abstract: A computer program has been designed and implemented to allow a researcher to analyze the oscillatory behavior of simulated neural networks with cyclic con(cid:173) nectivity. The computer program, implemented on the Texas Instruments Ex(cid:173) plorer / Odyssey system, and the results of numerous experiments are discussed. The program, CYCLES, allows a user to construct, operate, and inspect neural networks containing cyclic connection paths with the aid of a powerful graphics(cid:173) based interface. Numerous cycles have been studied, including cycles with one or more activation points, non-interruptible cycles, cycles with variable path lengths, and interacting cycles. The final class, interacting cycles, is important due to its ability to implement time-dependent goal processing in neural networks.

paragraphs: CYCLES is a simulation program for studying neural networks whose connections contain loops. Its focus is oscillatory behavior: activity that evolves through repeated circulation along cyclic paths. The program gives researchers a graphical interface for building networks, running them, and inspecting the behavior produced by their connectivity.

The authors implemented the tool on the Texas Instruments Explorer/Odyssey system and used it to investigate several kinds of cycles. These include cycles activated at one or more points, cycles that cannot be interrupted, cycles with different path lengths, and cycles that interact. The variety makes network timing and interaction explicit subjects of experimentation.

Interacting cycles receive particular attention because they can implement goal processing that depends on time. This connects the study of recurring neural activity with a computational purpose beyond simply observing oscillations. The paper's contribution combines a working research interface with experiments on cyclic structures, making it possible to construct and examine networks in which the timing of activity is part of the computation.
summary.tldr: CYCLES provides a graphical simulation environment for exploring oscillatory neural circuits and time-dependent goal processing.

title: Cycles: A Simulation Tool for Studying Cyclic Neural Networks

abstract: This work introduces a new method called Self Organizing Neural Network (SONN) algorithm and compares its performance with Back Propagation in a signal separation application. The problem is to separate two signals; a modem data signal and a male speech signal, added and transmitted through a 4 khz channel. The signals are sam(cid:173) pled at 8 khz, and using supervised learning, an attempt is made to reconstruct them. The SONN is an algorithm that constructs its own network topology during training, which is shown to be much smaller than the BP network, faster to trained, and free from the trial-and(cid:173) error network design that characterize BP.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a Self Organizing Neural Network algorithm, SONN, for separating a mixture of two signals. The specific task combines male speech with a modem data signal, transmits the sum through a 4 kHz channel, and samples it at 8 kHz. Supervised learning is used in an attempt to reconstruct the original signals.

The comparison is with a network trained by backpropagation. SONN's distinctive feature is that it constructs its network topology during training. Architecture selection therefore becomes part of the learning procedure, addressing the trial-and-error process associated with designing the backpropagation network used for comparison.

The authors report that SONN produces a much smaller network and trains faster. These findings concern the resources and design effort needed for the separation application. The contribution is a supervised approach that adapts its structure while learning, demonstrated on a mixture of speech and data. The reported advantages connect automatic topology construction to network compactness and training efficiency in that setting.
summary.tldr: SONN builds its own topology and yields a smaller, faster-training network for supervised speech-and-data signal separation.

title: The Cocktail Party Problem: Speech/Data Signal Separation Comparison between Backpropagation and SONN

abstract: Previous work (M.I. Sereno, 1989; cf. M.E. Sereno, 1987) showed that a feedforward network with area VI-like input-layer units and a Hebb rule can develop area MT-like second layer units that solve the aperture problem for pattern motion. The present study extends this earlier work to more complex motions. Saito et al. (1986) showed that neurons with large receptive fields in macaque visual area MST are sensitive to different senses of rotation and dilation, irrespective of the receptive field location of the movement singularity. A network with an MT-like second layer was trained and tested on combinations of rotating, dilating, and translating patterns. Third-layer units learn to detect specific senses of rotation or dilation in a position-independent fashion, despite having position-dependent direction selectivity within their receptive fields.

The present study extends this earlier work to more complex motions. Saito et al. (1986) showed that neurons with large receptive fields in macaque visual area MST are sensitive to different senses of rotation and dilation, irrespective of the receptive field location of the movement singularity. paragraphs: The study investigates how a layered neural network can learn to recognize rotation and dilation despite changes in where those motions are centered. It extends earlier work in which a Hebbian learning rule produced motion-processing units resembling those in visual area MT. The new task requires combining those motion signals into descriptions of more complex movement.

The network is trained and tested on combinations of rotating, dilating, and translating patterns. Its second layer is MT-like, while third-layer units learn to detect particular senses of rotation or dilation. The biological motivation comes from neurons in macaque visual area MST that respond to such motions across different locations of the movement singularity.

The reported result is position-independent detection in the third layer, even though direction preferences within each unit's receptive field remain position-dependent. This distinction matters: local responses can vary across space while their combination indicates the same overall motion. The study shows that this relationship between local selectivity and broader motion recognition can emerge through the stated learning approach.
summary.tldr: Hebbian learning produces units that recognize rotation or dilation across positions by combining locally position-dependent motion responses.

title: Learning to See Rotation and Dilation with a Hebb Rule

abstract: We propose a computational model for how the cortex discriminates shape and depth from texture. The model consists of four stages: (1) extraction of local spatial frequency, (2) frequency characterization, (3) detection of texture compression by normalization, and (4) integration of the normalized frequency over space. The model accounts for a number of psychophysical observations including experiments based on novel random textures. These textures are generated from white noise and manipulated in Fourier domain in order to produce specific frequency spectra. Simulations with a range of stimuli, including real images, show qualitative and quantitative agreement with human perception.

The model consists of four stages: (1) extraction of local spatial frequency, (2) frequency characterization, (3) detection of texture compression by normalization, and (4) integration of the normalized frequency over space. The model accounts for a number of psychophysical observations including experiments based on novel random textures. These textures are generated from white noise and manipulated in Fourier domain in order to produce specific frequency spectra. Simulations with a range of stimuli, including real images, show qualitative and quantitative agreement with human perception.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a model of how the cortex could infer surface shape and depth from texture. Its central idea is to examine how the spatial frequency of texture changes across an image. Spatial frequency describes how closely packed image variations are, giving the model a way to characterize texture locally before combining information across a surface.

The computation proceeds through four stages. First, the network extracts local spatial frequencies and characterizes them. It then uses normalization to detect texture compression, before integrating the normalized frequency information over space. This sequence connects small, local measurements to a larger interpretation of shape: the final estimate depends on how texture measurements fit together across the image.

The authors compare the model with human perception using several kinds of stimuli, including real images and specially constructed random textures. Those random textures begin as white noise and are manipulated to control their frequency spectra. The simulations show both qualitative and quantitative agreement with perception, supporting the proposed processing sequence as an account of the reported texture-based judgments.
summary.tldr: A four-stage network uses local texture frequencies to estimate shape and depth, producing results that agree with human perception.

title: A Network Mechanism for the Determination of Shape-From-Texture

abstract: Most current methods for prediction of protein secondary structure use a small window of the protein sequence to predict the structure of the central amino acid. We describe a new method for prediction of the non-local structure called ,8-sheet, which consists of two or more ,8-strands that are connected by hydrogen bonds. Since,8- strands are often widely separated in the protein chain, a network with two windows is introduced. After training on a set of proteins the network predicts the sheets well, but there are many false pos(cid:173) itives. By using a global energy function the ,8-sheet prediction is combined with a local prediction of the three secondary structures a-helix, ,8-strand and coil. The energy function is minimized using simulated annealing to give a final prediction.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a difficulty in predicting protein structure from amino-acid sequences: beta sheets connect strands that can be far apart along the chain. Methods that examine only a small neighborhood around each amino acid do not directly capture these distant relationships. The authors introduce a network with two sequence windows to predict sheet structure.

After training on proteins, the network predicts sheets well but also produces many false positives. This makes local acceptance of every predicted pairing problematic. The method therefore combines its sheet predictions with a separate local prediction of three secondary-structure types: alpha helix, beta strand, and coil.

A global energy function brings these predictions together, and simulated annealing searches for a final assignment with low energy. This lets the final prediction reflect both distant strand relationships and local structural evidence. The contribution is a coordinated treatment of protein structure: the two-window network supplies nonlocal information, while global optimization reconciles that information with predictions about individual sequence regions.
summary.tldr: A two-window network predicts distant beta-strand relationships, then global optimization combines them with local protein-structure predictions.

title: Prediction of Beta Sheets in Proteins

abstract: This paper discusses the use of multilayer feed forward neural net(cid:173) works for predicting a stock's excess return based on its exposure to various technical and fundamental factors. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach a hedged portfolio which consists of equally capitalized long and short positions is constructed and its historical returns are benchmarked against T-bill returns and the S&P500 index.

paragraphs: This paper uses multilayer feedforward neural networks to predict a stock's excess return from its exposure to technical and fundamental factors. The prediction problem combines several descriptions of a stock into one estimated return outcome. The nonlinear model provides a way to relate those factor exposures to the quantity used for stock selection.

The evaluation connects the forecasts to a portfolio. The authors construct a hedged portfolio with equal amounts of capital allocated to long and short positions. This turns the modeling approach into a concrete investment arrangement whose historical returns can be examined, rather than assessing the prediction model only in isolation.

The portfolio's historical returns are compared with Treasury-bill returns and the S&P 500 index. These comparisons frame the demonstration around investment outcomes from the proposed approach. The abstract describes this evaluation as demonstrating effectiveness but supplies no numerical return comparison. Its stated contribution is the combination of nonlinear factor-based prediction, a balanced long–short portfolio, and historical benchmarking.
summary.tldr: Neural networks predict stock excess returns from multiple factors, with the approach evaluated through a hedged portfolio's historical returns.

title: Stock Selection via Nonlinear Multi-Factor Models

abstract: A self-organizing architecture is developed for image region classi(cid:173) fication. The system consists of a preprocessor that utilizes multi(cid:173) scale filtering, competition, cooperation, and diffusion to compute a vector of image boundary and surface properties, notably texture and brightness properties. This vector inputs to a system that incrementally learns noisy multidimensional mappings and their probabilities. The architecture is applied to difficult real-world image classification problems, including classification of synthet(cid:173) ic aperture radar and natural texture images, and outperforms a recent state-of-the-art system at classifying natural textures.

This vector inputs to a system that incrementally learns noisy multidimensional mappings and their probabilities. paragraphs: ARTEX is a self-organizing system for classifying image regions from their visual properties. Its architecture connects an image-processing stage with an incremental learning stage. This arrangement addresses both how to describe a region and how to learn useful classifications from descriptions that can be multidimensional and noisy.

The preprocessor combines filtering at multiple scales with competition, cooperation, and diffusion. These operations produce a vector describing boundaries and surfaces, especially texture and brightness. The resulting vector becomes the input to a system that incrementally learns mappings and their probabilities. Thus, the classifier works with a structured description of regional appearance and associates that description with learned probabilistic relationships.

The authors apply the architecture to synthetic aperture radar imagery and natural texture images, presenting both as difficult real-world classification problems. On natural textures, ARTEX outperforms a recent state-of-the-art system. That comparison supports the usefulness of combining the proposed visual preprocessing with incremental probabilistic learning for the tested texture-classification task. The radar application additionally demonstrates use with another type of image data.
summary.tldr: ARTEX combines multiscale image descriptions with incremental probabilistic learning and outperforms a contemporary system on natural-texture classification.

title: ARTEX: A Self-organizing Architecture for Classifying Image Regions

paragraphs: Optimal stopping asks when to stop a stochastic process rather than continue observing its evolution. This paper proposes an approximate solution for a discounted Markov-chain setting. The chain is assumed to be irreducible and aperiodic, conditions that restrict its long-run transition behavior and form part of the theoretical setting.

The algorithm represents a Q-function as a weighted combination of fixed basis functions. It updates those weights incrementally using simulated transitions from the underlying chain, following an iterative procedure similar to Q-learning. This representation lets the method express decision values through shared functions instead of requiring an independently adjustable value for every possible situation.

The paper outlines a proof of convergence with probability one and gives approximation-error bounds. These results establish theoretical support for combining a Q-learning-like update with arbitrary linear function approximators in this stopping problem. The treatment focuses on finite state spaces; the abstract states that continuous and unbounded extensions belong to a fuller treatment. The guarantee is therefore tied to the specified sequential decision setting.
summary.tldr: A Q-learning-like algorithm approximates optimal stopping values with fixed basis functions and comes with convergence and approximation-error results.

title: Approximate Solutions to Optimal Stopping Problems

paragraphs: The paper examines how people's causal judgments develop during learning. Its motivation is that existing psychological theories primarily emphasize long-run predictions. Explaining judgments after learning has progressed is a different task from explaining the short-run behavior that occurs as a person is still learning about causal relationships.

The authors consider three theories of causal learning and judgment. Two describe learning through the estimation of parameters in causal Bayesian networks, using different parameterizations. The third describes learning through changes in structure. These alternatives distinguish learning about the numerical properties of a causal model from learning about the organization of the model itself.

The paper develops dynamical versions of these theories and compares their predictions with a real-world dataset. The contribution is to bring their accounts of the learning process into direct comparison, rather than considering only their long-run predictions. This makes the evolution of causal judgments the object of explanation and provides a way to examine how different theories describe short-run human behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper compares dynamical versions of three causal-learning theories to study people's short-run judgments.

title: Dynamical Causal Learning

abstract: In the analysis of natural images, Gaussian scale mixtures (GSM) have been used to account for the statistics of filter responses, and to inspire hierarchical cortical representational learning schemes. GSMs pose a critical assignment problem, working out which filter responses were generated by a common multiplicative factor. We present a new approach to solving this assignment problem through a probabilistic extension to the basic GSM, and show how to perform inference in the model using Gibbs sampling. We demonstrate the efficacy of the approach on both synthetic and image data.
originalAbstract: In the analysis of natural images, Gaussian scale mixtures (GSM) have been used to account for the statistics of filter responses, and to inspire hierarchical cortical representational learning schemes. GSMs pose a critical assignment problem, working out which filter responses were generated by a common multiplicative factor. We present a new approach to solving this assignment problem through a probabilistic extension to the basic GSM, and show how to perform inference in the model using Gibbs sampling. We demonstrate the efficacy of the approach on both synthetic and image data.

paragraphs: The paper studies a grouping problem that arises when modeling natural images with Gaussian scale mixtures. These models describe image filter responses using multiplicative factors and have also motivated hierarchical accounts of cortical representation learning. Their usefulness depends on an important assignment question: which responses should be treated as sharing the same factor?

Sharing a multiplicative factor means that a collection of responses is explained partly through a common influence on their scale. Determining that collection is therefore part of understanding the structure of the image responses. The authors extend the basic Gaussian scale mixture probabilistically so that this assignment problem can be addressed within the model.

They then show how to carry out inference using Gibbs sampling, providing a computational procedure for working with the extension. Demonstrations on synthetic data and image data support the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to infer the grouping associated with multiplicative influences, adding an explicit assignment mechanism to an existing model of image statistics.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic extension of Gaussian scale mixtures infers which image filter responses share a multiplicative factor.

title: Assignment of Multiplicative Mixtures in Natural Images

abstract: We prove the strongest known bound for the risk of hypotheses selected from the ensemble generated by running a learning algorithm incremen(cid:173) tally on the training data. Our result is based on proof techniques that are remarkably different from the standard risk analysis based on uniform convergence arguments.
originalAbstract: We prove the strongest known bound for the risk of hypotheses selected from the ensemble generated by running a learning algorithm incremen(cid:173) tally on the training data. Our result is based on proof techniques that are remarkably different from the standard risk analysis based on uniform convergence arguments.

paragraphs: An incremental learning algorithm produces a sequence of candidate predictors as it works through training data. This paper studies the risk of hypotheses selected from that resulting collection. The question concerns the predictive quality of a selected hypothesis, making the sequence generated during learning the central object of the analysis.

The contribution is a theoretical risk bound, described by the authors as the strongest known for this selection setting. As the title indicates, the focus is on risk tail bounds: guarantees concerning the possibility of larger prediction risk. The result therefore addresses how much assurance can be attached to a predictor selected from the online learning process.

The authors emphasize that their proof uses techniques substantially different from standard analyses based on uniform convergence. Uniform convergence arguments seek control across a collection of candidate hypotheses; this paper establishes its stated bound through another proof approach. Its significance lies in strengthening the guarantee available for selected online hypotheses and broadening the analytical methods used to obtain such guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a stronger risk guarantee for hypotheses selected from an incremental learner's outputs using a different proof approach.

title: Improved risk tail bounds for on-line algorithms

abstract: We present a novel approach to the characterization of complex sensory neurons. One of the main goals of characterizing sensory neurons is to characterize dimensions in stimulus space to which the neurons are highly sensitive (causing large gradients in the neural responses) or al- ternatively dimensions in stimulus space to which the neuronal response are invariant (deﬁning iso-response manifolds). We formulate this prob- lem as that of learning a geometry on stimulus space that is compatible with the neural responses: the distance between stimuli should be large when the responses they evoke are very different, and small when the re- sponses they evoke are similar. Here we show how to successfully train such distance functions using rather limited amount of information. The data consisted of the responses of neurons in primary auditory cortex (A1) of anesthetized cats to 32 stimuli derived from natural sounds. For each neuron, a subset of all pairs of stimuli was selected such that the responses of the two stimuli in a pair were either very similar or very dissimilar. The distance function was trained to ﬁt these constraints. The resulting distance functions generalized to predict the distances between the responses of a test stimulus and the trained stimuli.

We formulate this prob- lem as that of learning a geometry on stimulus space that is compatible with the neural responses: the distance between stimuli should be large when the responses they evoke are very different, and small when the re- sponses they evoke are similar. paragraphs: The paper characterizes sensory neurons by learning which differences between sounds matter to their responses. Some changes in a stimulus produce large response changes, while others leave the response nearly unchanged. Rather than treating all stimulus differences alike, the authors learn a distance function shaped by a particular neuron's behavior.

The training principle is direct: sounds that evoke similar responses should be close together, and sounds that evoke very different responses should be far apart. The data comprise responses from primary auditory cortex neurons in anesthetized cats to 32 stimuli derived from natural sounds. For each neuron, training uses selected stimulus pairs with either very similar or very dissimilar responses.

The learned distances generalize to comparisons between a test stimulus and the training stimuli. This shows that the selected pairwise constraints contain information beyond the examples used to fit them. The resulting geometry offers a way to describe neural sensitivity and invariance using limited response information, with the reported demonstration tied to this auditory recording setting.
summary.tldr: Learning distances from selected sound pairs reveals response-relevant stimulus differences and generalizes to test stimuli in auditory neuron recordings.

title: Analyzing Auditory Neurons by Learning Distance Functions

abstract: Integrating semantic and syntactic analysis is essential for document analysis. Using an analogous reasoning, we present an approach that combines bag-of-words and spatial models to perform semantic and syntactic analysis for recognition of an object based on its internal appearance and its context. We argue that while object recognition requires modeling relative spatial locations of image features within the object, a bag-of-word is sufficient for representing context. Learning such a model from weakly labeled data involves labeling of features into two classes: foreground(object) or ''informative'' background(context). labeling. We present a ''shape-aware'' model which utilizes contour information for efficient and accurate labeling of features in the image. Our approach iterates between an MCMC-based labeling and contour based labeling of features to integrate co-occurrence of features and shape similarity.
originalAbstract: Integrating semantic and syntactic analysis is essential for document analysis. Using an analogous reasoning, we present an approach that combines bag-of-words and spatial models to perform semantic and syntactic analysis for recognition of an object based on its internal appearance and its context. We argue that while object recognition requires modeling relative spatial locations of image features within the object, a bag-of-word is sufficient for representing context. Learning such a model from weakly labeled data involves labeling of features into two classes: foreground(object) or ''informative'' background(context). labeling. We present a ''shape-aware'' model which utilizes contour information for efficient and accurate labeling of features in the image. Our approach iterates between an MCMC-based labeling and contour based labeling of features to integrate co-occurrence of features and shape similarity.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object involves both its own appearance and clues from its surroundings. This paper proposes representing those two sources of information differently. Within the object, the relative positions of image features matter. For the surrounding context, the authors argue that a bag-of-words representation, which records feature occurrences without their spatial arrangement, is sufficient.

Learning this combined representation from weak labels requires deciding which features belong to the object and which belong to informative background. The proposed model uses contour information to help make that assignment. Shape therefore contributes directly to how the training image is interpreted, rather than serving only as another appearance cue after the foreground has already been identified.

The learning procedure alternates between feature labeling based on Markov chain Monte Carlo and labeling based on contours. These steps bring together evidence about which features occur together and how their shapes agree. The stated contribution is an efficient, accurate way to distinguish object features from contextual features while learning a recognition model that uses both.
summary.tldr: A shape-aware recognition model alternates probabilistic and contour-based labeling to learn objects and informative context from weak labels.

title: A ``Shape Aware'' Model for semi-supervised Learning of Objects and its Context

abstract: Working memory is a central topic of cognitive neuroscience because it is critical for solving real world problems in which information from multiple temporally distant sources must be combined to generate appropriate behavior. However, an often neglected fact is that learning to use working memory effectively is itself a difficult problem. The Gating" framework is a collection of psychological models that show how dopamine can train the basal ganglia and prefrontal cortex to form useful working memory representations in certain types of problems. We bring together gating with ideas from machine learning about using finite memory systems in more general problems. Thus we present a normative Gating model that learns, by online temporal difference methods, to use working memory to maximize discounted future rewards in general partially observable settings. The model successfully solves a benchmark working memory problem, and exhibits limitations similar to those observed in human experiments. Moreover, the model introduces a concise, normative definition of high level cognitive concepts such as working memory and cognitive control in terms of maximizing discounted future rewards."

paragraphs: Working memory helps combine information encountered at different times, but learning what to retain and how to use it is itself a difficult problem. This paper connects psychological gating models with machine learning ideas about finite memory. Gating models describe how dopamine can train the basal ganglia and prefrontal cortex to form useful memory representations.

The authors develop a normative model: memory use is evaluated according to an explicit objective, maximizing discounted future rewards. Online temporal-difference learning trains the model to use working memory in general partially observable settings, where currently available information does not fully describe the situation. This broadens the connection between gating and reward-based learning beyond the problem types addressed by earlier gating models.

The model solves a benchmark working-memory problem and displays limitations resembling those observed in human experiments. These results connect successful task performance with some human-like constraints. The formulation also defines working memory and cognitive control in terms of their contribution to future reward, providing a concise computational interpretation of these higher-level cognitive concepts.
summary.tldr: A reward-driven gating model learns to use working memory under partial observability and exhibits limitations resembling those seen in human experiments.

title: Learning to Use Working Memory in Partially Observable Environments through Dopaminergic Reinforcement

abstract: Gaussian graphical models with sparsity in the inverse covariance matrix are of significant interest in many modern applications. For the problem of recovering the graphical structure, information criteria provide useful optimization objectives for algorithms searching through sets of graphs or for selection of tuning parameters of other methods such as the graphical lasso, which is a likelihood penalization technique. In this paper we establish the asymptotic consistency of an extended Bayesian information criterion for Gaussian graphical models in a scenario where both the number of variables p and the sample size n grow. Compared to earlier work on the regression case, our treatment allows for growth in the number of non-zero parameters in the true model, which is necessary in order to cover connected graphs. We demonstrate the performance of this criterion on simulated data when used in conjuction with the graphical lasso, and verify that the criterion indeed performs better than either cross-validation or the ordinary Bayesian information criterion when p and the number of non-zero parameters q both scale with n.

For the problem of recovering the graphical structure, information criteria provide useful optimization objectives for algorithms searching through sets of graphs or for selection of tuning parameters of other methods such as the graphical lasso, which is a likelihood penalization technique. In this paper we establish the asymptotic consistency of an extended Bayesian information criterion for Gaussian graphical models in a scenario where both the number of variables p and the sample size n grow. Compared to earlier work on the regression case, our treatment allows for growth in the number of non-zero parameters in the true model, which is necessary in order to cover connected graphs. We demonstrate the performance of this criterion on simulated data when used in conjuction with the graphical lasso, and verify that the criterion indeed performs better than either cross-validation or the ordinary Bayesian information criterion when p and the number of non-zero parameters q both scale with n.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models describe relationships through the structure of an inverse covariance matrix. Recovering a sparse graph requires choosing which connections to retain. This paper studies an extended Bayesian information criterion as a selection objective, usable either when searching across graphs or when choosing a tuning parameter for methods such as the graphical lasso.

The authors establish asymptotic consistency in a setting where both the number of variables and the sample size increase. Their treatment also permits the number of nonzero parameters in the true model to grow. That allowance matters because connected graphs require increasing numbers of connections as their number of variables grows.

In simulations, the criterion is combined with the graphical lasso and compared with cross-validation and ordinary Bayesian information criterion. It performs better in the studied setting where both the variable count and the number of nonzero parameters scale with sample size. The theoretical and empirical contributions therefore address model selection when the underlying graph can become larger and more complex as more data arrive.
summary.tldr: An extended Bayesian information criterion has consistency guarantees and favorable simulation results for Gaussian graph selection as model size grows.

title: Extended Bayesian Information Criteria for Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: Bayesian approaches to preference elicitation (PE) are particularly attractive due to their ability to explicitly model uncertainty in users' latent utility functions. However, previous approaches to Bayesian PE have ignored the important problem of generalizing from previous users to an unseen user in order to reduce the elicitation burden on new users. In this paper, we address this deficiency by introducing a Gaussian Process (GP) prior over users' latent utility functions on the joint space of user and item features. We learn the hyper-parameters of this GP on a set of preferences of previous users and use it to aid in the elicitation process for a new user. This approach provides a flexible model of a multi-user utility function, facilitates an efficient value of information (VOI) heuristic query selection strategy, and provides a principled way to incorporate the elicitations of multiple users back into the model. We show the effectiveness of our method in comparison to previous work on a real dataset of user preferences over sushi types.

paragraphs: Preference elicitation learns what a user values by asking questions about their preferences. Bayesian approaches represent uncertainty about the user’s hidden utility function. This paper addresses how preferences collected from earlier users can help with a new user, with the aim of reducing the amount of questioning that newcomer needs.

The authors place a Gaussian process prior over utility functions defined jointly through user and item features. They learn its hyperparameters from previous users’ preferences and use the resulting model during elicitation for a new user. This gives a flexible shared utility model that can carry information across users while retaining uncertainty about their preferences.

The approach supports an efficient value-of-information heuristic for choosing questions and a principled way to feed newly elicited preferences back into the shared model. Comparisons with previous work on a real dataset of sushi preferences demonstrate its effectiveness. The result supports combining knowledge transfer and query selection within a single probabilistic preference model, rather than treating each new elicitation session independently.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process preference model transfers information from previous users and supports value-of-information query selection for new users.

title: Gaussian Process Preference Elicitation

abstract: Games of incomplete information, or Bayesian games, are an important game-theoretic model and have many applications in economics. We propose Bayesian action-graph games (BAGGs), a novel graphical representation for Bayesian games. BAGGs can represent arbitrary Bayesian games, and furthermore can compactly express Bayesian games exhibiting commonly encountered types of structure including symmetry, action- and type-specific utility independence, and probabilistic independence of type distributions. We provide an algorithm for computing expected utility in BAGGs, and discuss conditions under which the algorithm runs in polynomial time. Bayes-Nash equilibria of BAGGs can be computed by adapting existing algorithms for complete-information normal form games and leveraging our expected utility algorithm. We show both theoretically and empirically that our approaches improve significantly on the state of the art.

paragraphs: Bayesian games model strategic situations in which players do not have complete information. The paper introduces Bayesian action-graph games, or BAGGs, as a graphical representation for these problems. The representation can express arbitrary Bayesian games, while offering compact descriptions when a game contains useful structure.

The structures it can exploit include symmetry, independence in how actions or player types affect utilities, and probabilistic independence among type distributions. These properties matter because they can reduce how much information must be represented and processed. The authors provide an algorithm for computing expected utility and identify conditions under which its running time is polynomial.

Expected-utility computation also supports finding Bayes-Nash equilibria. The paper explains how existing algorithms for complete-information normal-form games can be adapted using the new utility algorithm. Theoretical and empirical results show significant improvements over prior approaches. The key distinction is between broad representational coverage and conditional computational efficiency: BAGGs can represent any Bayesian game, but compactness and polynomial-time utility computation depend on exploitable structure and the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: Bayesian action-graph games exploit structure in incomplete-information games to improve representation, expected-utility computation, and equilibrium calculations.

title: Bayesian Action-Graph Games

abstract: We introduce hierarchically supervised latent Dirichlet allocation (HSLDA), a model for hierarchically and multiply labeled bag-of-word data. Examples of such data include web pages and their placement in directories, product descriptions and associated categories from product hierarchies, and free-text clinical records and their assigned diagnosis codes. Out-of-sample label prediction is the primary goal of this work, but improved lower-dimensional representations of the bag-of-word data are also of interest. We demonstrate HSLDA on large-scale data from clinical document labeling and retail product categorization tasks. We show that leveraging the structure from hierarchical labels improves out-of-sample label prediction substantially when compared to models that do not.

We demonstrate HSLDA on large-scale data from clinical document labeling and retail product categorization tasks. We show that leveraging the structure from hierarchical labels improves out-of-sample label prediction substantially when compared to models that do not.

paragraphs: Many text collections attach multiple labels to a document, and those labels often belong to a hierarchy. Product categories and diagnosis codes are examples: their organization contains information beyond the individual labels. This paper introduces hierarchically supervised latent Dirichlet allocation, or HSLDA, for bag-of-word data with both hierarchical and multiple labels.

The primary goal is to predict labels for previously unseen documents. A second interest is obtaining improved lower-dimensional representations of the text. The model brings the structure of the labels into this learning problem, allowing the organization of categories to inform the relationship between a document’s words and its assigned labels.

The authors demonstrate HSLDA on large-scale clinical document labeling and retail product categorization tasks. In those evaluations, using the hierarchical label structure substantially improves prediction on unseen examples compared with models that do not use it. The findings support treating a label hierarchy as useful supervision, with value for prediction beyond simply knowing which labels appear on each training document.
summary.tldr: HSLDA uses hierarchical, multiple labels to improve prediction for unseen text documents in clinical and retail evaluations.

title: Hierarchically Supervised Latent Dirichlet Allocation

abstract: Unsupervised clustering of scattered, noisy and high-dimensional data points is an important and difficult problem. Continuous relaxations of balanced cut problems yield excellent clustering results. This paper provides rigorous convergence results for two algorithms that solve the relaxed Cheeger Cut minimization. The first algorithm is a new steepest descent algorithm and the second one is a slight modification of the Inverse Power Method algorithm \cite{pro:HeinBuhler10OneSpec}. While the steepest descent algorithm has better theoretical convergence properties, in practice both algorithm perform equally. We also completely characterize the local minima of the relaxed problem in terms of the original balanced cut problem, and relate this characterization to the convergence of the algorithms.

paragraphs: Clustering noisy, scattered, high-dimensional data can be formulated through balanced cut problems. Continuous relaxations make these problems accessible to numerical optimization and can produce strong clustering results. This paper examines the relaxed Cheeger Cut objective, focusing on whether algorithms converge and what the local minima of that objective represent.

The authors provide rigorous convergence results for two algorithms: a new steepest descent method and a slightly modified Inverse Power Method. The steepest descent method has stronger theoretical convergence properties. In practice, however, the two methods perform equally, separating the strength of a mathematical guarantee from the observed performance of an implementation.

The paper also fully characterizes the relaxed problem’s local minima in terms of the original balanced cut problem. This connects the continuous objective back to the discrete clustering task that motivated it. Relating that characterization to algorithm convergence helps explain both where optimization can settle and how those destinations correspond to the underlying partitioning problem.
summary.tldr: The paper proves convergence results for two Cheeger Cut algorithms and characterizes how relaxed local minima relate to balanced cuts.

title: Convergence and Energy Landscape for Cheeger Cut Clustering

abstract: We uncover relations between robust MDPs and risk-sensitive MDPs. The objective of a robust MDP is to minimize a function, such as the expectation of cumulative cost, for the worst case when the parameters have uncertainties. The objective of a risk-sensitive MDP is to minimize a risk measure of the cumulative cost when the parameters are known. We show that a risk-sensitive MDP of minimizing the expected exponential utility is equivalent to a robust MDP of minimizing the worst-case expectation with a penalty for the deviation of the uncertain parameters from their nominal values, which is measured with the Kullback-Leibler divergence. We also show that a risk-sensitive MDP of minimizing an iterated risk measure that is composed of certain coherent risk measures is equivalent to a robust MDP of minimizing the worst-case expectation when the possible deviations of uncertain parameters from their nominal values are characterized with a concave function.

The objective of a robust MDP is to minimize a function, such as the expectation of cumulative cost, for the worst case when the parameters have uncertainties. The objective of a risk-sensitive MDP is to minimize a risk measure of the cumulative cost when the parameters are known. We show that a risk-sensitive MDP of minimizing the expected exponential utility is equivalent to a robust MDP of minimizing the worst-case expectation with a penalty for the deviation of the uncertain parameters from their nominal values, which is measured with the Kullback-Leibler divergence. We also show that a risk-sensitive MDP of minimizing an iterated risk measure that is composed of certain coherent risk measures is equivalent to a robust MDP of minimizing the worst-case expectation when the possible deviations of uncertain parameters from their nominal values are characterized with a concave function.

paragraphs: The paper connects two approaches to decision-making over time. A robust Markov decision process evaluates decisions against unfavorable choices of uncertain model parameters. A risk-sensitive Markov decision process instead assumes known parameters and evaluates cumulative cost through a risk measure. The authors identify settings in which these seemingly different objectives are mathematically equivalent.

The first equivalence concerns minimizing expected exponential utility. This risk-sensitive objective corresponds to minimizing worst-case expected cost while penalizing deviations from nominal parameters. The penalty is measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence. Thus, in this formulation, sensitivity to risk can also be interpreted as protection against model changes whose departures from the nominal model carry a cost.

The second equivalence concerns iterated risk measures constructed from certain coherent risk measures. These correspond to robust objectives whose permitted parameter deviations are described through a concave function. Together, the results give precise connections between attitudes toward uncertain outcomes and uncertainty about model parameters. Their scope depends on the specified utility, risk measures, and descriptions of parameter deviations.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes equivalences between specified risk-sensitive MDP objectives and robust MDPs with corresponding penalties or constraints on parameter deviations.

title: Robustness and risk-sensitivity in Markov decision processes

abstract: Applying linear templates is an integral part of many object detection systems and accounts for a significant portion of computation time. We describe a method that achieves a substantial end-to-end speedup over the best current methods, without loss of accuracy. Our method is a combination of approximating scores by vector quantizing feature windows and a number of speedup techniques including cascade. Our procedure allows speed and accuracy to be traded off in two ways: by choosing the number of Vector Quantization levels, and by choosing to rescore windows or not. Our method can be directly plugged into any recognition system that relies on linear templates. We demonstrate our method to speed up the original Exemplar SVM detector [1] by an order of magnitude and Deformable Part models [2] by two orders of magnitude with no loss of accuracy.

This paper targets that operation directly, aiming to accelerate the full recognition system rather than only an isolated calculation. The proposed method approximates template scores by vector-quantizing feature windows and combines this with additional acceleration techniques, including a cascade.

The procedure exposes two ways to balance speed and accuracy. One is choosing the number of vector-quantization levels, which controls the representation used for approximate scoring. The other is deciding whether to rescore windows. These choices allow the same basic method to support different computational and accuracy requirements.

The authors state that the method can be plugged into recognition systems using linear templates. Their demonstrations speed up the original Exemplar SVM detector by one order of magnitude and Deformable Part models by two, without accuracy loss in those evaluations. The reported findings show that approximate intermediate scoring can deliver substantial end-to-end acceleration while preserving final detection accuracy.
summary.tldr: Vector-quantized template scoring substantially accelerates two object detectors without accuracy loss in the reported evaluations.

title: Fast Template Evaluation with Vector Quantization

abstract: In this paper, we present a new approach for lifted MAP inference in Markov logic networks (MLNs). The key idea in our approach is to compactly encode the MAP inference problem as an Integer Polynomial Program (IPP) by schematically applying three lifted inference steps to the MLN: lifted decomposition, lifted conditioning, and partial grounding. Our IPP encoding is lifted in the sense that an integer assignment to a variable in the IPP may represent a truth-assignment to multiple indistinguishable ground atoms in the MLN. We show how to solve the IPP by first converting it to an Integer Linear Program (ILP) and then solving the latter using state-of-the-art ILP techniques. Experiments on several benchmark MLNs show that our new algorithm is substantially superior to ground inference and existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and solution quality.

Our IPP encoding is lifted in the sense that an integer assignment to a variable in the IPP may represent a truth-assignment to multiple indistinguishable ground atoms in the MLN. We show how to solve the IPP by first converting it to an Integer Linear Program (ILP) and then solving the latter using state-of-the-art ILP techniques. paragraphs: The paper tackles maximum a posteriori inference in Markov logic networks: finding a most probable assignment of truth values under the model. Its approach uses a compact optimization representation that can group indistinguishable ground atoms. This grouping matters because a single optimization variable can then describe assignments involving multiple atoms.

The authors construct an integer polynomial program by systematically combining lifted decomposition, lifted conditioning, and partial grounding. The resulting representation remains lifted because an integer value can stand for a truth assignment to a collection of indistinguishable atoms. They then convert the polynomial program into an integer linear program, allowing established integer linear programming techniques to solve the encoded inference problem.

Experiments on several benchmark Markov logic networks report substantial improvements in both computational efficiency and solution quality over ground inference and existing methods. These findings support the usefulness of combining compact logical representations with integer optimization. The contribution is both an encoding framework and a practical route from that encoding to available solution techniques.
summary.tldr: The paper converts lifted MAP inference into compact integer optimization problems, improving efficiency and solution quality on benchmark Markov logic networks.

title: An Integer Polynomial Programming Based Framework for Lifted MAP Inference

abstract: We consider the problem of subspace clustering: given points that lie on or near the union of many low-dimensional linear subspaces, recover the subspaces. To this end, one first identifies sets of points close to the same subspace and uses the sets to estimate the subspaces. As the geometric structure of the clusters (linear subspaces) forbids proper performance of general distance based approaches such as K-means, many model-specific methods have been proposed. In this paper, we provide new simple and efficient algorithms for this problem. Our statistical analysis shows that the algorithms are guaranteed exact (perfect) clustering performance under certain conditions on the number of points and the affinity be- tween subspaces. These conditions are weaker than those considered in the standard statistical literature. Experimental results on synthetic data generated from the standard unions of subspaces model demonstrate our theory. We also show that our algorithm performs competitively against state-of-the-art algorithms on real-world applications such as motion segmentation and face clustering, with much simpler implementation and lower computational cost.

The goal is to identify points belonging to the same subspace and then estimate those subspaces. This geometry calls for methods tailored to linear structure: ordinary distance-based clustering, such as K-means, does not adequately address the structure described in the paper.

The authors propose simple, efficient algorithms and analyze when they recover the clusters exactly. Their guarantees depend on the number of available points and the affinity between subspaces, which captures how closely the subspaces align. The required conditions are weaker than those used in the standard statistical literature considered by the authors.

Synthetic experiments generated from a union-of-subspaces model support the theoretical analysis. On motion segmentation and face clustering, the method performs competitively with leading alternatives while offering simpler implementation and lower computational cost. The paper therefore combines conditional exact-recovery guarantees with practical evidence of efficiency. Perfect clustering is the theoretical conclusion under the stated conditions, while the real-data finding is competitive performance.
summary.tldr: Simple subspace-clustering algorithms offer conditional exact-recovery guarantees and competitive real-data performance at lower computational cost.

title: Greedy Subspace Clustering

abstract: Linear regression studies the problem of estimating a model parameter $\beta^* \in \R^p$, from $n$ observations $\{(y_i,x_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ from linear model $y_i = \langle \x_i,\beta^* \rangle + \epsilon_i$. We consider a significant generalization in which the relationship between $\langle x_i,\beta^* \rangle$ and $y_i$ is noisy, quantized to a single bit, potentially nonlinear, noninvertible, as well as unknown. This model is known as the single-index model in statistics, and, among other things, it represents a significant generalization of one-bit compressed sensing. We propose a novel spectral-based estimation procedure and show that we can recover $\beta^*$ in settings (i.e., classes of link function $f$) where previous algorithms fail. In general, our algorithm requires only very mild restrictions on the (unknown) functional relationship between $y_i$ and $\langle x_i,\beta^* \rangle$. We also consider the high dimensional setting where $\beta^*$ is sparse, and introduce a two-stage nonconvex framework that addresses estimation challenges in high dimensional regimes where $p \gg n$. For a broad class of link functions between $\langle x_i,\beta^* \rangle$ and $y_i$, we establish minimax lower bounds that demonstrate the optimality of our estimators in both the classical and high dimensional regimes.

That transformation may be noisy, nonlinear, noninvertible, or reduced to a single bit. The significance is that unknown nonlinear observation mechanisms need not prevent optimal estimation within the analyzed classes, including settings where sparsity is used to address limited observations.
summary.tldr: Spectral and two-stage nonconvex estimators recover linear parameters through broad classes of unknown nonlinear observation functions with optimality guarantees.

title: Optimal Linear Estimation under Unknown Nonlinear Transform

abstract: The robust principal component analysis (RPCA) problem seeks to separate low-rank trends from sparse outlierswithin a data matrix, that is, to approximate a $n\times d$ matrix $D$ as the sum of a low-rank matrix $L$ and a sparse matrix $S$.We examine the robust principal component analysis (RPCA) problem under data compression, wherethe data $Y$ is approximately given by $(L + S)\cdot C$, that is, a low-rank $+$ sparse data matrix that has been compressed to size $n\times m$ (with $m$ substantially smaller than the original dimension $d$) via multiplication witha compression matrix $C$. We give a convex program for recovering the sparse component $S$ along with the compressed low-rank component $L\cdot C$, along with upper bounds on the error of this reconstructionthat scales naturally with the compression dimension $m$ and coincides with existing results for the uncompressedsetting $m=d$. Our results can also handle error introduced through additive noise or through missing data.The scaling of dimension, compression, and signal complexity in our theoretical results is verified empirically through simulations, and we also apply our method to a data set measuring chlorine concentration acrossa network of sensors, to test its performance in practice.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis separates a data matrix into low-rank trends and sparse outliers. This paper studies the problem when only a compressed version of their sum is available. Compression reduces the original number of columns substantially, making the recovery task different from decomposing the full data matrix directly.

The authors propose a convex program that recovers the sparse component together with the compressed low-rank component. This distinction matters: the stated target includes the original sparse matrix, but only the compressed representation of the low-rank matrix. They derive upper bounds on reconstruction error that depend naturally on the compression dimension and agree with existing results when compression is absent.

The analysis also accommodates errors from additive noise or missing data. Simulations verify the predicted relationships among dimension, compression, and signal complexity. An application to chlorine measurements from a sensor network tests the method in practice. The contribution combines a recovery procedure with quantitative guarantees for separating structured trends and sparse contamination from compressed observations.
summary.tldr: A convex method recovers sparse outliers and compressed low-rank structure from compressed data, with reconstruction-error bounds.

title: Robust PCA with compressed data

abstract: The use of Bayesian methods in large-scale data settings is attractive because of the rich hierarchical models, uncertainty quantification, and prior specification they provide. Standard Bayesian inference algorithms are computationally expensive, however, making their direct application to large datasets difficult or infeasible. Recent work on scaling Bayesian inference has focused on modifying the underlying algorithms to, for example, use only a random data subsample at each iteration. We leverage the insight that data is often redundant to instead obtain a weighted subset of the data (called a coreset) that is much smaller than the original dataset. We can then use this small coreset in any number of existing posterior inference algorithms without modification. In this paper, we develop an efficient coreset construction algorithm for Bayesian logistic regression models. We provide theoretical guarantees on the size and approximation quality of the coreset -- both for fixed, known datasets, and in expectation for a wide class of data generative models. Crucially, the proposed approach also permits efficient construction of the coreset in both streaming and parallel settings, with minimal additional effort. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a number of synthetic and real-world datasets, and find that, in practice, the size of the coreset is independent of the original dataset size. Furthermore, constructing the coreset takes a negligible amount of time compared to that required to run MCMC on it.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference offers uncertainty estimates and a way to incorporate prior information, but processing a large dataset can be expensive. This paper reduces that burden for Bayesian logistic regression by constructing a coreset: a small, weighted subset intended to approximate the contribution of the full dataset. The approach exploits redundancy in the observations.

Once constructed, the coreset can be used with existing posterior inference algorithms without modifying those algorithms. The authors provide guarantees for its size and approximation quality, both for a fixed known dataset and in expectation under a broad class of data-generating models. Construction also supports streaming and parallel processing with little additional effort.

In the reported practice, coreset size is independent of the original dataset size, and construction takes negligible time compared with running MCMC on the coreset. These empirical findings support compressing the data before inference as a practical route to scaling Bayesian logistic regression.
summary.tldr: Small weighted subsets make Bayesian logistic regression more scalable while supporting existing inference algorithms and theoretical approximation guarantees.

title: Coresets for Scalable Bayesian Logistic Regression

abstract: The input-output mappings learned by state-of-the-art neural networks are significantly discontinuous. It is possible to cause a neural network used for image recognition to misclassify its input by applying very specific, hardly perceptible perturbations to the input, called adversarial perturbations. Many hypotheses have been proposed to explain the existence of these peculiar samples as well as several methods to mitigate them. A proven explanation remains elusive, however. In this work, we take steps towards a formal characterization of adversarial perturbations by deriving lower bounds on the magnitudes of perturbations necessary to change the classification of neural networks. The bounds are experimentally verified on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 data sets.

paragraphs: Neural image classifiers can change their predictions after carefully chosen changes to an input that are barely perceptible. Such adversarial perturbations raise a quantitative question: how much must the input change before a classification change becomes possible? This paper approaches that question through mathematical lower bounds on the required perturbation magnitude.

A lower bound identifies a threshold below which a perturbation cannot be large enough to change the classification covered by the bound. It does not, by itself, say that every larger change will cause an error or that a successful perturbation exists exactly at the threshold. This distinction makes the result a statement about guaranteed minimum size rather than a recipe for constructing attacks.

The authors derive these bounds for neural networks and experimentally verify them on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The work contributes to a formal characterization of adversarial behavior, an area where the abstract describes a proven explanation as still elusive. Its stated advance is therefore a mathematical constraint on vulnerability supported by experiments, rather than a complete explanation or elimination of adversarial examples.
summary.tldr: The paper derives and experimentally verifies lower bounds on the perturbation magnitude needed to change a neural network's classification.

title: Lower bounds on the robustness to adversarial perturbations

abstract: Compressive image recovery is a challenging problem that requires fast and accurate algorithms. Recently, neural networks have been applied to this problem with promising results. By exploiting massively parallel GPU processing architectures and oodles of training data, they can run orders of magnitude faster than existing techniques. However, these methods are largely unprincipled black boxes that are difficult to train and often-times specific to a single measurement matrix. It was recently demonstrated that iterative sparse-signal-recovery algorithms can be ``unrolled’' to form interpretable deep networks. Taking inspiration from this work, we develop a novel neural network architecture that mimics the behavior of the denoising-based approximate message passing (D-AMP) algorithm. We call this new network {\em Learned} D-AMP (LDAMP). The LDAMP network is easy to train, can be applied to a variety of different measurement matrices, and comes with a state-evolution heuristic that accurately predicts its performance. Most importantly, it outperforms the state-of-the-art BM3D-AMP and NLR-CS algorithms in terms of both accuracy and run time. At high resolutions, and when used with sensing matrices that have fast implementations, LDAMP runs over $50\times$ faster than BM3D-AMP and hundreds of times faster than NLR-CS.

Inspired by turning iterative algorithms into network layers, this architecture connects learned reconstruction to an established computational procedure. At high image resolutions, when the sensing matrices have fast implementations, it runs more than 50 times faster than BM3D-AMP and hundreds of times faster than NLR-CS. Those conditions are part of the large speedup claim.
summary.tldr: LDAMP turns a denoising-based recovery algorithm into a trainable network with improved reported reconstruction accuracy and runtime.

title: Learned D-AMP: Principled Neural Network based Compressive Image Recovery

abstract: A Triangle Generative Adversarial Network ($\Delta$-GAN) is developed for semi-supervised cross-domain joint distribution matching, where the training data consists of samples from each domain, and supervision of domain correspondence is provided by only a few paired samples. $\Delta$-GAN consists of four neural networks, two generators and two discriminators. The generators are designed to learn the two-way conditional distributions between the two domains, while the discriminators implicitly define a ternary discriminative function, which is trained to distinguish real data pairs and two kinds of fake data pairs. The generators and discriminators are trained together using adversarial learning. Under mild assumptions, in theory the joint distributions characterized by the two generators concentrate to the data distribution. In experiments, three different kinds of domain pairs are considered, image-label, image-image and image-attribute pairs. Experiments on semi-supervised image classification, image-to-image translation and attribute-based image generation demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Triangle GAN addresses learning relationships between two domains when examples from each domain are available but only a few are paired. The task is to learn their joint distribution, including which examples correspond across domains. This setting supports using limited correspondence supervision alongside the separate collections of samples.

The architecture has two generators and two discriminators. Each generator learns a conditional distribution in one direction between the domains. Together, the discriminators distinguish three kinds of pairs: real pairs and the two types of generated pairs. Adversarial training therefore evaluates the correspondence produced by both directions within a shared learning setup.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that the joint distributions represented by the generators concentrate toward the data distribution. Experiments cover image-label, image-image, and image-attribute relationships, with favorable results on semi-supervised classification, image translation, and attribute-based generation. The findings support the framework across these tested tasks, while the theoretical distribution-matching conclusion retains its stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Triangle GAN learns bidirectional relationships between domains using few paired examples and a three-way adversarial comparison.

title: Triangle Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Safety is a desirable property that can immensely increase the applicability of learning algorithms in real-world decision-making problems. It is much easier for a company to deploy an algorithm that is safe, i.e., guaranteed to perform at least as well as a baseline. In this paper, we study the issue of safety in contextual linear bandits that have application in many different fields including personalized ad recommendation in online marketing. We formulate a notion of safety for this class of algorithms. We develop a safe contextual linear bandit algorithm, called conservative linear UCB (CLUCB), that simultaneously minimizes its regret and satisfies the safety constraint, i.e., maintains its performance above a fixed percentage of the performance of a baseline strategy, uniformly over time. We prove an upper-bound on the regret of CLUCB and show that it can be decomposed into two terms: 1) an upper-bound for the regret of the standard linear UCB algorithm that grows with the time horizon and 2) a constant term that accounts for the loss of being conservative in order to satisfy the safety constraint. We empirically show that our algorithm is safe and validate our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: A learning system that explores new decisions may temporarily perform worse than an established strategy. This paper studies that deployment concern in contextual linear bandits, where decisions use contextual information and learning must balance exploration with performance. It defines safety through comparison with a baseline strategy.

The proposed conservative linear UCB algorithm, CLUCB, minimizes regret while maintaining performance above a fixed percentage of the baseline's performance throughout time. The percentage-based constraint is the precise safety requirement. It gives the learner a specified performance floor while still allowing it to seek better decisions.

The authors prove a regret bound with two components. One grows with the time horizon like a bound for standard linear UCB; the other is a constant term representing the cost of satisfying the conservative constraint. This decomposition identifies an additional cost of caution that does not itself keep growing with the horizon in the bound. Experiments demonstrate the stated safety behavior and support the theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: CLUCB learns contextual decisions while maintaining a fixed fraction of baseline performance, with a constant additional conservatism term in its regret bound.

title: Conservative Contextual Linear Bandits

abstract: The design of good heuristics or approximation algorithms for NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems often requires significant specialized knowledge and trial-and-error. Can we automate this challenging, tedious process, and learn the algorithms instead? In many real-world applications, it is typically the case that the same optimization problem is solved again and again on a regular basis, maintaining the same problem structure but differing in the data. This provides an opportunity for learning heuristic algorithms that exploit the structure of such recurring problems. In this paper, we propose a unique combination of reinforcement learning and graph embedding to address this challenge. The learned greedy policy behaves like a meta-algorithm that incrementally constructs a solution, and the action is determined by the output of a graph embedding network capturing the current state of the solution. We show that our framework can be applied to a diverse range of optimization problems over graphs, and learns effective algorithms for the Minimum Vertex Cover, Maximum Cut and Traveling Salesman problems.

paragraphs: Designing heuristics for hard combinatorial problems often takes specialized knowledge and considerable experimentation. This paper explores learning such heuristics when the same type of optimization problem occurs repeatedly with different input data. Repeated structure gives a learning system an opportunity to discover useful decision rules across problem instances.

The proposed framework combines reinforcement learning with graph embeddings. A learned greedy policy builds a solution incrementally, choosing each action using a graph embedding network that represents the current state of the partial solution. The resulting policy serves as a general procedure for constructing solutions, while the representation supplies information about the particular graph and the progress already made.

The authors demonstrate effective learned algorithms for Minimum Vertex Cover, Maximum Cut, and Traveling Salesman problems. These examples show that the framework applies across several graph optimization tasks. The stated findings support automating part of heuristic design by learning from recurring problem structure, with effectiveness demonstrated for the evaluated problems rather than an asserted guarantee of optimal solutions for every instance.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning and graph embeddings learn greedy solution-building heuristics for several hard graph optimization problems.

title: Learning Combinatorial Optimization Algorithms over Graphs

abstract: Variational Auto-Encoders (VAE) have become very popular techniques to perform inference and learning in latent variable models as they allow us to leverage the rich representational power of neural networks to obtain flexible approximations of the posterior of latent variables as well as tight evidence lower bounds (ELBO). Com- bined with stochastic variational inference, this provides a methodology scaling to large datasets. However, for this methodology to be practically efficient, it is neces- sary to obtain low-variance unbiased estimators of the ELBO and its gradients with respect to the parameters of interest. While the use of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) has been previously suggested to achieve this [23, 26], the proposed methods require specifying reverse kernels which have a large impact on performance. Additionally, the resulting unbiased estimator of the ELBO for most MCMC kernels is typically not amenable to the reparameterization trick. We show here how to optimally select reverse kernels in this setting and, by building upon Hamiltonian Importance Sampling (HIS) [17], we obtain a scheme that provides low-variance unbiased estimators of the ELBO and its gradients using the reparameterization trick. This allows us to develop a Hamiltonian Variational Auto-Encoder (HVAE). This method can be re-interpreted as a target-informed normalizing flow [20] which, within our context, only requires a few evaluations of the gradient of the sampled likelihood and trivial Jacobian calculations at each iteration.

paragraphs: Variational auto-encoders learn latent-variable models by approximating posterior distributions and optimizing an evidence lower bound, or ELBO. Efficient training requires estimates of this objective and its gradients that are unbiased and have low variance. Adding Markov chain Monte Carlo can enrich inference, but earlier approaches depend heavily on how reverse kernels are chosen.

The paper shows how to choose those reverse kernels optimally in its setting. Building on Hamiltonian Importance Sampling, it constructs low-variance, unbiased estimates of both the ELBO and its gradients that support the reparameterization trick. This addresses a difficulty with most MCMC kernels, whose unbiased ELBO estimators are typically unsuitable for that gradient-estimation technique.

The resulting Hamiltonian Variational Auto-Encoder can also be understood as a target-informed normalizing flow: its transformation uses information about the distribution being approximated. In the authors' context, each iteration requires only a few gradient evaluations of the sampled likelihood and straightforward Jacobian calculations. The contribution connects richer posterior inference with the computational requirements of practical variational learning.
summary.tldr: Hamiltonian Variational Auto-Encoders combine Hamiltonian importance sampling with optimal reverse kernels to obtain low-variance, unbiased, reparameterizable training estimates.

title: Hamiltonian Variational Auto-Encoder

abstract: We propose two randomized algorithms for low-rank Tucker decomposition of tensors. The algorithms, which incorporate sketching, only require a single pass of the input tensor and can handle tensors whose elements are streamed in any order. To the best of our knowledge, ours are the only algorithms which can do this. We test our algorithms on sparse synthetic data and compare them to multiple other methods. We also apply one of our algorithms to a real dense 38 GB tensor representing a video and use the resulting decomposition to correctly classify frames containing disturbances.
