To the best of our knowledge, ours are the only algorithms which can do this. We test our algorithms on sparse synthetic data and compare them to multiple other methods. We also apply one of our algorithms to a real dense 38 GB tensor representing a video and use the resulting decomposition to correctly classify frames containing disturbances.

paragraphs: The paper develops two randomized algorithms for computing low-rank Tucker decompositions of large tensors. A tensor is a multidimensional array, and a low-rank decomposition provides a compact structured representation. The practical focus is how to build that representation when the input is large and its entries arrive as a stream.

Both algorithms incorporate sketching and require only one pass over the input. They can process tensor entries in any arrival order, removing the need for a particular ordering of the stream. The authors state that, to their knowledge, no other algorithms provide this combination of capabilities. The contribution therefore concerns how the data can be accessed as well as how it is decomposed.

The algorithms are evaluated on sparse synthetic data against multiple other methods. One is also applied to a dense 38 GB tensor representing video. The resulting decomposition is used to correctly classify frames containing disturbances, demonstrating that the representation can retain information useful for a downstream task on a large real input.
summary.tldr: Two randomized Tucker-decomposition algorithms process arbitrarily ordered tensor streams in one pass, with a demonstrated application to a 38 GB video tensor.

title: Low-Rank Tucker Decomposition of Large Tensors Using TensorSketch

abstract: We consider the bilinear inverse problem of recovering two vectors, x in R^L and w in R^L, from their entrywise product. We consider the case where x and w have known signs and are sparse with respect to known dictionaries of size K and N, respectively. Here, K and N may be larger than, smaller than, or equal to L. We introduce L1-BranchHull, which is a convex program posed in the natural parameter space and does not require an approximate solution or initialization in order to be stated or solved. We study the case where x and w are S1- and S2-sparse with respect to a random dictionary, with the sparse vectors satisfying an effective sparsity condition, and present a recovery guarantee that depends on the number of measurements as L > Omega(S1+S2)(log(K+N))^2. Numerical experiments verify that the scaling constant in the theorem is not too large. One application of this problem is the sweep distortion removal task in dielectric imaging, where one of the signals is a nonnegative reflectivity, and the other signal lives in a known subspace, for example that given by dominant wavelet coefficients. We also introduce a variants of L1-BranchHull for the purposes of tolerating noise and outliers, and for the purpose of recovering piecewise constant signals. We provide an ADMM implementation of these variants and show they can extract piecewise constant behavior from real images.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover two unknown vectors when the observations contain their entry-by-entry products. It assumes that both vectors have known signs and sparse representations in known dictionaries. These assumptions give the recovery problem additional structure: each signal can be described using relatively few dictionary components, even when the dictionaries differ in size from the observation space.

The proposed method, L1-BranchHull, expresses recovery as a convex optimization problem in the original parameter space. It does not need an approximate answer or initialization to define or solve the program. summary.tldr: L1-BranchHull uses convex optimization to recover two sparse signals from their entrywise product under known-sign and dictionary assumptions.

title: A convex program for bilinear inversion of sparse vectors

abstract: We address the problem of learning accurate 3D shape and camera pose from a collection of unlabeled category-specific images. We train a convolutional network to predict both the shape and the pose from a single image by minimizing the reprojection error: given several views of an object, the projections of the predicted shapes to the predicted camera poses should match the provided views. To deal with pose ambiguity, we introduce an ensemble of pose predictors which we then distill to a single "student" model. To allow for efficient learning of high-fidelity shapes, we represent the shapes by point clouds and devise a formulation allowing for differentiable projection of these. Our experiments show that the distilled ensemble of pose predictors learns to estimate the pose accurately, while the point cloud representation allows to predict detailed shape models.

To deal with pose ambiguity, we introduce an ensemble of pose predictors which we then distill to a single "student" model. To allow for efficient learning of high-fidelity shapes, we represent the shapes by point clouds and devise a formulation allowing for differentiable projection of these. Our experiments show that the distilled ensemble of pose predictors learns to estimate the pose accurately, while the point cloud representation allows to predict detailed shape models.

paragraphs: This paper learns to recover an object's three-dimensional shape and camera pose from unlabeled images belonging to a particular object category. A convolutional network predicts both quantities from a single image. During training, several views of an object provide a consistency signal: the predicted shape, projected using predicted camera poses, should reproduce the observed views.

The shape is represented as a point cloud, and the authors develop a differentiable projection formulation so that reprojection error can train the model. This representation is intended to support efficient learning of detailed geometry. To address ambiguity in camera pose, they train an ensemble of pose predictors and then distill it into a single student predictor.

Experiments show that the distilled predictor estimates camera pose accurately, while the point-cloud representation supports detailed shape predictions. The approach brings shape and viewpoint estimation into a shared learning objective. Its supervision comes from agreement across the available views, connecting the image evidence used in training to the single-image predictions the network ultimately makes.
summary.tldr: Differentiable point-cloud projection and distilled pose predictors learn detailed 3D shape and camera pose from unlabeled multiview images.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Shape and Pose with Differentiable Point Clouds

abstract: Sketching and stochastic gradient methods are arguably the most common techniques to derive efficient large scale learning algorithms. In this paper, we investigate their application in the context of nonparametric statistical learning. More precisely, we study the estimator defined by stochastic gradient with mini batches and random features. The latter can be seen as form of nonlinear sketching and used to define approximate kernel methods. The considered estimator is not explicitly penalized/constrained and regularization is implicit. Indeed, our study highlights how different parameters, such as number of features, iterations, step-size and mini-batch size control the learning properties of the solutions. We do this by deriving optimal finite sample bounds, under standard assumptions. The obtained results are corroborated and illustrated by numerical experiments.

In this paper, we investigate their application in the context of nonparametric statistical learning. More precisely, we study the estimator defined by stochastic gradient with mini batches and random features. The latter can be seen as form of nonlinear sketching and used to define approximate kernel methods. The considered estimator is not explicitly penalized/constrained and regularization is implicit. Indeed, our study highlights how different parameters, such as number of features, iterations, step-size and mini-batch size control the learning properties of the solutions. We do this by deriving optimal finite sample bounds, under standard assumptions. The obtained results are corroborated and illustrated by numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies a scalable learning method that combines mini-batch stochastic gradients with random features. Random features provide a nonlinear sketch that approximates a kernel method, while stochastic updates reduce the work involved in processing training data. The question is how these computational choices affect statistical learning quality.

The estimator has no explicit penalty or constraint to regularize its solution. Instead, regularization arises implicitly through choices such as the number of random features, training iterations, step size, and mini-batch size. The authors analyze how these parameters control the learned solution, connecting implementation decisions with the model's ability to learn from finite data.

Under standard assumptions, they derive optimal finite-sample bounds and use numerical experiments to illustrate and corroborate the results. The significance is that approximation and optimization parameters have statistical roles as well as computational ones. Understanding them together provides a principled account of how an efficient approximate kernel learner can be controlled without an explicit regularization term.
summary.tldr: The paper derives optimal finite-sample bounds explaining implicit regularization in mini-batch stochastic-gradient learning with random features.

title: Learning with SGD and Random Features

abstract: In extreme classification problems, learning algorithms are required to map instances to labels from an extremely large label set. We build on a recent extreme classification framework with logarithmic time and space (LTLS), and on a general approach for error correcting output coding (ECOC) with loss-based decoding, and introduce a flexible and efficient approach accompanied by theoretical bounds. Our framework employs output codes induced by graphs, for which we show how to perform efficient loss-based decoding to potentially improve accuracy. In addition, our framework offers a tradeoff between accuracy, model size and prediction time. We show how to find the sweet spot of this tradeoff using only the training data. Our experimental study demonstrates the validity of our assumptions and claims, and shows that our method is competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms.

We build on a recent extreme classification framework with logarithmic time and space (LTLS), and on a general approach for error correcting output coding (ECOC) with loss-based decoding, and introduce a flexible and efficient approach accompanied by theoretical bounds. Our framework employs output codes induced by graphs, for which we show how to perform efficient loss-based decoding to potentially improve accuracy. In addition, our framework offers a tradeoff between accuracy, model size and prediction time. We show how to find the sweet spot of this tradeoff using only the training data. Our experimental study demonstrates the validity of our assumptions and claims, and shows that our method is competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Extreme classification requires choosing labels from a very large set, making prediction cost and model size central concerns. This paper combines ideas from the logarithmic time and space classification framework with error-correcting output codes. The aim is to retain efficient prediction while allowing a more flexible way to evaluate candidate labels.

The framework uses graphs to define output codes and supplies an efficient procedure for loss-based decoding. Decoding determines a label from the model's coded outputs; using a loss gives that decision a criterion tied to prediction quality. The authors show how to perform this operation efficiently on their graph-induced codes, with theoretical bounds supporting the framework and the possibility of improved accuracy.

The method also exposes a tradeoff among accuracy, storage requirements, and prediction time. The authors describe how to choose a favorable operating point using only training data. Their experiments support the assumptions and claims behind the approach and show competitive performance against state-of-the-art algorithms. The result is a configurable classification framework rather than a claim that one configuration dominates every alternative.
summary.tldr: Graph-induced output codes enable efficient loss-based decoding with adjustable accuracy, model size, and prediction-time tradeoffs.

title: Efficient Loss-Based Decoding on Graphs for Extreme Classification

abstract: Progress in deep learning has spawned great successes in many engineering applications. As a prime example, convolutional neural networks, a type of feedforward neural networks, are now approaching -- and sometimes even surpassing -- human accuracy on a variety of visual recognition tasks. Here, however, we show that these neural networks and their recent extensions struggle in recognition tasks where co-dependent visual features must be detected over long spatial ranges. We introduce a visual challenge, Pathfinder, and describe a novel recurrent neural network architecture called the horizontal gated recurrent unit (hGRU) to learn intrinsic horizontal connections -- both within and across feature columns. We demonstrate that a single hGRU layer matches or outperforms all tested feedforward hierarchical baselines including state-of-the-art architectures with orders of magnitude more parameters.

As a prime example, convolutional neural networks, a type of feedforward neural networks, are now approaching -- and sometimes even surpassing -- human accuracy on a variety of visual recognition tasks. We demonstrate that a single hGRU layer matches or outperforms all tested feedforward hierarchical baselines including state-of-the-art architectures with orders of magnitude more parameters.

paragraphs: Strong visual recognition performance does not necessarily imply an ability to connect mutually dependent features across large distances in an image. This paper investigates that capability and shows that convolutional networks and their recent extensions struggle on tasks requiring long-range spatial dependencies. It introduces Pathfinder as a visual challenge for studying this problem.

The proposed horizontal gated recurrent unit, or hGRU, learns horizontal connections within and across feature columns. Its recurrent architecture provides a way to process relationships among spatially separated features. The design directly addresses the dependency structure highlighted by the challenge, placing learned interactions among features at the center of the model.

On the reported evaluation, a single hGRU layer matches or exceeds every tested feedforward hierarchical baseline, including state-of-the-art architectures with orders of magnitude more parameters. This is evidence that the proposed recurrent interactions can be valuable for the particular long-range recognition demands being tested. The comparison also shows that a much larger parameter count in the tested feedforward models did not by itself resolve those demands.
summary.tldr: A single hGRU layer matches or outperforms all tested feedforward baselines on a challenge requiring long-range visual dependencies.

title: Learning long-range spatial dependencies with horizontal gated recurrent units

abstract: Continuing advances in neural interfaces have enabled simultaneous monitoring of spiking activity from hundreds to thousands of neurons. To interpret these large-scale data, several methods have been proposed to infer latent dynamic structure from high-dimensional datasets. One recent line of work uses recurrent neural networks in a sequential autoencoder (SAE) framework to uncover dynamics. SAEs are an appealing option for modeling nonlinear dynamical systems, and enable a precise link between neural activity and behavior on a single-trial basis. However, the very large parameter count and complexity of SAEs relative to other models has caused concern that SAEs may only perform well on very large training sets. We hypothesized that with a method to systematically optimize hyperparameters (HPs), SAEs might perform well even in cases of limited training data. Such a breakthrough would greatly extend their applicability. However, we find that SAEs applied to spiking neural data are prone to a particular form of overfitting that cannot be detected using standard validation metrics, which prevents standard HP searches. We develop and test two potential solutions: an alternate validation method (“sample validation”) and a novel regularization method (“coordinated dropout”). These innovations prevent overfitting quite effectively, and allow us to test whether SAEs can achieve good performance on limited data through large-scale HP optimization. When applied to data from motor cortex recorded while monkeys made reaches in various directions, large-scale HP optimization allowed SAEs to better maintain performance for small dataset sizes. Our results should greatly extend the applicability of SAEs in extracting latent dynamics from sparse, multidimensional data, such as neural population spiking activity.

summary.tldr: New validation and regularization methods enable hyperparameter searches that help neural sequential autoencoders retain performance with limited data.

title: Enabling hyperparameter optimization in sequential autoencoders for spiking neural data

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) is inherently subject to the gap of architectures during searching and validating. To bridge this gap, we develop Differentiable ArchiTecture Approximation (DATA) with an Ensemble Gumbel-Softmax (EGS) estimator to automatically approximate architectures during searching and validating in a differentiable manner. Technically, the EGS estimator consists of a group of Gumbel-Softmax estimators, which is capable of converting probability vectors to binary codes and passing gradients from binary codes to probability vectors. Benefiting from such modeling, in searching, architecture parameters and network weights in the NAS model can be jointly optimized with the standard back-propagation, yielding an end-to-end learning mechanism for searching deep models in a large enough search space. Conclusively, during validating, a high-performance architecture that approaches to the learned one during searching is readily built. Extensive experiments on a variety of popular datasets strongly evidence that our method is capable of discovering high-performance architectures for image classification, language modeling and semantic segmentation, while guaranteeing the requisite efficiency during searching.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can optimize one architectural representation during search and evaluate a different architecture afterward. This mismatch can separate what was learned from what is ultimately tested. DATA addresses the gap by making architecture approximation differentiable during both search and validation, aiming to keep the resulting architecture close to the searched one.

Its main component is an Ensemble Gumbel-Softmax estimator, which combines multiple Gumbel-Softmax estimators. It converts probability vectors into binary codes while allowing gradients to pass back from those codes to the probabilities. This permits architectural parameters and ordinary network weights to be optimized jointly using standard backpropagation within a sufficiently large search space.

At validation time, the method constructs a high-performing architecture that approximates the architecture learned during search. Experiments on multiple datasets report effective architecture discovery for image classification, language modeling, and semantic segmentation while maintaining search efficiency. The significance is the connection between a trainable search representation and the architecture actually evaluated, with reported benefits spanning several types of prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: DATA uses differentiable binary architecture approximations to reduce the mismatch between architecture search and validation.

title: DATA: Differentiable ArchiTecture Approximation

abstract: Work on adversarial examples has shown that neural nets are surprisingly sensitive to adversarially chosen changes of small magnitude. In this paper, we show the opposite: neural nets could be surprisingly insensitive to adversarially chosen changes of large magnitude. We observe that this phenomenon can arise from the intrinsic properties of the ReLU activation function. As a result, two very different examples could share the same feature activation and therefore the same classification decision. We refer to this phenomenon as feature collision and the corresponding examples as colliding examples. We find that colliding examples are quite abundant: we empirically demonstrate the existence of polytopes of approximately colliding examples in the neighbourhood of practically any example.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples usually highlight how a small input change can cause a neural network to change its answer. This paper investigates a different problem: large, deliberately chosen changes can sometimes leave the network's internal representation essentially unchanged. The network can therefore overlook substantial differences between inputs, even while being sensitive to other, much smaller changes.

The authors connect this behavior to intrinsic properties of the ReLU activation function. They call it a feature collision when different examples produce the same feature activation and consequently receive the same classification decision. This shifts attention from the final prediction to the intermediate representation: two inputs can become indistinguishable to the classifier because their differences disappear in its features.

The empirical findings suggest these collisions are abundant. The authors demonstrate geometric regions called polytopes containing approximately colliding examples near practically any example examined. The result concerns approximate agreement across regions, rather than only isolated matching pairs. It identifies excessive insensitivity as another way neural representations can fail to preserve meaningful input differences.
summary.tldr: Neural networks can map substantially different inputs to nearly identical features, with experiments finding abundant regions of such collisions.

title: Approximate Feature Collisions in Neural Nets

abstract: A linear restriction of a function is the same function with its domain restricted to points on a given line. This paper addresses the problem of computing a succinct representation for a linear restriction of a piecewise-linear neural network. This primitive, which we call ExactLine, allows us to exactly characterize the result of applying the network to all of the infinitely many points on a line. In particular, ExactLine computes a partitioning of the given input line segment such that the network is affine on each partition. We present an efficient algorithm for computing ExactLine for networks that use ReLU, MaxPool, batch normalization, fully-connected, convolutional, and other layers, along with several applications. First, we show how to exactly determine decision boundaries of an ACAS Xu neural network, providing significantly improved confidence in the results compared to prior work that sampled finitely many points in the input space. Next, we demonstrate how to exactly compute integrated gradients, which are commonly used for neural network attributions, allowing us to show that the prior heuristic-based methods had relative errors of 25-45% and show that a better sampling method can achieve higher accuracy with less computation. Finally, we use ExactLine to empirically falsify the core assumption behind a well-known hypothesis about adversarial examples, and in the process identify interesting properties of adversarially-trained networks.

paragraphs: A neural network may behave differently at many locations along a single input line segment. Checking a finite collection of points leaves the behavior between them unresolved. ExactLine addresses this problem for piecewise-linear networks by constructing an exact, compact description of their output over the entire segment.

The method divides the segment into pieces on which the network is affine: within each piece, its output follows a linear transformation plus an offset. The algorithm supports common layers including ReLU, MaxPool, convolution, fully connected layers, and batch normalization. This makes a continuous set of infinitely many inputs accessible through a finite representation.

The method also empirically falsifies the central assumption of a hypothesis about adversarial examples and reveals properties of adversarially trained networks.
summary.tldr: ExactLine exactly describes a piecewise-linear network along an input segment, supporting precise boundary analysis and feature attribution.

title: Computing Linear Restrictions of Neural Networks

abstract: Predicting the motion of agents such as pedestrians or human-driven vehicles is one of the most critical problems in the autonomous driving domain. The overall safety of driving and the comfort of a passenger directly depend on its successful solution. The motion prediction problem also remains one of the most challenging problems in autonomous driving engineering, mainly due to high variance of the possible agent’s future behavior given a situation. The two phenomena responsible for the said variance are the multimodality caused by the uncertainty of the agent’s intent (e.g., turn right or move forward) and uncertainty in the realization of a given intent (e.g., which lane to turn into). To be useful within a real-time autonomous driving pipeline, a motion prediction system must provide efficient ways to describe and quantify this uncertainty, such as computing posterior modes and their probabilities or estimating density at the point corresponding to a given trajectory. It also should not put substantial density on physically impossible trajectories, as they can confuse the system processing the predictions. In this paper, we introduce the PRANK method, which satisfies these requirements. PRANK takes rasterized bird-eye images of agent’s surroundings as an input and extracts features of the scene with a convolutional neural network. It then produces the conditional distribution of agent’s trajectories plausible in the given scene. The key contribution of PRANK is a way to represent that distribution using nearest-neighbor methods in latent trajectory space, which allows for efficient inference in real time. We evaluate PRANK on the in-house and Argoverse datasets, where it shows competitive results.

Uncertainty arises both from what an agent intends to do, such as turning or continuing forward, and from how that intention is carried out. An autonomous driving system also needs to query these possibilities quickly without assigning substantial probability to physically impossible motion.

PRANK takes rasterized bird's-eye views of an agent's surroundings and uses a convolutional network to extract scene features. It produces a conditional distribution over trajectories plausible in that scene. Its central contribution is a representation of this distribution using nearest-neighbor methods in a latent trajectory space, enabling efficient real-time inference.

This representation supports operations such as identifying likely trajectory modes and their probabilities or evaluating density for a particular trajectory. Those operations make uncertainty usable by the rest of a driving pipeline. Evaluations on an in-house dataset and Argoverse show competitive results. The contribution combines a distribution over possible motion with an efficient way to access it, rather than reducing prediction to a single future path.
summary.tldr: PRANK represents plausible future trajectories through latent-space nearest neighbors, enabling real-time probabilistic motion prediction with competitive reported results.

title: PRANK: motion Prediction based on RANKing

abstract: Modularity maximization has been a fundamental tool for understanding the community structure of a network, but the underlying optimization problem is nonconvex and NP-hard to solve. State-of-the-art algorithms like the Louvain or Leiden methods focus on different heuristics to help escape local optima, but they still depend on a greedy step that moves node assignment locally and is prone to getting trapped. In this paper, we propose a new class of low-cardinality algorithm that generalizes the local update to maximize a semidefinite relaxation derived from max-k-cut. This proposed algorithm is scalable, empirically achieves the global semidefinite optimality for small cases, and outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithms in real-world datasets with little additional time cost. From the algorithmic perspective, it also opens a new avenue for scaling-up semidefinite programming when the solutions are sparse instead of low-rank.

paragraphs: Community detection often groups network nodes by maximizing modularity, but that optimization problem is nonconvex and NP-hard. Established methods such as Louvain and Leiden use heuristics to escape poor solutions. Their local greedy node moves can still become trapped, motivating an update mechanism that explores community assignments through a different optimization formulation.

The authors propose a class of low-cardinality algorithms that generalizes the local update using a semidefinite relaxation derived from max-k-cut. A relaxation replaces the original difficult optimization with a related problem that can be approached differently. Here, that change allows the algorithm to pursue a broader optimization objective than the usual discrete local reassignment step while preserving scalability.

On small cases, the method empirically reaches the global optimum of the semidefinite relaxation. On real-world datasets, it outperforms leading algorithms with little additional time cost. The distinction between the relaxed optimum and the original modularity problem matters. The work also suggests a route to scaling semidefinite programming by exploiting sparse solutions rather than relying on low rank.
summary.tldr: A low-cardinality semidefinite approach improves empirical community detection with little extra runtime and reaches relaxed global optima on small cases.

title: Community detection using fast low-cardinality semidefinite programming

abstract: The key distinguishing property of a Bayesian approach is marginalization, rather than using a single setting of weights. Bayesian marginalization can particularly improve the accuracy and calibration of modern deep neural networks, which are typically underspecified by the data, and can represent many compelling but different solutions. We show that deep ensembles provide an effective mechanism for approximate Bayesian marginalization, and propose a related approach that further improves the predictive distribution by marginalizing within basins of attraction, without significant overhead. We also investigate the prior over functions implied by a vague distribution over neural network weights, explaining the generalization properties of such models from a probabilistic perspective. From this perspective, we explain results that have been presented as mysterious and distinct to neural network generalization, such as the ability to fit images with random labels, and show that these results can be reproduced with Gaussian processes. We also show that Bayesian model averaging alleviates double descent, resulting in monotonic performance improvements with increased flexibility.

paragraphs: A neural network can admit many plausible weight settings consistent with its training data. This paper emphasizes Bayesian marginalization: combining predictions across possible solutions. The authors argue that this is particularly relevant for modern networks whose behavior is not uniquely determined by the available data, and that it can improve both accuracy and calibration.

They show that deep ensembles offer an effective approximation to Bayesian marginalization. They then propose a related approach that also averages within basins of attraction, regions associated with individual solutions, improving the predictive distribution without significant overhead. This broadens the averaging performed around the solutions represented by an ensemble.

The paper also examines what a vague distribution over weights implies about possible functions. This perspective helps explain generalization phenomena, including fitting images with random labels, which the authors reproduce with Gaussian processes. They further show that Bayesian model averaging alleviates double descent, with performance improving monotonically as flexibility increases in their findings. Together, the results connect predictive averaging with a probabilistic account of network behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper connects deep ensembles and Bayesian averaging to improved predictions and a probabilistic explanation of neural-network generalization.

title: Bayesian Deep Learning and a Probabilistic Perspective of Generalization

abstract: One of the most efficient methods to solve L2 -regularized primal problems, such as logistic regression and linear support vector machine (SVM) classification, is the widely used trust region Newton algorithm, TRON. While TRON has recently been shown to enjoy substantial speedups on shared-memory multi-core systems, exploiting graphical processing units (GPUs) to speed up the method is significantly more difficult, owing to the highly complex and heavily sequential nature of the algorithm. In this work, we show that using judicious GPU-optimization principles, TRON training time for different losses and feature representations may be drastically reduced. For sparse feature sets, we show that using GPUs to train logistic regression classifiers in LIBLINEAR is up to an order-of-magnitude faster than solely using multithreading. For dense feature sets–which impose far more stringent memory constraints–we show that GPUs substantially reduce the lengthy SVM learning times required for state-of-the-art proteomics analysis, leading to dramatic improvements over recently proposed speedups. Furthermore, we show how GPU speedups may be mixed with multithreading to enable such speedups when the dataset is too large for GPU memory requirements; on a massive dense proteomics dataset of nearly a quarter-billion data instances, these mixed-architecture speedups reduce SVM analysis time from over half a week to less than a single day while using limited GPU memory.

paragraphs: TRON is a trust-region Newton algorithm used to train models such as regularized logistic regression and linear support vector machines. Although it benefits from multicore processors, its complex and strongly sequential structure makes GPU acceleration difficult. This paper shows how carefully chosen GPU optimizations can substantially reduce training time across different losses and feature representations.

For sparse features, the authors accelerate logistic regression training in LIBLINEAR by up to an order of magnitude compared with multithreading alone. For dense features, they tackle the more demanding memory requirements of support vector machine training in proteomics. In that setting, they report substantial reductions in lengthy learning times and improvements over recently proposed acceleration methods.

The paper also combines GPU computation with CPU multithreading when a dataset exceeds GPU memory capacity. On a dense proteomics dataset with nearly a quarter-billion instances, this mixed approach reduces analysis from more than half a week to less than one day while using limited GPU memory. The results demonstrate practical computational gains for established classifiers, including workloads too large to fit entirely on the accelerator.
summary.tldr: Careful GPU optimization and CPU–GPU cooperation substantially accelerate TRON-based classification, including dense datasets larger than GPU memory.

title: GPU-Accelerated Primal Learning for Extremely Fast Large-Scale Classification

abstract: The sliding window model of computation captures scenarios in which data is arriving continuously, but only the latest $w$ elements should be used for analysis. The goal is to design algorithms that update the solution efficiently with each arrival rather than recomputing it from scratch. In this work, we focus on $k$-clustering problems such as $k$-means and $k$-median. In this setting, we provide simple and practical algorithms that offer stronger performance guarantees than previous results. Empirically, we show that our methods store only a small fraction of the data, are orders of magnitude faster, and find solutions with costs only slightly higher than those returned by algorithms with access to the full dataset.

In this setting, we provide simple and practical algorithms that offer stronger performance guarantees than previous results. paragraphs: In a continuously arriving data stream, an analysis may need to reflect only the most recent observations. The sliding-window model captures this by retaining a horizon of the latest w elements. This paper studies clustering in that setting, including k-means and k-median, where the desired groups must evolve as the window advances.

Recomputing a clustering from scratch after every arrival would repeatedly process much of the same information. The authors instead develop algorithms that update solutions efficiently as new data enter the window. They describe the methods as simple and practical, and establish stronger performance guarantees than previous results for these clustering problems.

The empirical findings address memory, speed, and clustering quality together. The methods store only a small fraction of the data and run orders of magnitude faster, while their clustering costs are only slightly above those of algorithms that can access the full dataset. This supports maintaining compact information about a changing window as a practical way to keep clustering current without paying the full cost of repeated batch analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper develops efficient sliding-window clustering algorithms with stronger guarantees and reported savings in memory and runtime.

title: Sliding Window Algorithms for k-Clustering Problems

abstract: Visual illusions may be explained by the likelihood of patches in real-world images, as argued by input-driven paradigms in Neuro-Science. However, neither the data nor the tools existed in the past to extensively support these explanations. The era of big data opens a new opportunity to study input-driven approaches. We introduce a tool that computes the likelihood of patches, given a large dataset to learn from. Given this tool, we present a model that supports the approach and explains lightness and color visual illusions in a unified manner. Furthermore, our model generates visual illusions in natural images, by applying the same tool, reversely.

paragraphs: One explanation of visual illusions is that perception reflects how likely particular image patches are in the visual world. On this view, the statistical regularities of ordinary images help explain why some arrangements produce misleading impressions of lightness or color. The paper develops a computational way to investigate that explanation.

The authors introduce a tool that learns from a large image dataset and estimates the likelihood of image patches. They use it to construct a model that accounts for both lightness and color illusions within one framework. Treating both kinds of illusion through the same statistical tool connects them to a shared explanatory principle.

The tool can also be applied in reverse to generate visual illusions in natural images. This extends its role from explaining existing effects to producing images that exhibit them. Together, the explanatory model and the generation capability support the input-driven account described in the paper. The findings provide computational support for that approach, rather than establishing it as the only possible explanation of visual perception.
summary.tldr: A model of image-patch likelihoods provides a unified statistical explanation of lightness and color illusions and can generate new illusions.

title: Color Visual Illusions: A Statistics-based Computational Model

abstract: We analyze in a closed form the learning dynamics of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for a single layer neural network classifying a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture where each cluster is assigned one of two labels. This problem provides a prototype of a non-convex loss landscape with interpolating regimes and a large generalization gap. We define a particular stochastic process for which SGD can be extended to a continuous-time limit that we call stochastic gradient flow. In the full-batch limit we recover the standard gradient flow. We apply dynamical mean-field theory from statistical physics to track the dynamics of the algorithm in the high-dimensional limit via a self-consistent stochastic process. We explore the performance of the algorithm as a function of control parameters shedding light on how it navigates the loss landscape.

This paper studies that evolution for a single-layer neural network classifying a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture with two possible labels. The setting provides a model of a non-convex loss landscape that includes interpolating regimes and a large generalization gap.

The authors define a stochastic process that gives SGD a continuous-time extension, called stochastic gradient flow. In the full-batch limit, this construction recovers standard gradient flow. They then use dynamical mean-field theory from statistical physics to describe learning through a self-consistent stochastic process in the high-dimensional limit.

This produces a closed-form analysis of the learning dynamics in the specified model. By varying control parameters, the authors explore algorithm performance and how optimization moves through the loss landscape. The value of the framework is an analytically tractable view of stochastic learning behavior. Its conclusions concern the stated Gaussian-mixture classification setting and high-dimensional analysis, rather than arbitrary neural-network training problems.
summary.tldr: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a closed-form description of SGD learning dynamics for a single-layer Gaussian-mixture classifier in high dimensions.

title: Dynamical mean-field theory for stochastic gradient descent in Gaussian mixture classification

abstract: The Frank-Wolfe algorithm is a classic method for constrained optimization problems. It has recently been popular in many machine learning applications because its projection-free property leads to more efficient iterations. In this paper, we study projection-free algorithms for convex-strongly-concave saddle point problems with complicated constraints. Our method combines Conditional Gradient Sliding with Mirror-Prox and show that it only requires $\tilde{\cO}(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ gradient evaluations and $\tilde{\cO}(1/\epsilon^2)$ linear optimizations in the batch setting. We also extend our method to the stochastic setting and propose first stochastic projection-free algorithms for saddle point problems. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms and verify our theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Constrained optimization can be expensive when each update requires projecting a point back into a complicated feasible set. Projection-free methods avoid that operation, which can make individual iterations more efficient. This paper develops such methods for saddle point problems that are convex in one variable and strongly concave in the other.

The proposed algorithm combines Conditional Gradient Sliding with Mirror-Prox. In the batch setting, its stated requirements are approximately 1/√ε gradient evaluations and 1/ε² linear optimizations, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Reporting these separately matters: the method controls the number of gradient calculations while using linear optimization to handle the constraints without projection.

The authors also extend the approach to stochastic optimization and present what they describe as the first stochastic projection-free algorithms for saddle point problems. Their experiments demonstrate effectiveness and support the theoretical guarantees. Together, the results provide an approach for the specified convex–strongly-concave setting that makes the computational roles of gradients and constraint handling explicit, especially when the geometry of the constraints makes projection inconvenient.
summary.tldr: Combining Conditional Gradient Sliding with Mirror-Prox yields projection-free saddle point algorithms with theoretical guarantees in batch and stochastic settings.

title: Efficient Projection-free Algorithms for Saddle Point Problems

abstract: Deep learning models are increasingly popular in many machine learning applications where the training data may contain sensitive information. To provide formal and rigorous privacy guarantee, many learning systems now incorporate differential privacy by training their models with (differentially) private SGD. A key step in each private SGD update is gradient clipping that shrinks the gradient of an individual example whenever its l2 norm exceeds a certain threshold. We first demonstrate how gradient clipping can prevent SGD from converging to a stationary point. We then provide a theoretical analysis on private SGD with gradient clipping. Our analysis fully characterizes the clipping bias on the gradient norm, which can be upper bounded by the Wasserstein distance between the gradient distribution and a geometrically symmetric distribution. Our empirical evaluation further suggests that the gradient distributions along the trajectory of private SGD indeed exhibit such symmetric structure. Together, our results provide an explanation why private SGD with gradient clipping remains effective in practice despite its potential clipping bias. Finally, we develop a new perturbation-based technique that can provably correct the clipping bias even for instances with highly asymmetric gradient distributions.

paragraphs: Private stochastic gradient descent clips each example's gradient when its length exceeds a threshold. This is a key part of the training procedure, but clipping can distort the update direction. The paper first demonstrates that this distortion can prevent SGD from reaching a stationary point, making clipping bias a genuine optimization issue.

The authors then analyze that bias geometrically. They characterize its effect on the gradient norm and bound it using the Wasserstein distance between the gradient distribution and a geometrically symmetric distribution. This relates the potential harm from clipping to the shape of the gradients encountered during training.

Their experiments suggest that gradient distributions along private-SGD training trajectories do exhibit the relevant symmetry. Combined with the theory, this offers an explanation for why clipping can work well in practice despite its possible bias; the empirical symmetry is evidence, not a universal property of training. The authors also propose a perturbation-based technique that provably corrects clipping bias even for highly asymmetric gradient distributions. The paper therefore supplies both an account of practical effectiveness and a method for addressing problematic asymmetry.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis links private-SGD clipping bias to gradient asymmetry and motivates a provable perturbation-based correction.

title: Understanding Gradient Clipping in Private SGD: A Geometric Perspective

abstract: Most machine learning tasks are inherently multi-objective. This means that the learner has to come up with a model that performs well across a number of base objectives $\cL_{1}, \ldots, \cL_{p}$, as opposed to a single one. Since optimizing with respect to multiple objectives at the same time is often computationally expensive, the base objectives are often combined in an ensemble $\sum_{k=1}^{p}\lambda_{k}\cL_{k}$, thereby reducing the problem to scalar optimization. The mixture weights $\lambda_{k}$ are set to uniform or some other fixed distribution, based on the learner's preferences. We argue that learning with a fixed distribution on the mixture weights runs the risk of overfitting to some individual objectives and significantly harming others, despite performing well on an entire ensemble. Moreover, in reality, the true preferences of a learner across multiple objectives are often unknown or hard to express as a specific distribution. Instead, we propose a new framework of \emph{Agnostic Learning with Multiple Objectives} ($\almo$), where a model is optimized for \emph{any} weights in the mixture of base objectives. We present data-dependent Rademacher complexity guarantees for learning in the $\almo$ framework, which are used to guide a scalable optimization algorithm and the corresponding regularization. We present convergence guarantees for this algorithm, assuming convexity of the loss functions and the underlying hypothesis space. We further implement the algorithm in a popular symbolic gradient computation framework and empirically demonstrate on a number of datasets the benefits of $\almo$ framework versus learning with a fixed mixture weights distribution.

paragraphs: When a learning task has several objectives, a common shortcut combines them using fixed weights. An implementation in a symbolic gradient computation framework is evaluated on several datasets, where the authors report benefits over learning with fixed mixture weights. The results support accounting explicitly for uncertainty in objective preferences, while the stated convergence result depends on the convexity assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a learning framework that accounts for arbitrary mixtures of objectives instead of committing to fixed preference weights.

title: Agnostic Learning with Multiple Objectives

abstract: Recent research on graph embedding has achieved success in various applications. Most graph embedding methods preserve the proximity in a graph into a manifold in an embedding space. We argue an important but neglected problem about this proximity-preserving strategy: Graph topology patterns, while preserved well into an embedding manifold by preserving proximity, may distort in the ambient embedding Euclidean space, and hence to detect them becomes difficult for machine learning models. To address the problem, we propose curvature regularization, to enforce flatness for embedding manifolds, thereby preventing the distortion. We present a novel angle-based sectional curvature, termed ABS curvature, and accordingly three kinds of curvature regularization to induce flat embedding manifolds during graph embedding. We integrate curvature regularization into five popular proximity-preserving embedding methods, and empirical results in two applications show significant improvements on a wide range of open graph datasets.

paragraphs: Graph embedding represents a graph in a geometric space so that machine learning models can use its structure. Many methods focus on preserving which graph elements are close to one another. This paper argues that doing so can preserve topological patterns along an embedding manifold while still distorting those patterns in the surrounding Euclidean space.

That distinction matters because a downstream model may have difficulty detecting a pattern that is preserved on a curved manifold but distorted in the space where it operates. The authors propose curvature regularization to encourage flatter embedding manifolds. They introduce an angle-based measure called ABS curvature and use it to develop three forms of regularization.

The regularizers are integrated into five established proximity-preserving embedding methods. Across two applications and a range of public graph datasets, the authors report significant empirical improvements. These results support treating the geometry of the embedding manifold as an additional design concern: preserving local proximity alone may leave useful graph structure difficult for subsequent models to recognize.
summary.tldr: Curvature regularization encourages flatter graph embeddings so that preserved graph patterns are easier for downstream models to detect.

title: Curvature Regularization to Prevent Distortion in Graph Embedding

abstract: Market equilibrium is a solution concept with many applications such as digital ad markets, fair division, and resource sharing. For many classes of utility functions, equilibria can be captured by convex programs. We develop simple first-order methods suitable for solving these convex programs for large-scale markets. We focus on three practically-relevant utility classes: linear, quasilinear, and Leontief utilities. Using structural properties of market equilibria under each utility class, we show that the corresponding convex programs can be reformulated as optimization of a structured smooth convex function over a polyhedral set, for which projected gradient achieves linear convergence. To do so, we utilize recent linear convergence results under weakened strong-convexity conditions, and further refine the relevant constants in existing convergence results. Then, we show that proximal gradient (a generalization of projected gradient) with a practical linesearch scheme achieves linear convergence under the Proximal-PL condition, a recently developed error bound condition for convex composite problems. For quasilinear utilities, we show that Mirror Descent applied to a new convex program achieves sublinear last-iterate convergence and yields a form of Proportional Response dynamics, an elegant, interpretable algorithm for computing market equilibria originally developed for linear utilities. Numerical experiments show that Proportional Response is highly efficient for computing approximate market equilibria, while projected gradient with linesearch can be much faster when higher-accuracy solutions are needed.

summary.tldr: Structured convex reformulations yield efficient first-order market-equilibrium algorithms with convergence guarantees and different advantages at different accuracy levels.

title: First-Order Methods for Large-Scale Market Equilibrium Computation

abstract: We investigate a stochastic counterpart of majority votes over finite ensembles of classifiers, and study its generalization properties. While our approach holds for arbitrary distributions, we instantiate it with Dirichlet distributions: this allows for a closed-form and differentiable expression for the expected risk, which then turns the generalization bound into a tractable training objective.The resulting stochastic majority vote learning algorithm achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and benefits from (non-vacuous) tight generalization bounds, in a series of numerical experiments when compared to competing algorithms which also minimize PAC-Bayes objectives -- both with uninformed (data-independent) and informed (data-dependent) priors.
originalAbstract: We investigate a stochastic counterpart of majority votes over finite ensembles of classifiers, and study its generalization properties. While our approach holds for arbitrary distributions, we instantiate it with Dirichlet distributions: this allows for a closed-form and differentiable expression for the expected risk, which then turns the generalization bound into a tractable training objective.The resulting stochastic majority vote learning algorithm achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and benefits from (non-vacuous) tight generalization bounds, in a series of numerical experiments when compared to competing algorithms which also minimize PAC-Bayes objectives -- both with uninformed (data-independent) and informed (data-dependent) priors.

paragraphs: An ensemble can classify an input by combining the votes of several classifiers. This paper studies a stochastic version of majority voting over a finite ensemble and asks how well it generalizes beyond training examples. Its goal is to make a generalization guarantee useful for learning the voting rule itself.

The theoretical approach accommodates arbitrary distributions, while the concrete implementation uses Dirichlet distributions. This choice yields an expected-risk expression that is both closed-form and differentiable. As a result, the PAC-Bayes generalization bound becomes a tractable training objective. The guarantee therefore plays an operational role: the algorithm can directly optimize a quantity designed to connect training performance with generalization.

Numerical experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy and tight, non-vacuous bounds when comparing against competing algorithms that also optimize PAC-Bayes objectives. The evaluation includes both data-independent priors and priors informed by data. These results indicate that, in the studied comparisons, learning with a theoretically motivated objective can deliver strong predictive performance while retaining informative bounds on how the stochastic vote generalizes.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet formulation makes a PAC-Bayes bound directly trainable for stochastic majority votes with strong accuracy and informative guarantees.

title: Learning Stochastic Majority Votes by Minimizing a PAC-Bayes Generalization Bound

abstract: We consider the problem of optimizing a black-box function based on noisy bandit feedback. Kernelized bandit algorithms have shown strong empirical and theoretical performance for this problem. They heavily rely on the assumption that the model is well-specified, however, and can fail without it. Instead, we introduce and address a \emph{misspecified} kernelized bandit setting where the unknown function can be $\epsilon$--uniformly approximated by a function with a bounded norm in some Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). We design efficient and practical algorithms whose performance degrades minimally in the presence of model misspecification. Specifically, we present two algorithms based on Gaussian process (GP) methods: an optimistic EC-GP-UCB algorithm that requires knowing the misspecification error, and Phased GP Uncertainty Sampling, an elimination-type algorithm that can adapt to unknown model misspecification. We provide upper bounds on their cumulative regret in terms of $\epsilon$, the time horizon, and the underlying kernel, and we show that our algorithm achieves optimal dependence on $\epsilon$ with no prior knowledge of misspecification. In addition, in a stochastic contextual setting, we show that EC-GP-UCB can be effectively combined with the regret bound balancing strategy and attain similar regret bounds despite not knowing $\epsilon$.

paragraphs: Optimizing a black-box function from noisy evaluations requires deciding where to sample next. Kernel-based bandit methods can work well, but their guarantees often assume the function fits the model. This paper relaxes that assumption: the true function must be uniformly within an error epsilon of a bounded-norm function in the chosen reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

The authors propose two Gaussian-process methods. EC-GP-UCB uses optimism and requires the misspecification error to be known. Phased GP Uncertainty Sampling uses an elimination approach and adapts without prior knowledge of that error. The distinction matters because the degree of mismatch between a model and the actual function may itself be unknown.

The paper bounds cumulative regret using epsilon, the number of decisions, and the kernel. It establishes optimal dependence on epsilon for its method without prior misspecification knowledge. In a stochastic contextual setting, combining EC-GP-UCB with regret bound balancing also yields similar guarantees without knowing epsilon. These results quantify robustness under a specific approximation assumption.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-process bandit algorithms tolerate bounded model mismatch, including a method with optimal error dependence without knowing the mismatch in advance.

title: Misspecified Gaussian Process Bandit Optimization

abstract: Before the deep learning revolution, many perception algorithms were based on runtime optimization in conjunction with a strong prior/regularization penalty. A prime example of this in computer vision is optical and scene flow. Supervised learning has largely displaced the need for explicit regularization. Instead, they rely on large amounts of labeled data to capture prior statistics, which are not always readily available for many problems. Although optimization is employed to learn the neural network, at runtime, the weights of this network are frozen. As a result, these learning solutions are domain-specific and do not generalize well to other statistically different scenarios. This paper revisits the scene flow problem that relies predominantly on runtime optimization and strong regularization. A central innovation here is the inclusion of a neural scene flow prior, which utilizes the architecture of neural networks as a new type of implicit regularizer. Unlike learning-based scene flow methods, optimization occurs at runtime, and our approach needs no offline datasets---making it ideal for deployment in new environments such as autonomous driving. We show that an architecture based exclusively on multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) can be used as a scene flow prior. Our method attains competitive---if not better---results on scene flow benchmarks. Also, our neural prior's implicit and continuous scene flow representation allows us to estimate dense long-term correspondences across a sequence of point clouds. The dense motion information is represented by scene flow fields where points can be propagated through time by integrating motion vectors. We demonstrate such a capability by accumulating a sequence of lidar point clouds.

paragraphs: Scene flow describes how points in a three-dimensional scene move over time. This paper revisits estimating that motion through optimization performed at runtime. Its central idea is to use a neural network's architecture as an implicit regularizer, so the structure of the network helps constrain the motion estimate without requiring an offline training dataset.

The authors demonstrate this capability by accumulating lidar point clouds, showing how the representation supports a temporal reconstruction task beyond estimating motion between individual observations.
summary.tldr: A neural architecture serves as a scene flow prior for runtime optimization, achieving competitive results without offline datasets.

title: Neural Scene Flow Prior

abstract: Multiple lines of evidence suggest that predictive models may benefit from algorithmic triage. Under algorithmic triage, a predictive model does not predict all instances but instead defers some of them to human experts. However, the interplay between the prediction accuracy of the model and the human experts under algorithmic triage is not well understood. In this work, we start by formally characterizing under which circumstances a predictive model may benefit from algorithmic triage. In doing so, we also demonstrate that models trained for full automation may be suboptimal under triage. Then, given any model and desired level of triage, we show that the optimal triage policy is a deterministic threshold rule in which triage decisions are derived deterministically by thresholding the difference between the model and human errors on a per-instance level. Building upon these results, we introduce a practical gradient-based algorithm that is guaranteed to find a sequence of predictive models and triage policies of increasing performance. Experiments on a wide variety of supervised learning tasks using synthetic and real data from two important applications---content moderation and scientific discovery---illustrate our theoretical results and show that the models and triage policies provided by our gradient-based algorithm outperform those provided by several competitive baselines.

paragraphs: Algorithmic triage assigns some predictions to a model and defers others to human experts. The paper studies when this division can improve performance and how the model should be trained for it. A key finding is that a model optimized to handle every instance may be suboptimal once humans handle part of the workload.

For a given model and desired amount of triage, the authors characterize the optimal allocation as a deterministic threshold rule. It compares model and human errors for each instance and thresholds their difference. The decision therefore depends on relative performance on that instance, connecting the allocation of work directly to the strengths of both predictors.

Building on this analysis, the paper introduces a gradient-based algorithm guaranteed to produce a sequence of models and triage policies with improving performance. Experiments use synthetic data and real applications in content moderation and scientific discovery. The resulting models and policies outperform several competitive baselines, supporting the value of learning prediction and delegation together.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a predictive model and a human-deferral policy can improve triage performance over training for full automation.

title: Differentiable Learning Under Triage

abstract: We develop new parameter-free and scale-free algorithms for solving convex-concave saddle-point problems. Our results are based on a new simple regret minimizer, the Conic Blackwell Algorithm$^+$ (CBA$^+$), which attains $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ average regret. Intuitively, our approach generalizes to other decision sets of interest ideas from the Counterfactual Regret minimization (CFR$^+$) algorithm, which has very strong practical performance for solving sequential games on simplexes.We show how to implement CBA$^+$ for the simplex, $\ell_{p}$ norm balls, and ellipsoidal confidence regions in the simplex, and we present numerical experiments for solving matrix games and distributionally robust optimization problems.Our empirical results show that CBA$^+$ is a simple algorithm that outperforms state-of-the-art methods on synthetic data and real data instances, without the need for any choice of step sizes or other algorithmic parameters.

paragraphs: Convex-concave saddle-point problems involve coupled minimization and maximization decisions. This paper develops algorithms for these problems that require no chosen step sizes or other algorithmic parameters. Its central component is the Conic Blackwell Algorithm+, abbreviated CBA+, a regret-minimization procedure that is also scale-free.

CBA+ extends ideas from CFR+, a method with strong practical performance in sequential games, to additional decision sets. The paper gives implementations for the simplex, norm balls, and ellipsoidal confidence regions within the simplex. Its theoretical guarantee bounds average regret at order one over the square root of the number of iterations, connecting repeated decision quality to a diminishing error measure.

The authors test the approach on matrix games and distributionally robust optimization problems, using synthetic and real-data instances. They report that CBA+ outperforms state-of-the-art methods in those experiments without parameter tuning. The contribution combines a regret guarantee, support for several useful constraint geometries, and empirical evidence that a simple untuned procedure can perform well on these saddle-point applications.
summary.tldr: CBA+ provides parameter-free, scale-free saddle-point algorithms with a square-root average-regret rate and strong reported performance on games and robust optimization.

title: Conic Blackwell Algorithm: Parameter-Free Convex-Concave Saddle-Point Solving

abstract: Federated learning (FL) coordinates with numerous heterogeneous devices to collaboratively train a shared model while preserving user privacy. Despite its multiple advantages, FL faces new challenges. One challenge arises when devices drop out of the training process. In this case, the convergence of popular FL algorithms such as FedAvg is severely influenced by the straggling devices. To tackle this challenge, we study federated learning algorithms in the presence of arbitrary device unavailability and propose an algorithm named Memory-augmented Impatient Federated Averaging (MIFA). Our algorithm efficiently avoids excessive latency induced by inactive devices, and corrects the gradient bias using the memorized latest updates from them. We prove that MIFA achieves minimax optimal convergence rates on non-i.i.d. data for both strongly convex and non-convex smooth functions. originalAbstract: Federated learning (FL) coordinates with numerous heterogeneous devices to collaboratively train a shared model while preserving user privacy. Despite its multiple advantages, FL faces new challenges. One challenge arises when devices drop out of the training process. In this case, the convergence of popular FL algorithms such as FedAvg is severely influenced by the straggling devices. To tackle this challenge, we study federated learning algorithms in the presence of arbitrary device unavailability and propose an algorithm named Memory-augmented Impatient Federated Averaging (MIFA). Our algorithm efficiently avoids excessive latency induced by inactive devices, and corrects the gradient bias using the memorized latest updates from them. We prove that MIFA achieves minimax optimal convergence rates on non-i.i.d. data for both strongly convex and non-convex smooth functions. We also provide an explicit characterization of the improvement over baseline algorithms through a case study, and validate the results by numerical experiments on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model across devices that can differ in both data and availability. When devices stop participating, methods such as FedAvg can suffer in convergence. Waiting for inactive devices introduces latency, while their absence also affects the updates used to train the shared model.

Memory-augmented Impatient Federated Averaging, or MIFA, addresses these two effects together. It avoids excessive waiting and retains the latest updates from unavailable devices. Those remembered updates are used to correct gradient bias, allowing the algorithm to account for devices that are currently absent from training.

The paper proves minimax-optimal convergence rates with non-identically distributed data for strongly convex objectives and for smooth nonconvex objectives. It also characterizes improvement over baseline algorithms through a case study and supports its results with numerical experiments on real-world datasets. The central contribution is a principled use of update memory: device unavailability becomes something the optimization procedure explicitly handles, with both latency considerations and convergence analysis informing the design.
summary.tldr: MIFA reuses unavailable devices’ latest updates to reduce waiting and correct gradient bias, with optimal convergence results in the studied settings.

title: Fast Federated Learning in the Presence of Arbitrary Device Unavailability

abstract: We consider off-policy evaluation (OPE) in continuous treatment settings, such as personalized dose-finding. In OPE, one aims to estimate the mean outcome under a new treatment decision rule using historical data generated by a different decision rule. Most existing works on OPE focus on discrete treatment settings. To handle continuous treatments, we develop a novel estimation method for OPE using deep jump learning. The key ingredient of our method lies in adaptively discretizing the treatment space using deep discretization, by leveraging deep learning and multi-scale change point detection. This allows us to apply existing OPE methods in discrete treatments to handle continuous treatments. Our method is further justified by theoretical results, simulations, and a real application to Warfarin Dosing.

The proposed method, deep jump learning, builds an adaptive discretization of the treatment space. It combines deep learning with change-point detection operating at multiple scales to construct that discretization. This step is the bridge to existing evaluation methods: after organizing continuous treatments into discrete regions, the method can use techniques developed for discrete treatment decisions.

The approach matters because much of the existing off-policy evaluation literature concentrates on discrete treatments. It provides a way to bring those tools into a continuous setting through a learned representation of treatment choices. The authors support the method with theoretical results, simulations, and an application to Warfarin dosing, addressing both its mathematical basis and its use on a real treatment problem.

title: Deep Jump Learning for Off-Policy Evaluation in Continuous Treatment Settings

abstract: The design of optimal auctions is a problem of interest in economics, game theory and computer science. Despite decades of effort, strategyproof, revenue-maximizing auction designs are still not known outside of restricted settings. However, recent methods using deep learning have shown some success in approximating optimal auctions, recovering several known solutions and outperforming strong baselines when optimal auctions are not known. In addition to maximizing revenue, auction mechanisms may also seek to encourage socially desirable constraints such as allocation fairness or diversity. However, these philosophical notions neither have standardization nor do they have widely accepted formal definitions. In this paper, we propose PreferenceNet, an extension of existing neural-network-based auction mechanisms to encode constraints using (potentially human-provided) exemplars of desirable allocations. In addition, we introduce a new metric to evaluate an auction allocations' adherence to such socially desirable constraints and demonstrate that our proposed method is competitive with current state-of-the-art neural-network based auction designs. We validate our approach through human subject research and show that we are able to effectively capture real human preferences.

Those examples can potentially come from people, giving the method a way to represent preferences without requiring a single standardized mathematical definition. It supports treating socially desirable allocation behavior as something that can be learned from expressed preferences.
summary.tldr: PreferenceNet learns auction-allocation constraints from desirable examples and demonstrates that this approach can capture human preferences.

title: PreferenceNet: Encoding Human Preferences in Auction Design with Deep Learning

abstract: In this work, we propose to use out-of-distribution samples, i.e., unlabeled samples coming from outside the target classes, to improve few-shot learning. Specifically, we exploit the easily available out-of-distribution samples to drive the classifier to avoid irrelevant features by maximizing the distance from prototypes to out-of-distribution samples while minimizing that of in-distribution samples (i.e., support, query data). Our approach is simple to implement, agnostic to feature extractors, lightweight without any additional cost for pre-training, and applicable to both inductive and transductive settings. Extensive experiments on various standard benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves the performance of pretrained networks with different architectures.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning must distinguish target classes using very few labeled examples. POODLE adds another source of information: unlabeled examples from outside those classes. Such examples indicate what the classifier should separate from its target categories, helping it avoid features that are irrelevant to the current classification task.

The method adjusts class prototypes by increasing their distance from out-of-distribution examples while reducing their distance from in-distribution examples, including support and query data in the described approach. This creates complementary signals: target examples draw prototypes toward useful regions, while outside examples push them away from regions associated with irrelevant content.

POODLE is lightweight, does not add pretraining cost, and can work with different feature extractors. The authors describe its applicability to both inductive and transductive settings and report consistent improvements across standard benchmarks using pretrained networks with different architectures. The findings suggest that readily available examples outside the target classes can be a useful resource for few-shot adaptation, even though they do not supply additional labels for the classes being learned.
summary.tldr: POODLE improves few-shot classification by moving class prototypes away from unlabeled examples outside the target classes.

title: POODLE: Improving Few-shot Learning via Penalizing Out-of-Distribution Samples

abstract: This paper investigates the problem of computing the equilibrium of competitive games, which is often modeled as a constrained saddle-point optimization problem with probability simplex constraints. Despite recent efforts in understanding the last-iterate convergence of extragradient methods in the unconstrained setting, the theoretical underpinnings of these methods in the constrained settings, especially those using multiplicative updates, remain highly inadequate, even when the objective function is bilinear. Motivated by the algorithmic role of entropy regularization in single-agent reinforcement learning and game theory, we develop provably efficient extragradient methods to find the quantal response equilibrium (QRE)---which are solutions to zero-sum two-player matrix games with entropy regularization---at a linear rate. The proposed algorithms can be implemented in a decentralized manner, where each player executes symmetric and multiplicative updates iteratively using its own payoff without observing the opponent's actions directly. In addition, by controlling the knob of entropy regularization, the proposed algorithms can locate an approximate Nash equilibrium of the unregularized matrix game at a sublinear rate without assuming the Nash equilibrium to be unique. Our methods also lead to efficient policy extragradient algorithms for solving entropy-regularized zero-sum Markov games at a linear rate. All of our convergence rates are nearly dimension-free, which are independent of the size of the state and action spaces up to logarithm factors, highlighting the positive role of entropy regularization for accelerating convergence.
