summary.tldr: Entropy-regularized extragradient methods achieve fast equilibrium convergence in zero-sum matrix and Markov games with nearly dimension-free rates.

title: Fast Policy Extragradient Methods for Competitive Games with Entropy Regularization

abstract: Abstract Consider $N$ cooperative agents such that for $T$ turns, each agent n takes an action $a_{n}$ and receives a stochastic reward $r_{n}\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\right)$. Agents cannot observe the actions of other agents and do not know even their own reward function. The agents can communicate with their neighbors on a connected graph $G$ with diameter $d\left(G\right)$. We want each agent $n$ to achieve an expected average reward of at least $\lambda_{n}$ over time, for a given quality of service (QoS) vector $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$. A QoS vector $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is not necessarily achievable. By giving up on immediate reward, knowing that the other agents will compensate later, agents can improve their achievable capacity region. Our main observation is that the gap between $\lambda_{n}t$ and the accumulated reward of agent $n$, which we call the QoS regret, behaves like a queue. Inspired by this observation, we propose a distributed algorithm that aims to learn a max-weight matching of agents to actions. In each epoch, the algorithm employs a consensus phase where the agents agree on a certain weighted sum of rewards by communicating only $O\left(d\left(G\right)\right)$ numbers every turn. Then, the algorithm uses distributed successive elimination on a random subset of action profiles to approximately maximize this weighted sum of rewards. We prove a bound on the accumulated sum of expected QoS regrets of all agents, that holds if $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is a safety margin $\varepsilon_{T}$ away from the boundary of the capacity region, where $\varepsilon_{T}\rightarrow0$ as $T\rightarrow\infty$. This bound implies that, for large $T$, our algorithm can achieve any $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ in the interior of the dynamic capacity region, while all agents are guaranteed an empirical average expected QoS regret of $\tilde{O}\left(1\right)$ over $t=1,\ldots,T$ which never exceeds $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{t}\right)$ for any $t$. We then extend our result to time-varying i.i.d. communication graphs.

The central idea treats an agent's accumulated shortfall from its target as a queue. A distributed algorithm uses these shortfalls to guide weighted reward optimization. Agents first communicate through a connected graph to agree on weights, then use distributed successive elimination over a random subset of joint action profiles to approximately maximize the weighted objective.

The authors also extend the result to independently sampled, time-varying communication graphs.
summary.tldr: Treating reward shortfalls as queues enables distributed bandit agents to learn cooperative allocations that achieve interior long-run service targets.

title: Queue Up Your Regrets: Achieving the Dynamic Capacity Region of Multiplayer Bandits

abstract: We study the Bayesian regret of the renowned Thompson Sampling algorithm in contextual bandits with binary losses and adversarially-selected contexts. We adapt the information-theoretic perspective of Russo and Van Roy [2016] to the contextual setting by considering a lifted version of the information ratio defined in terms of the unknown model parameter instead of the optimal action or optimal policy as done in previous works on the same setting. This allows us to bound the regret in terms of the entropy of the prior distribution through a remarkably simple proof, and with no structural assumptions on the likelihood or the prior. The extension to priors with infinite entropy only requires a Lipschitz assumption on the log-likelihood. An interesting special case is that of logistic bandits with $d$-dimensional parameters, $K$ actions, and Lipschitz logits, for which we provide a $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{dKT})$ regret upper-bound that does not depend on the smallest slope of the sigmoid link function.

Its focus is Bayesian regret, a measure of accumulated decision-making loss averaged under a prior over the unknown model. The challenge is to relate that loss to what the algorithm learns.

The authors modify an information-theoretic analysis by measuring information about the unknown model parameter itself. Earlier approaches in the same setting tracked information about the optimal action or policy. summary.tldr: Tracking information about unknown model parameters yields broad Thompson Sampling regret bounds for contextual bandits with binary losses.

title: Lifting the Information Ratio: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Thompson Sampling for Contextual Bandits

abstract: In this paper, we advocate for two stages in a neural network's decision making process. The first is the existing feed-forward inference framework where patterns in given data are sensed and associated with previously learned patterns. The second stage is a slower reflection stage where we ask the network to reflect on its feed-forward decision by considering and evaluating all available choices. Together, we term the two stages as introspective learning. We use gradients of trained neural networks as a measurement of this reflection. A simple three-layered Multi Layer Perceptron is used as the second stage that predicts based on all extracted gradient features. We perceptually visualize the post-hoc explanations from both stages to provide a visual grounding to introspection. For the application of recognition, we show that an introspective network is 4% more robust and 42% less prone to calibration errors when generalizing to noisy data. We also illustrate the value of introspective networks in downstream tasks that require generalizability and calibration including active learning, out-of-distribution detection, and uncertainty estimation. Finally, we ground the proposed machine introspection to human introspection for the application of image quality assessment.

The second, slower stage considers the available choices and uses additional information to reassess the decision. The authors call the combined process introspective learning.

Reflection is implemented through gradients extracted from trained networks. A three-layer multilayer perceptron uses these gradient features to make the second-stage prediction. The technical contribution is a concrete two-stage predictor that turns gradient information into an additional basis for decision making.
summary.tldr: Introspective learning adds a gradient-based reflection stage that improves reported robustness and calibration when recognizing noisy data.

title: Introspective Learning : A Two-Stage approach for Inference in Neural Networks

abstract: Estimating personalized effects of treatments is a complex, yet pervasive problem. To tackle it, recent developments in the machine learning (ML) literature on heterogeneous treatment effect estimation gave rise to many sophisticated, but opaque, tools: due to their flexibility, modularity and ability to learn constrained representations, neural networks in particular have become central to this literature. Unfortunately, the assets of such black boxes come at a cost: models typically involve countless nontrivial operations, making it difficult to understand what they have learned. Yet, understanding these models can be crucial -- in a medical context, for example, discovered knowledge on treatment effect heterogeneity could inform treatment prescription in clinical practice. In this work, we therefore use post-hoc feature importance methods to identify features that influence the model's predictions. This allows us to evaluate treatment effect estimators along a new and important dimension that has been overlooked in previous work: We construct a benchmarking environment to empirically investigate the ability of personalized treatment effect models to identify predictive covariates -- covariates that determine differential responses to treatment. Our benchmarking environment then enables us to provide new insight into the strengths and weaknesses of different types of treatment effects models as we modulate different challenges specific to treatment effect estimation -- e.g. the ratio of prognostic to predictive information, the possible nonlinearity of potential outcomes and the presence and type of confounding.

paragraphs: Personalized treatment-effect models estimate how the effect of a treatment varies between people. Flexible models can capture complicated patterns, but their predictions alone do not reveal which characteristics drive those differences. This paper evaluates whether such models identify the variables that determine different responses to treatment.

The authors use post-hoc feature importance methods to examine which inputs influence a trained model's predictions. They build a benchmarking environment around the recovery of predictive covariates: characteristics that determine treatment-effect differences. This introduces an interpretability-focused evaluation dimension, allowing models to be assessed for what they appear to have learned about treatment heterogeneity.

The environment varies challenges specific to treatment-effect estimation, including the balance of prognostic and predictive information, nonlinear potential outcomes, and different forms of confounding. These controlled changes reveal strengths and weaknesses across model types. The contribution is a way to investigate whether a model's influential features reflect the relevant treatment-response structure, knowledge that could matter when interpreting personalized estimates in settings such as medicine.
summary.tldr: This benchmark uses feature importance to assess whether treatment-effect models identify the characteristics that drive different treatment responses.

title: Benchmarking Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Models through the Lens of Interpretability

abstract: Identifying the relevant variables for a classification model with correct confidence levels is a central but difficult task in high-dimension. Despite the core role of sparse logistic regression in statistics and machine learning, it still lacks a good solution for accurate inference in the regime where the number of features $p$ is as large as or larger than the number of samples $n$. Here we tackle this problem by improving the Conditional Randomization Test (CRT). The original CRT algorithm shows promise as a way to output p-values while making few assumptions on the distribution of the test statistics. As it comes with a prohibitive computational cost even in mildly high-dimensional problems, faster solutions based on distillation have been proposed. Yet, they rely on unrealistic hypotheses and result in low-power solutions. To improve this, we propose \emph{CRT-logit}, an algorithm that combines a variable-distillation step and a decorrelation step that takes into account the geometry of $\ell_1$-penalized logistic regression problem. We provide a theoretical analysis of this procedure, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulations, along with experiments on large-scale brain-imaging and genomics datasets.

paragraphs: Selecting useful predictors is different from determining how confidently each predictor can be called relevant. This distinction becomes especially difficult in classification when the number of features matches or exceeds the number of samples. The paper addresses statistical inference for sparse logistic regression in this high-dimensional setting.

Its starting point is the Conditional Randomization Test, which can produce p-values while requiring relatively few assumptions about the distribution of its test statistic. The original procedure is computationally expensive. Faster approaches based on distillation exist, but the authors argue that their assumptions are unrealistic and that they have limited power to detect relevant variables.

The proposed CRT-logit algorithm combines variable distillation with a decorrelation step tailored to the geometry of logistic regression with an L1 penalty. This makes the structure of the fitted classification problem central to the testing procedure. The authors provide theoretical analysis and evaluate the method through simulations and large brain-imaging and genomics datasets. These results support its effectiveness as an approach to identifying relevant variables with statistical confidence.
summary.tldr: CRT-logit adapts conditional randomization testing to sparse logistic regression through variable distillation and geometry-aware decorrelation.

title: A Conditional Randomization Test for Sparse Logistic Regression in High-Dimension

abstract: The recent success of Transformer has benefited many real-world applications, with its capability of building long dependency through pairwise dot-products. However, the strong assumption that elements are directly attentive to each other limits the performance of tasks with high-order dependencies such as natural language understanding and Image captioning. To solve such problems, we are the first to define the Jump Self-attention (JAT) to build Transformers. Inspired by the pieces moving of English Draughts, we introduce the spectral convolutional technique to calculate JAT on the dot-product feature map. This technique allows JAT's propagation in each self-attention head and is interchangeable with the canonical self-attention. We further develop the higher-order variants under the multi-hop assumption to increase the generality. Moreover, the proposed architecture is compatible with the pre-trained models. With extensive experiments, we empirically show that our methods significantly increase the performance on ten different tasks.

Inspired by the pieces moving of English Draughts, we introduce the spectral convolutional technique to calculate JAT on the dot-product feature map. We further develop the higher-order variants under the multi-hop assumption to increase the generality. Moreover, the proposed architecture is compatible with the pre-trained models. With extensive experiments, we empirically show that our methods significantly increase the performance on ten different tasks.

paragraphs: Standard transformer self-attention builds relationships through pairwise dot products. The authors argue that assuming elements attend directly to one another limits performance on tasks involving higher-order dependencies, including language understanding and image captioning. Jump Self-attention, or JAT, is proposed to let attention represent richer relationships within a transformer.

Inspired by movement in English draughts, JAT applies a spectral convolution technique to the dot-product feature map. This supports propagation within each attention head. The authors also construct higher-order variants under a multi-hop assumption, extending the ways relationships can be represented. JAT is interchangeable with conventional self-attention and compatible with pretrained models, which makes the proposed mechanism usable within existing transformer architectures.

Experiments across ten tasks show significant performance improvements for the proposed methods. The findings support the usefulness of enriching the attention computation beyond direct pairwise relationships in the tested settings. The contribution combines a new attention mechanism with architectural compatibility, connecting the goal of modeling higher-order structure to a component that can replace ordinary self-attention.
summary.tldr: Jump Self-attention uses spectral convolution and multi-hop relationships to enrich transformer attention, with reported gains across ten tasks.

title: Jump Self-attention: Capturing High-order Statistics in Transformers

abstract: Inspired by a recent breakthrough of Mishchenko et al. [2022], who for the first time showed that local gradient steps can lead to provable communication acceleration, we propose an alternative algorithm which obtains the same communication acceleration as their method (ProxSkip). Our approach is very different, however: it is based on the celebrated method of Chambolle and Pock [2011], with several nontrivial modifications: i) we allow for an inexact computation of the prox operator of a certain smooth strongly convex function via a suitable gradient-based method (e.g., GD or Fast GD), ii) we perform a careful modification of the dual update step in order to retain linear convergence. Our general results offer the new state-of-the-art rates for the class of strongly convex-concave saddle-point problems with bilinear coupling characterized by the absence of smoothness in the dual function. When applied to federated learning, we obtain a theoretically better alternative to ProxSkip: our method requires fewer local steps ($\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{1/3})$ or $\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{1/4})$, compared to $\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{1/2})$ of ProxSkip), and performs a deterministic number of local steps instead. Like ProxSkip, our method can be applied to optimization over a connected network, and we obtain theoretical improvements here as well.

paragraphs: In distributed optimization, local computation and communication are different costs. This paper proposes an algorithm that achieves the same provable communication acceleration as ProxSkip while improving the theoretical requirements for local work. Its construction starts from a primal-dual optimization method and changes how its internal computations and dual updates are performed.

A key modification allows a proximal operation for a smooth, strongly convex function to be computed approximately using gradient descent or accelerated gradient descent. The authors also adjust the dual update to retain linear convergence despite this inexact computation. Their general analysis gives improved rates for strongly convex-concave saddle-point problems with bilinear coupling and a dual function that need not be smooth.

For federated learning, the reported local-step requirements scale as O(kappa^(1/3)) or O(kappa^(1/4)), compared with ProxSkip's O(kappa^(1/2)). The number of local steps is deterministic as well. The method also applies to optimization over a connected network, where the authors obtain further theoretical improvements. These findings distinguish communication efficiency from the local computational effort needed to achieve it.
summary.tldr: An inexact primal-dual method matches ProxSkip’s communication acceleration while requiring theoretically fewer, deterministically scheduled local steps.

title: Communication Acceleration of Local Gradient Methods via an Accelerated Primal-Dual Algorithm with an Inexact Prox

abstract: Contextual Bayesian optimization (CBO) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making given side information, with important applications, e.g., in wind energy systems. In this setting, the learner receives context (e.g., weather conditions) at each round, and has to choose an action (e.g., turbine parameters). Standard algorithms assume no cost for switching their decisions at every round. However, in many practical applications, there is a cost associated with such changes, which should be minimized. We introduce the episodic CBO with movement costs problem and, based on the online learning approach for metrical task systems of Coester and Lee (2019), propose a novel randomized mirror descent algorithm that makes use of Gaussian Process confidence bounds. We compare its performance with the offline optimal sequence for each episode and provide rigorous regret guarantees. We further demonstrate our approach on the important real-world application of altitude optimization for Airborne Wind Energy Systems. In the presence of substantial movement costs, our algorithm consistently outperforms standard CBO algorithms.

paragraphs: Contextual Bayesian optimization selects actions repeatedly while receiving side information, such as weather conditions. In wind energy, an action could specify operating parameters. Standard approaches assume that changing the action between rounds is free, but physical adjustments can carry costs. This paper incorporates those costs into an episodic version of the decision problem.

The proposed algorithm combines randomized mirror descent with Gaussian-process confidence bounds. It builds on an online-learning approach for metrical task systems, connecting uncertainty about action performance with the expense of moving between decisions. The authors analyze regret against the offline optimal sequence within each episode, providing rigorous guarantees relative to that comparison.

The application is altitude optimization for airborne wind energy systems, where changing altitude introduces the kind of movement tradeoff the formulation captures. When movement costs are substantial, the method consistently outperforms standard contextual Bayesian optimization algorithms in the reported evaluation. The result shows why evaluating a sequence of decisions must account for the cost of transitions as well as the value of individual actions.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian optimization method accounts for costly action changes and improves reported wind-energy optimization when movement costs are substantial.

title: Movement Penalized Bayesian Optimization with Application to Wind Energy Systems

abstract: Is dynamics prediction indispensable for physical reasoning? If so, what kind of roles do the dynamics prediction modules play during the physical reasoning process? Most studies focus on designing dynamics prediction networks and treating physical reasoning as a downstream task without investigating the questions above, taking for granted that the designed dynamics prediction would undoubtedly help the reasoning process. In this work, we take a closer look at this assumption, exploring this fundamental hypothesis by comparing two learning mechanisms: Learning from Dynamics (LfD) and Learning from Intuition (LfI). In the first experiment, we directly examine and compare these two mechanisms. Results show a surprising finding: Simple LfI is better than or on par with state-of-the-art LfD. This observation leads to the second experiment with Ground-truth Dynamics (GD), the ideal case of LfD wherein dynamics are obtained directly from a simulator. Results show that dynamics, if directly given instead of approximated, would achieve much higher performance than LfI alone on physical reasoning; this essentially serves as the performance upper bound. Yet practically, LfD mechanism can only predict Approximate Dynamics (AD) using dynamics learning modules that mimic the physical laws, making the following downstream physical reasoning modules degenerate into the LfI paradigm; see the third experiment. We note that this issue is hard to mitigate, as dynamics prediction errors inevitably accumulate in the long horizon. Finally, in the fourth experiment, we note that LfI, the extremely simpler strategy when done right, is more effective in learning to solve physical reasoning problems. Taken together, the results on the challenging benchmark of PHYRE show that LfI is, if not better, as good as LfD with bells and whistles for dynamics prediction. However, the potential improvement from LfD, though challenging, remains lucrative.

paragraphs: The paper questions whether predicting physical dynamics is indispensable for physical reasoning. It compares Learning from Dynamics, which uses a dynamics-prediction component, with Learning from Intuition, a simpler alternative. On the PHYRE benchmark, the authors initially find that the intuition approach matches or exceeds state-of-the-art dynamics-based approaches.

They then supply exact dynamics directly from a simulator. In this idealized setting, dynamics substantially improve reasoning performance beyond intuition alone, establishing the potential value of accurate physical information. The important distinction is therefore between having correct dynamics and relying on a learned approximation of them.

Further experiments suggest that approximate dynamics can cause downstream reasoning to fall back into the intuition paradigm. The authors identify accumulated prediction error over long horizons as a difficult obstacle. Their final experiment reinforces the effectiveness of a properly implemented intuition strategy. Taken together, the findings favor the simpler approach in the tested practical setting while preserving the possibility of substantial gains from better dynamics-based reasoning.
summary.tldr: On PHYRE, simple intuition-based learning matches or beats learned-dynamics approaches, although exact simulator dynamics reveal substantial potential gains.

title: On the Learning Mechanisms in Physical Reasoning

abstract: Learning-based methods have shown promising performance for accelerating motion planning, but mostly in the setting of static environments. For the more challenging problem of planning in dynamic environments, such as multi-arm assembly tasks and human-robot interaction, motion planners need to consider the trajectories of the dynamic obstacles and reason about temporal-spatial interactions in very large state spaces. We propose a GNN-based approach that uses temporal encoding and imitation learning with data aggregation for learning both the embeddings and the edge prioritization policies. Experiments show that the proposed methods can significantly accelerate online planning over state-of-the-art complete dynamic planning algorithms. The learned models can often reduce costly collision checking operations by more than 1000x, and thus accelerating planning by up to 95%, while achieving high success rates on hard instances as well.

paragraphs: Planning a robot's motion around moving obstacles requires reasoning about both location and timing. A route that is clear at one moment may be blocked at another, making the search space much larger than in a static environment. This paper develops a learned approach to accelerate planning in dynamic settings such as multi-arm assembly and human-robot interaction.

The method combines a graph neural network with temporal encoding. It uses imitation learning with data aggregation to learn both representations and policies for prioritizing graph edges. Edge prioritization directs the planner's search effort, while temporal encoding incorporates the time-dependent information needed to reason about interactions with moving obstacles.

Experiments show significant online-planning acceleration relative to leading complete dynamic-planning algorithms. The learned models often reduce expensive collision checks by more than a factor of 1,000 and achieve planning acceleration of up to 95%, while retaining high success rates on difficult instances. These are reported experimental outcomes, highlighting how learned search priorities can reduce the costly geometric checking involved in dynamic motion planning.
summary.tldr: A graph neural network with temporal encoding learns search priorities that substantially accelerate motion planning around moving obstacles in experiments.

title: Learning-based Motion Planning in Dynamic Environments Using GNNs and Temporal Encoding

abstract: We introduce Contrastive Intrinsic Control (CIC), an unsupervised reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that maximizes the mutual information between state-transitions and latent skill vectors. CIC utilizes contrastive learning between state-transitions and skills vectors to learn behaviour embeddings and maximizes the entropy of these embeddings as an intrinsic reward to encourage behavioural diversity. We evaluate our algorithm on the Unsupervised RL Benchmark (URLB) in the asymptotic state-based setting, which consists of a long reward-free pre-training phase followed by a short adaptation phase to downstream tasks with extrinsic rewards. We find that CIC improves over prior exploration algorithms in terms of adaptation efficiency to downstream tasks on state-based URLB.

We evaluate our algorithm on the Unsupervised RL Benchmark (URLB) in the asymptotic state-based setting, which consists of a long reward-free pre-training phase followed by a short adaptation phase to downstream tasks with extrinsic rewards. paragraphs: Contrastive Intrinsic Control prepares a reinforcement-learning agent before a specific task reward is available. The aim is to learn varied behaviors during reward-free pretraining that can later support adaptation to rewarded tasks. The method connects latent skill vectors with state transitions, making the changes an agent produces central to its learned skills.

CIC uses contrastive learning to build behavior embeddings from transitions and skill vectors. It seeks high mutual information between them, so the skill representation and resulting behavior are informative about each other. It also rewards high entropy in the behavior embeddings, creating an internal incentive to explore a diverse range of behaviors during pretraining.

The evaluation uses the state-based Unsupervised RL Benchmark in its asymptotic setting: a long reward-free training period followed by a short adaptation phase with external rewards. CIC improves adaptation efficiency over prior exploration algorithms in that setting. The finding supports learning diverse transition-based skills as preparation for later tasks, with the stated evidence specifically tied to state-based inputs and extended pretraining.
summary.tldr: CIC learns diverse skills through contrastive transition embeddings and improves downstream adaptation after long reward-free pretraining.

title: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning with Contrastive Intrinsic Control

abstract: A machine learning model is traditionally considered robust if its prediction remains (almost) constant under input perturbations with small norm. However, real-world tasks like molecular property prediction or point cloud segmentation have inherent equivariances, such as rotation or permutation equivariance. In such tasks, even perturbations with large norm do not necessarily change an input's semantic content. Furthermore, there are perturbations for which a model's prediction explicitly needs to change. For the first time, we propose a sound notion of adversarial robustness that accounts for task equivariance. We then demonstrate that provable robustness can be achieved by (1) choosing a model that matches the task's equivariances (2) certifying traditional adversarial robustness. Certification methods are, however, unavailable for many models, such as those with continuous equivariances. We close this gap by developing the framework of equivariance-preserving randomized smoothing, which enables architecture-agnostic certification. We additionally derive the first architecture-specific graph edit distance certificates, i.e. sound robustness guarantees for isomorphism equivariant tasks like node classification. Overall, a sound notion of robustness is an important prerequisite for future work at the intersection of robust and geometric machine learning.

paragraphs: Traditional adversarial robustness asks whether small input changes leave a prediction nearly unchanged. That definition can be inadequate for geometric tasks: rotations or permutations may substantially alter the numerical input while preserving its meaning. Other transformations require a corresponding change in the output. The paper develops a robustness notion that explicitly accounts for such task equivariances.

The authors show that provable robustness can be obtained by choosing a model with the task's equivariances and certifying its traditional adversarial robustness. This establishes a sufficient route from familiar certificates to guarantees aligned with the task. However, certification tools are unavailable for many relevant architectures, including models with continuous equivariances.

To address that gap, the paper introduces equivariance-preserving randomized smoothing, enabling certification without depending on a specific architecture. It also derives architecture-specific graph edit distance certificates for isomorphism-equivariant tasks such as node classification. The contribution is a definition and certification framework that respects how a task's outputs should respond to meaningful transformations, extending robustness analysis beyond numerical input closeness alone.
summary.tldr: The paper defines robustness that respects task symmetries and develops certification methods for equivariant models and graph tasks.

title: Provable Adversarial Robustness for Group Equivariant Tasks: Graphs, Point Clouds, Molecules, and More

abstract: MCMC algorithms offer empirically efficient tools for sampling from a target distribution $\pi(x) \propto \exp(-V(x))$. However, on the theory side, MCMC algorithms suffer from slow mixing rate when $\pi(x)$ is non-log-concave. Our work examines this gap and shows that when Poincar\'e-style inequality holds on a subset $\mathcal{X}$ of the state space, the conditional distribution of MCMC iterates over $\mathcal{X}$ mixes fast to the true conditional distribution. This fast mixing guarantee can hold in cases when global mixing is provably slow. We formalize the statement and quantify the conditional mixing rate. We further show that conditional mixing can have interesting implications for sampling from mixtures of Gaussians, parameter estimation for Gaussian mixture models, and Gibbs-sampling with well-connected local minima.

However, on the theory side, MCMC algorithms suffer from slow mixing rate when $\pi(x)$ is non-log-concave. Our work examines this gap and shows that when Poincar\'e-style inequality holds on a subset $\mathcal{X}$ of the state space, the conditional distribution of MCMC iterates over $\mathcal{X}$ mixes fast to the true conditional distribution. paragraphs: MCMC methods generate samples intended to approximate a target probability distribution, but their theoretical convergence can be slow for non-log-concave targets. This creates a tension with their practical usefulness. The paper studies a more focused question: whether the distribution of sampled states, conditioned on being inside a particular region, can become accurate quickly.

The central result assumes that a Poincaré-style inequality holds within the chosen subset of the state space. Under this condition, the conditional distribution of MCMC iterates converges rapidly to the target’s conditional distribution on that subset. The authors formalize this statement and quantify its rate, including situations where convergence across the entire state space is provably slow.

The distinction matters because local conditional accuracy and global accuracy are different objectives. The result does not require rapid global mixing to establish the former. The paper explores implications for sampling Gaussian mixtures, estimating parameters of Gaussian mixture models, and Gibbs sampling with well-connected local minima, showing how this conditional perspective can inform several sampling and estimation problems.
summary.tldr: Under a regional Poincaré-style condition, MCMC can rapidly approximate a conditional distribution even when global convergence is provably slow.

title: Fast Conditional Mixing of MCMC Algorithms for Non-log-concave Distributions

abstract: Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) is a common name for an emerging family of approaches that infer the model parameters when the likelihood is intractable. Existing SBI methods either approximate the likelihood, such as Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) or directly model the posterior, such as Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation (SNPE). While ABC is efficient on low-dimensional problems, on higher-dimensional tasks, it is generally outperformed by SNPE, which leverages function approximation. In this paper, we propose Pseudo-Likelihood Inference (PLI), a new method that brings neural approximation into ABC, making it competitive on challenging Bayesian system identification tasks. By utilizing integral probability metrics, we introduce a smooth likelihood kernel with an adaptive bandwidth that is updated based on information-theoretic trust regions. Thanks to this formulation, our method (i) allows for optimizing neural posteriors via gradient descent, (ii) does not rely on summary statistics, and (iii) enables multiple observations as input. In comparison to SNPE, it leads to improved performance when more data is available. The effectiveness of PLI is evaluated on four classical SBI benchmark tasks and on a highly dynamic physical system, showing particular advantages on stochastic simulations and multi-modal posterior landscapes.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference estimates model parameters when the likelihood cannot be evaluated tractably. Approximate Bayesian Computation approaches this through likelihood approximation, while Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation directly learns a posterior. This paper introduces Pseudo-Likelihood Inference to bring neural approximation into the former approach and improve its competitiveness on demanding system-identification problems.

PLI uses integral probability metrics to construct a smooth likelihood kernel. Its bandwidth adapts through information-theoretic trust regions, providing a controlled way to update that kernel during inference. The resulting formulation permits gradient-based optimization of neural posteriors, accepts multiple observations, and does not depend on summary statistics. These properties connect the likelihood-approximation approach with flexible neural optimization.

The method is evaluated on four established simulation-based inference benchmarks and a highly dynamic physical system. The authors report improved performance relative to SNPE when more data are available, with particular advantages for stochastic simulations and posterior distributions containing multiple modes. The findings support PLI as a useful alternative in those tested settings, especially when inference must use several observations.
summary.tldr: Pseudo-Likelihood Inference brings neural optimization into approximate Bayesian computation through an adaptive smooth likelihood kernel that supports multiple observations.

title: Pseudo-Likelihood Inference

abstract: We propose SutraNets, a novel method for neural probabilistic forecasting of long-sequence time series. SutraNets use an autoregressive generative model to factorize the likelihood of long sequences into products of conditional probabilities. When generating long sequences, most autoregressive approaches suffer from harmful error accumulation, as well as challenges in modeling long-distance dependencies. SutraNets treat long, univariate prediction as multivariate prediction over lower-frequency sub-series. Autoregression proceeds across time and across sub-series in order to ensure coherent multivariate (and, hence, high-frequency univariate) outputs. Since sub-series can be generated using fewer steps, SutraNets effectively reduce error accumulation and signal path distances. We find SutraNets to significantly improve forecasting accuracy over competitive alternatives on six real-world datasets, including when we vary the number of sub-series and scale up the depth and width of the underlying sequence models.

SutraNets treat long, univariate prediction as multivariate prediction over lower-frequency sub-series. Autoregression proceeds across time and across sub-series in order to ensure coherent multivariate (and, hence, high-frequency univariate) outputs. Since sub-series can be generated using fewer steps, SutraNets effectively reduce error accumulation and signal path distances. We find SutraNets to significantly improve forecasting accuracy over competitive alternatives on six real-world datasets, including when we vary the number of sub-series and scale up the depth and width of the underlying sequence models.

paragraphs: Long-range probabilistic forecasting must represent possible future sequences while maintaining relationships across time. Autoregressive models build sequences through conditional predictions, but long chains can accumulate errors and make distant dependencies difficult to capture. SutraNets changes how a long sequence is organized to reduce these difficulties.

The method treats one high-frequency series as several lower-frequency sub-series and forecasts them as a multivariate problem. Autoregression proceeds both across time and between sub-series, maintaining coherence when their outputs are interpreted as the original series. Because each sub-series requires fewer generation steps, this organization reduces error accumulation and shortens the paths over which distant information must travel.

The authors report significantly better forecasting accuracy than competitive alternatives on six real-world datasets. Improvements also hold in experiments that vary the number of sub-series and increase the depth and width of the underlying sequence models. The findings support reorganizing the forecasting dependency structure as a useful component of long-sequence modeling, alongside choices about the capacity of the neural network itself.
summary.tldr: SutraNets forecasts linked lower-frequency sub-series to reduce long autoregressive chains, improving accuracy on six real-world datasets.

title: SutraNets: Sub-series Autoregressive Networks for Long-Sequence, Probabilistic Forecasting

abstract: One of the fundamental challenges found throughout the data sciences is to explain why things happen in specific ways, or through which mechanisms a certain variable $X$ exerts influences over another variable $Y$. In statistics and machine learning, significant efforts have been put into developing machinery to estimate correlations across variables efficiently. In causal inference, a large body of literature is concerned with the decomposition of causal effects under the rubric of mediation analysis. However, many variations are spurious in nature, including different phenomena throughout the applied sciences. Despite the statistical power to estimate correlations and the identification power to decompose causal effects, there is still little understanding of the properties of spurious associations and how they can be decomposed in terms of the underlying causal mechanisms. In this manuscript, we develop formal tools for decomposing spurious variations in both Markovian and Semi-Markovian models. We prove the first results that allow a non-parametric decomposition of spurious effects and provide sufficient conditions for the identification of such decompositions. The described approach has several applications, ranging from explainable and fair AI to questions in epidemiology and medicine, and we empirically demonstrate its use.

paragraphs: An observed association between two variables does not, by itself, explain how one influences the other. Causal mediation analysis studies how causal effects pass through different mechanisms, but spurious associations also need explanation. This paper asks how variation that is not a causal effect can be separated into contributions connected to the underlying causal structure.

The authors develop formal decomposition tools for both Markovian and Semi-Markovian causal models. Their results allow spurious effects to be decomposed nonparametrically, without restricting the analysis to a particular parametric form. They also provide sufficient conditions for identifying these decompositions: conditions under which the components can be recovered from the available information.

The contribution is an explanatory framework for associations that conventional causal-effect decomposition does not directly address. It connects the question of whether an association is causal to the further question of which mechanisms produce its spurious part. The authors demonstrate applications empirically and identify uses in explainable and fair AI, epidemiology, and medicine. Recovery remains tied to the stated sufficient identification conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops nonparametric tools and sufficient identification conditions for decomposing spurious associations into contributions from underlying causal mechanisms.

title: A Causal Framework for Decomposing Spurious Variations

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face the challenges in fine-tuning and deployment due to their high memory demands and computational costs. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods aim to reduce the memory usage of the optimizer state during fine-tuning, the inherent size of pre-trained LLM weights continues to be a pressing concern. Even though quantization techniques are widely proposed to ease memory demands and accelerate LLM inference, most of these techniques are geared towards the deployment phase.To bridge this gap, this paper presents Parameter-Efficient and Quantization-aware Adaptation (PEQA) – a simple yet effective method that combines the advantages of PEFT with quantized LLMs. By updating solely the quantization scales, PEQA can be directly applied to quantized LLMs, ensuring seamless task transitions. Parallel to existing PEFT methods, PEQA significantly reduces the memory overhead associated with the optimizer state. Furthermore, it leverages the advantages of quantization to substantially reduce model sizes. Even after fine-tuning, the quantization structure of a PEQA-tuned LLM remains intact, allowing for accelerated inference on the deployment stage.We employ PEQA-tuning for task-specific adaptation on LLMs with up to $65$ billion parameters. To assess the logical reasoning and language comprehension of PEQA-tuned LLMs, we fine-tune low-bit quantized LLMs using a instruction dataset. Our results show that even when LLMs are quantized to below 4-bit precision, their capabilities in language modeling, few-shot in-context learning, and comprehension can be resiliently restored to (or even improved over) their full-precision original performances with PEQA.

paragraphs: Reducing the number of parameters updated during fine-tuning lowers optimizer memory, but storing a large language model’s pretrained weights remains expensive. Quantization reduces weight storage, yet many quantization methods focus on deployment. This paper connects these two approaches so that a model can remain compressed while being adapted to a task.

Parameter-Efficient and Quantization-aware Adaptation, or PEQA, updates only the quantization scales. It applies directly to quantized models, reducing optimizer-state overhead while retaining the smaller model representation. The quantization structure remains intact after fine-tuning, which allows the adapted model to retain the inference advantages of its compressed form.

The authors apply PEQA to models with up to 65 billion parameters and use instruction data to assess reasoning and comprehension after adaptation. Their results show that models quantized below four-bit precision can recover, or sometimes improve on, their original full-precision performance in language modeling, few-shot in-context learning, and comprehension. This is evidence that adjusting quantization scales can provide useful adaptation despite the restricted set of trainable quantities.
summary.tldr: PEQA fine-tunes compressed language models by updating only quantization scales, preserving low-bit structure while recovering strong performance.

title: Memory-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Compressed Large Language Models via sub-4-bit Integer Quantization

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly benefit from Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting in performing various reasoning tasks. While CoT allows models to produce more comprehensive reasoning processes, its emphasis on intermediate reasoning steps can inadvertently introduce hallucinations and accumulated errors, thereby limiting models’ ability to solve complex reasoning tasks. Inspired by how humans engage in careful and meticulous deductive logical reasoning processes to solve tasks, we seek to enable language models to perform explicit and rigorous deductive reasoning, and also ensure the trustworthiness of their reasoning process through self-verification. However, directly verifying the validity of an entire deductive reasoning process is challenging, even with advanced models like ChatGPT. In light of this, we propose to decompose a reasoning verification process into a series of step-by-step subprocesses, each only receiving their necessary context and premises. To facilitate this procedure, we propose Natural Program, a natural language-based deductive reasoning format. Our approach enables models to generate precise reasoning steps where subsequent steps are more rigorously grounded on prior steps. It also empowers language models to carry out reasoning self-verification in a step-by-step manner. By integrating this verification process into each deductive reasoning stage, we significantly enhance the rigor and trustfulness of generated reasoning steps. Along this process, we also improve the answer correctness on complex reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting asks language models to expose intermediate reasoning, but those extra steps can also introduce unsupported statements and propagate mistakes. Checking an entire argument at once is difficult even for advanced models. This paper instead treats verification as a sequence of smaller reasoning tasks tied to individual steps.

The authors introduce Natural Program, a natural-language format for deductive reasoning. It supports generating steps grounded in earlier statements and then verifying those steps using only the context and premises they need. Restricting each verification task this way makes the dependency between a conclusion and its supporting information explicit, rather than asking the model to assess a whole reasoning chain at once.

Verification is integrated throughout the deductive process. The authors report that this improves the rigor and trustworthiness of intermediate reasoning and also improves final-answer correctness on complex reasoning tasks. The stated result is an improvement in model reasoning and self-checking; the format uses natural language and does not itself establish that every generated argument is correct.
summary.tldr: Natural Program structures reasoning into explicit steps that language models can verify individually, improving reasoning quality and answer correctness.

title: Deductive Verification of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

abstract: Noisy partial label learning (noisy PLL) is an important branch of weakly supervised learning. Unlike PLL where the ground-truth label must conceal in the candidate label set, noisy PLL relaxes this constraint and allows the ground-truth label may not be in the candidate label set. To address this challenging problem, most of the existing works attempt to detect noisy samples and estimate the ground-truth label for each noisy sample. However, detection errors are unavoidable. These errors can accumulate during training and continuously affect model optimization. To this end, we propose a novel framework for noisy PLL with theoretical interpretations, called ``Adjusting Label Importance Mechanism (ALIM)''. It aims to reduce the negative impact of detection errors by trading off the initial candidate set and model outputs. ALIM is a plug-in strategy that can be integrated with existing PLL approaches. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method can achieve state-of-the-art performance on noisy PLL. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zeroQiaoba/ALIM.

paragraphs: Partial label learning trains a model from a set of possible labels for each example. Its usual assumption is that the correct label appears somewhere in that set. This paper addresses the noisier setting where even that assumption can fail, so choosing among the supplied candidates may never produce the right answer.

Existing approaches often try to identify examples with faulty candidate sets and then estimate their true labels. The problem is that mistakes in this detection process can accumulate and continue influencing training. ALIM addresses that issue by adjusting label importance through a tradeoff between the original candidate set and the model's own outputs. Its aim is to reduce the harm caused by detection errors.

The framework includes theoretical interpretations and is designed as a plug-in strategy for existing partial label learning methods. Across multiple benchmark datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance for noisy partial label learning. The result supports balancing candidate information with model predictions as a useful approach when supplied label sets themselves may be unreliable.
summary.tldr: ALIM balances candidate labels with model predictions to reduce the impact of detection errors in noisy partial label learning.

title: ALIM: Adjusting Label Importance Mechanism for Noisy Partial Label Learning

abstract: Predicting upcoming events is critical to our ability to effectively interact with ourenvironment and conspecifics. In natural language processing, transformer models,which are trained on next-word prediction, appear to construct a general-purposerepresentation of language that can support diverse downstream tasks. However, westill lack an understanding of how a predictive objective shapes such representations.Inspired by recent work in vision neuroscience Hénaff et al. (2019), here we test ahypothesis about predictive representations of autoregressive transformer models.In particular, we test whether the neural trajectory of a sequence of words in asentence becomes progressively more straight as it passes through the layers of thenetwork. The key insight behind this hypothesis is that straighter trajectories shouldfacilitate prediction via linear extrapolation. We quantify straightness using a 1-dimensional curvature metric, and present four findings in support of the trajectorystraightening hypothesis: i) In trained models, the curvature progressively decreasesfrom the first to the middle layers of the network. ii) Models that perform better onthe next-word prediction objective, including larger models and models trained onlarger datasets, exhibit greater decreases in curvature, suggesting that this improvedability to straighten sentence neural trajectories may be the underlying driver ofbetter language modeling performance. iii) Given the same linguistic context, thesequences that are generated by the model have lower curvature than the groundtruth (the actual continuations observed in a language corpus), suggesting thatthe model favors straighter trajectories for making predictions. iv) A consistentrelationship holds between the average curvature and the average surprisal ofsentences in the middle layers of models, such that sentences with straighter neuraltrajectories also have lower surprisal. Importantly, untrained models don’t exhibitthese behaviors. In tandem, these results support the trajectory straighteninghypothesis and provide a possible mechanism for how the geometry of the internalrepresentations of autoregressive models supports next word prediction.

paragraphs: This paper examines how next-word prediction shapes a language model's internal representations. It treats successive words in a sentence as a trajectory through representation space and asks whether that trajectory becomes straighter across network layers. The motivating hypothesis is that a straighter path could make upcoming representations easier to predict through linear extrapolation.

Using a one-dimensional curvature measure, the authors find that trained models straighten trajectories from their first layers toward their middle layers. Models with better next-word prediction performance show greater curvature reductions. For the same context, model-generated continuations also follow straighter trajectories than the continuations found in the language corpus.

In middle layers, sentences with lower average curvature also have lower average surprisal. Untrained models do not show these patterns. Together, the results support trajectory straightening as a possible mechanism for predictive language representations. The association with performance suggests a role for representational geometry, while the proposed explanation remains a hypothesis supported by the reported observations.
summary.tldr: Trained language models straighten sentence representation trajectories, supporting a possible geometric mechanism for next-word prediction.

title: Large language models implicitly learn to straighten neural sentence trajectories to construct a predictive representation of natural language.

abstract: To achieve reliable and precise scene understanding, autonomous vehicles typically incorporate multiple sensing modalities to capitalize on their complementary attributes. However, existing cross-modal 3D detectors do not fully utilize the image domain information to address the bottleneck issues of the LiDAR-based detectors. This paper presents a new cross-modal 3D object detector, namely UPIDet, which aims to unleash the potential of the image branch from two aspects. First, UPIDet introduces a new 2D auxiliary task called normalized local coordinate map estimation. This approach enables the learning of local spatial-aware features from the image modality to supplement sparse point clouds. Second, we discover that the representational capability of the point cloud backbone can be enhanced through the gradients backpropagated from the training objectives of the image branch, utilizing a succinct and effective point-to-pixel module. Extensive experiments and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our method. Notably, we achieved the top rank in the highly competitive cyclist class of the KITTI benchmark at the time of submission. The source code is available at https://github.com/Eaphan/UPIDet.

paragraphs: Camera images and LiDAR point clouds provide complementary information for three-dimensional object detection. However, existing combined detectors do not fully use image information to address weaknesses of LiDAR-based detection. UPIDet develops two ways for the image branch to contribute more strongly, particularly when the point cloud is sparse.

First, it adds a two-dimensional auxiliary task called normalized local coordinate map estimation. This encourages image features to encode local spatial information that can supplement the point cloud. Second, a point-to-pixel module allows training objectives from the image branch to send gradients into the point-cloud backbone, improving its learned representations.

These mechanisms give images a role both in providing spatial features and in shaping how point-cloud features are learned. Experiments and ablation studies support the effectiveness of the approach. The authors report the top position in the cyclist category of KITTI at submission time. That result is specific to the stated category and timing, while the broader finding is that image-branch supervision can strengthen a combined three-dimensional detector.
summary.tldr: UPIDet strengthens 3D detection by learning spatial image features and using image-training gradients to improve point-cloud representations.

title: Unleash the Potential of Image Branch for Cross-modal 3D Object Detection

abstract: Pose estimation is remarkably successful under supervised learning, but obtaining annotations, especially for new deployments, is costly and time-consuming. This work tackles adapting models trained on synthetic data to real-world target domains with only unlabelled data. A common approach is model fine-tuning with pseudo-labels from the target domain; yet many pseudo-labelling strategies cannot provide sufficient high-quality pose labels. This work proposes a reconstruction-based strategy as a complement to pseudo-labelling for synthetic-to-real domain adaptation. We generate the driving image by geometrically transforming a base image according to the predicted keypoints and enforce a reconstruction loss to refine the predictions. It provides a novel solution to effectively correct confident yet inaccurate keypoint locations through image reconstruction in domain adaptation. Our approach outperforms the previous state-of-the-arts by 8% for PCK on four large-scale hand and human real-world datasets. In particular, we excel on endpoints such as fingertips and head, with 7.2% and 29.9% improvements in PCK.

paragraphs: Pose models trained on synthetic images need adaptation before working well on real images, but obtaining new pose annotations is costly. Pseudo-labeling can use a model's own predictions as training targets on unlabeled data. Its usefulness is limited when those targets contain errors, including predictions that appear confident despite placing keypoints incorrectly.

This paper complements pseudo-labeling with geometric image reconstruction. Predicted keypoints determine how a base image is transformed to reconstruct a driving image. A reconstruction loss then refines the keypoint predictions. The method provides another training signal for adaptation, allowing image reconstruction to help correct confident but inaccurate locations.

Across four large-scale real-world hand and human datasets, the authors report an 8% improvement in PCK over previous state-of-the-art approaches. They also report gains of 7.2% for fingertips and 29.9% for the head. These results support reconstruction as a useful complement to pseudo-labels when adapting from synthetic training data to an unlabeled real-world target domain.
summary.tldr: Geometric image reconstruction helps correct pose predictions during synthetic-to-real adaptation using unlabeled target images.

title: Synthetic-to-Real Pose Estimation with Geometric Reconstruction

abstract: Learning graphical conditional independence structures is an important machine learning problem and a cornerstone of causal discovery. However, the accuracy and execution time of learning algorithms generally struggle to scale to problems with hundreds of highly connected variables---for instance, recovering brain networks from fMRI data. We introduce the best order score search (BOSS) and grow-shrink trees (GSTs) for learning directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in this paradigm. BOSS greedily searches over permutations of variables, using GSTs to construct and score DAGs from permutations. GSTs efficiently cache scores to eliminate redundant calculations. BOSS achieves state-of-the-art performance in accuracy and execution time, comparing favorably to a variety of combinatorial and gradient-based learning algorithms under a broad range of conditions. To demonstrate its practicality, we apply BOSS to two sets of resting-state fMRI data: simulated data with pseudo-empirical noise distributions derived from randomized empirical fMRI cortical signals and clinical data from 3T fMRI scans processed into cortical parcels. BOSS is available for use within the TETRAD project which includes Python and R wrappers.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph can reveal patterns of conditional independence among variables, an important component of causal discovery. Existing methods can struggle with both accuracy and runtime when hundreds of variables are strongly connected. The paper addresses this scaling challenge with best order score search, or BOSS, supported by grow-shrink trees.

BOSS greedily searches over orderings of variables. Grow-shrink trees construct and score candidate graphs associated with those orderings, while caching scores to avoid repeating calculations. The search strategy and the caching mechanism therefore address complementary parts of the computation: deciding which candidates to examine and reducing the work needed to evaluate them.

The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy and execution time across a broad range of tested conditions, comparing favorably with combinatorial and gradient-based algorithms. They also apply BOSS to simulated resting-state fMRI data with empirically derived noise and to clinical fMRI data represented as cortical parcels. These applications demonstrate practical use on brain-network data. The method is available through TETRAD with Python and R wrappers.
summary.tldr: BOSS combines greedy variable-order search with cached graph scoring to improve the speed and accuracy of DAG discovery.

title: Fast Scalable and Accurate Discovery of DAGs Using the Best Order Score Search and Grow Shrink Trees

abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from forgetting previously learned information when trained on new data. This problem is exacerbated in federated learning (FL), where the data is distributed and can change independently for each user. Many solutions are proposed to resolve this catastrophic forgetting in a centralized setting. However, they do not apply directly to FL because of its unique complexities, such as privacy concerns and resource limitations. To overcome these challenges, this paper presents a framework for \textbf{federated class incremental learning} that utilizes a generative model to synthesize samples from past distributions. This data can be later exploited alongside the training data to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. To preserve privacy, the generative model is trained on the server using data-free methods at the end of each task without requesting data from clients. Moreover, our solution does not demand the users to store old data or models, which gives them the freedom to join/leave the training at any time. Additionally, we introduce SuperImageNet, a new regrouping of the ImageNet dataset specifically tailored for federated continual learning. We demonstrate significant improvements compared to existing baselines through extensive experiments on multiple datasets.

paragraphs: Learning new visual categories can make a model forget categories it learned earlier. Federated learning makes this harder because users hold separate datasets that can change independently. Approaches developed for centralized training do not transfer directly when users face privacy concerns and limits on storage or computation.

The paper introduces a federated class incremental learning framework that generates synthetic examples representing past data distributions. Those examples can accompany current training data, giving the model a way to revisit earlier learning. After each task, a generative model is trained on the server through a data-free procedure that does not request client data. Users also do not need to retain old datasets or models.

These choices support users joining or leaving training without maintaining their own historical training resources. The researchers additionally introduce SuperImageNet, a regrouping of ImageNet designed for federated continual learning. Experiments across multiple datasets report significant improvements over existing baselines, supporting synthetic replay as a practical way to reduce forgetting in this distributed setting.
summary.tldr: Server-trained synthetic replay reduces forgetting in federated vision learning without requiring clients to retain old data or models.

title: A Data-Free Approach to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Class Incremental Learning for Vision Tasks

abstract: Unsupervised face animation aims to generate a human face video based on theappearance of a source image, mimicking the motion from a driving video. Existingmethods typically adopted a prior-based motion model (e.g., the local affine motionmodel or the local thin-plate-spline motion model). While it is able to capturethe coarse facial motion, artifacts can often be observed around the tiny motionin local areas (e.g., lips and eyes), due to the limited ability of these methodsto model the finer facial motions. In this work, we design a new unsupervisedface animation approach to learn simultaneously the coarse and finer motions. Inparticular, while exploiting the local affine motion model to learn the global coarsefacial motion, we design a novel motion refinement module to compensate forthe local affine motion model for modeling finer face motions in local areas. Themotion refinement is learned from the dense correlation between the source anddriving images. Specifically, we first construct a structure correlation volume basedon the keypoint features of the source and driving images. Then, we train a modelto generate the tiny facial motions iteratively from low to high resolution. Thelearned motion refinements are combined with the coarse motion to generate thenew image. Extensive experiments on widely used benchmarks demonstrate thatour method achieves the best results among state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Unsupervised face animation generates a video using the appearance of a source image and motion from a driving video. Existing motion models can capture broad facial movement but struggle with smaller changes around areas such as the lips and eyes. This paper addresses the resulting artifacts by learning coarse motion and finer refinements together.

The approach retains a local affine model for coarse facial movement and adds a module that learns the motion this model misses. It builds a structure correlation volume from keypoint features in the source and driving images. Those dense correlations provide the information used to estimate finer facial movement through repeated refinement from low to high resolution.

The refined motion is combined with the coarse estimate to generate each new image. Experiments on widely used benchmarks report the best results among the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. The approach matters because it gives detailed local motion its own learned correction mechanism, while continuing to use the coarse model for the larger facial movements it already represents.
summary.tldr: A learned motion-refinement module improves face animation by adding fine local movements to a coarse facial-motion model.

title: Learning Motion Refinement for Unsupervised Face Animation

abstract: In protein biophysics, the separation between the functionally important residues (forming the active site or binding surface) and those that create the overall structure (the fold) is a well-established and fundamental concept. Identifying and modifying those functional sites is critical for protein engineering but computationally non-trivial, and requires significant domain knowledge. To automate this process from a data-driven perspective, we propose a disentangled Wasserstein autoencoder with an auxiliary classifier, which isolates the function-related patterns from the rest with theoretical guarantees. This enables one-pass protein sequence editing and improves the understanding of the resulting sequences and editing actions involved. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply it to T-cell receptors (TCRs), a well-studied structure-function case. We show that our method can be used to alter the function of TCRs without changing the structural backbone, outperforming several competing methods in generation quality and efficiency, and requiring only 10\% of the running time needed by baseline models. To our knowledge, this is the first approach that utilizes disentangled representations for TCR engineering.

paragraphs: Protein engineering often aims to change what a protein does while preserving its overall structural organization. Functionally important residues form active sites or binding surfaces, whereas other residues help establish the fold. Identifying which sequence patterns to modify is computationally difficult and typically requires substantial domain knowledge. This paper develops a data-driven way to separate those roles.

The proposed model combines a disentangled Wasserstein autoencoder with an auxiliary classifier. It isolates function-related patterns from the remaining representation, with theoretical guarantees for that separation. This organization enables protein sequences to be edited in one pass and makes the relationship between the editing action and the resulting sequence easier to understand.

The authors apply the method to T-cell receptors, where structure and function provide a suitable test case. They show that receptor function can be altered without changing the structural backbone. Against several competing methods, the approach improves generation quality and efficiency, using only 10% of the running time required by baseline models. These findings support targeted sequence editing through separated representations.
summary.tldr: A disentangled autoencoder enables efficient T-cell receptor sequence edits that change function while preserving the structural backbone.

title: Disentangled Wasserstein Autoencoder for T-Cell Receptor Engineering

abstract: We extend metric learning by studying the Riemannian manifold structure of the underlying data space induced by similarity measures between data points. The key quantity of interest here is the Riemannian metric, which characterizes the Riemannian geometry and defines straight lines and derivatives on the manifold. Being able to estimate the Riemannian metric allows us to gain insights into the underlying manifold and compute geometric features such as the geodesic curves. We model the observed similarity measures as noisy responses generated from a function of the intrinsic geodesic distance between data points. A new local regression approach is proposed to learn the Riemannian metric tensor and its derivatives based on a Taylor expansion for the squared geodesic distances, accommodating different types of data such as continuous, binary, or comparative responses. We develop theoretical foundation for our method by deriving the rates of convergence for the asymptotic bias and variance of the estimated metric tensor. The proposed method is shown to be versatile in simulation studies and real data applications involving taxi trip time in New York City and MNIST digits.

The contribution links noisy observations to an estimated local geometry from which broader geometric features can be computed.
summary.tldr: A local regression method estimates manifold geometry and its derivatives from noisy observations related to intrinsic distances.

title: Estimating Riemannian Metric with Noise-Contaminated Intrinsic Distance

abstract: Understanding when neural networks can be learned efficientlyis a fundamental question in learning theory.Existing hardness results suggest that assumptions on both the input distribution and the network's weights are necessary for obtaining efficient algorithms. Moreover, it was previously shown that depth-$2$ networks can be efficiently learned under the assumptions that the input distribution is Gaussian, and the weight matrix is non-degenerate. In this work, we study whether such assumptions may suffice for learning deeper networks and prove negative results. We show that learning depth-$3$ ReLU networks under the Gaussian input distribution is hard even in the smoothed-analysis framework, where a random noise is added to the network's parameters. It implies that learning depth-$3$ ReLU networks under the Gaussian distribution is hard even if the weight matrices are non-degenerate. Moreover, we consider depth-$2$ networks, and show hardness of learning in the smoothed-analysis framework, where both the network parameters and the input distribution are smoothed. Our hardness results are under a well-studied assumption on the existence of local pseudorandom generators.

The authors investigate whether similarly favorable conditions are sufficient when the network becomes deeper.

For depth-three ReLU networks, they prove hardness even with Gaussian inputs and random perturbations added to the parameters. This perturbation setting, called smoothed analysis, tests whether difficulty persists after the parameters are randomly disturbed. Their result also implies hardness with non-degenerate weight matrices, showing that the earlier depth-two assumptions do not suffice for this deeper setting.

The authors additionally establish hardness for depth-two networks when both the parameters and input distribution undergo smoothing. All these hardness results depend on a stated assumption about the existence of local pseudorandom generators. Under that assumption, the findings identify limits to using Gaussian inputs, non-degeneracy, or smoothing as guarantees of efficient learning. They concern the studied learning problems rather than asserting that practical neural-network training always fails.
summary.tldr: Conditional hardness results show that smoothing and non-degeneracy do not suffice for efficient learning in the studied neural-network settings.

title: Computational Complexity of Learning Neural Networks: Smoothness and Degeneracy

abstract: We consider the class of noisy multi-layered sigmoid recurrent neural networks with $w$ (unbounded) weights for classification of sequences of length $T$, where independent noise distributed according to $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ is added to the output of each neuron in the network. Our main result shows that the sample complexity of PAC learning this class can be bounded by $O (w\log(T/\sigma))$. For the non-noisy version of the same class (i.e., $\sigma=0$), we prove a lower bound of $\Omega (wT)$ for the sample complexity. Our results indicate an exponential gap in the dependence of sample complexity on $T$ for noisy versus non-noisy networks. Moreover, given the mild logarithmic dependence of the upper bound on $1/\sigma$, this gap still holds even for numerically negligible values of $\sigma$.
