More precisely, our theoretical analysis show that DKRR-NY and DKRR-NY-PCG achieve the same learning rates as the exact KRR requiring essentially $\mathcal{O}(|D|^{1.5})$ time and $\mathcal{O}(|D|)$ memory with relaxing the restriction on $p$ in expectation, where $|D|$ is the number of data, which exhibits the average effectiveness of multiple trials. Furthermore, for showing the generalization performance in a single trial, we deduce the learning rates for DKRR-NY and DKRR-NY-PCG in probability. Finally, we propose a novel algorithm DKRR-NY-CM based on DKRR-NY, which employs a communication strategy to further improve the learning performance, whose effectiveness of communications is validated in theoretical and experimental analysis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to scale kernel ridge regression across local processors while preserving statistical accuracy. It analyzes distributed methods that use the Nyström approximation, including a version with iterative solvers. The central question is how much computation can be distributed without weakening the learning rates achieved by exact kernel ridge regression.

The authors derive optimal learning rates and improve the permitted range of processor counts relative to existing bounds. Their expectation results match exact kernel ridge regression’s learning rates while requiring essentially O(|D|^1.5) time and O(|D|) memory, where |D| denotes dataset size. They distinguish these average-over-trials guarantees from bounds in probability, which address performance in a single trial.

The paper also introduces a communication-based extension, DKRR-NY-CM, designed to improve learning performance through exchanges among processors. Both theoretical analysis and experiments support the effectiveness of this communication strategy. The work therefore addresses two connected issues: the statistical consequences of distributing approximate kernel learning and the additional value that communication can provide.
summary.tldr: Distributed Nyström kernel methods attain optimal learning rates under improved processor-count bounds, with communication providing further supported gains.

title: Distributed Nyström Kernel Learning with Communications

abstract: Learning to collaborate is critical in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). Previous works promote collaboration by maximizing the correlation of agents’ behaviors, which is typically characterized by Mutual Information (MI) in different forms. However, we reveal sub-optimal collaborative behaviors also emerge with strong correlations, and simply maximizing the MI can, surprisingly, hinder the learning towards better collaboration. To address this issue, we propose a novel MARL framework, called Progressive Mutual Information Collaboration (PMIC), for more effective MI-driven collaboration. PMIC uses a new collaboration criterion measured by the MI between global states and joint actions. Based on this criterion, the key idea of PMIC is maximizing the MI associated with superior collaborative behaviors and minimizing the MI associated with inferior ones. The two MI objectives play complementary roles by facilitating better collaborations while avoiding falling into sub-optimal ones. Experiments on a wide range of MARL benchmarks show the superior performance of PMIC compared with other algorithms.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need coordinated behavior, but strong statistical dependence between their behaviors does not by itself establish good teamwork. The paper shows that suboptimal collaboration can also have high mutual information. Consequently, maximizing mutual information without distinguishing the quality of the behavior can hinder progress toward better collaboration.

Progressive Mutual Information Collaboration, or PMIC, uses a criterion based on mutual information between global states and joint actions. It separates the learning objective into two complementary directions: increasing mutual information associated with superior collaboration and decreasing it for inferior collaboration. The first encourages useful coordination, while the second discourages becoming committed to poor coordinated behavior.

Experiments across a wide range of multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks report better performance than the compared algorithms. The results support a more selective use of dependence as a learning signal. PMIC’s contribution is to connect mutual-information optimization to the quality of collaboration, making the direction of the objective depend on whether the associated behavior is desirable.
summary.tldr: PMIC encourages mutual information linked to superior collaboration and suppresses it for inferior collaboration, improving tested multi-agent learning performance.

title: PMIC: Improving Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Progressive Mutual Information Collaboration

abstract: In this work we introduce Constrained Offline Policy Optimization (COPO), an offline policy optimization algorithm for learning in MDPs with cost constraints. COPO is built upon a novel offline cost-projection method, which we formally derive and analyze. Our method improves upon the state-of-the-art in offline constrained policy optimization by explicitly accounting for distributional shift and by offering non-asymptotic confidence bounds on the cost of a policy. These formal properties are superior to those of existing techniques, which only guarantee convergence to a point estimate. We formally analyze our method and empirically demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on discrete and continuous control problems, while offering the aforementioned improved, stronger, and more robust theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Offline policy optimization learns decision-making behavior from previously collected data. When a task also imposes cost constraints, evaluating a policy requires more than estimating its reward: the learning method must account for its costs as well. This paper introduces Constrained Offline Policy Optimization, or COPO, for Markov decision processes with those constraints.

COPO centers on an offline cost-projection method that the authors formally derive and analyze. A key feature is its explicit treatment of distributional shift, the mismatch that can arise between the available data and a policy's behavior. The method also provides non-asymptotic confidence bounds on policy cost, giving a finite-data uncertainty statement beyond convergence to a single cost estimate.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on both discrete and continuous control problems, alongside stronger formal properties than the compared existing techniques. The significance is the combination of effective policy learning and a more informative treatment of cost uncertainty. Its confidence bounds address how firmly a cost estimate is supported, rather than treating the estimate alone as sufficient evidence.
summary.tldr: COPO learns cost-constrained policies offline while accounting for distribution shift and providing finite-data confidence bounds on policy costs.

title: Constrained Offline Policy Optimization

abstract: Many bandit problems are characterized by the learner making decisions under constraints. The learner in Linear Contextual Bandits with Knapsacks (LinCBwK) receives a resource consumption vector in addition to a scalar reward in each time step which are both linear functions of the context corresponding to the chosen arm. For a fixed time horizon $T$, the goal of the learner is to maximize rewards while ensuring resource consumptions do not exceed a pre-specified budget. We present algorithms and characterize regret for LinCBwK in the smoothed setting where base context vectors are assumed to be perturbed by Gaussian noise. We consider both the stochastic and adversarial settings for the base contexts, and our analysis of stochastic LinCBwK can be viewed as a warm-up to the more challenging adversarial LinCBwK. For the stochastic setting, we obtain $O(\sqrt{T})$ additive regret bounds compared to the best context dependent fixed policy. The analysis combines ideas for greedy parameter estimation in \cite{kmrw18, siwb20} and the primal-dual paradigm first explored in \cite{agde17, agde14}. Our main contribution is an algorithm with $O(\log T)$ competitive ratio relative to the best context dependent fixed policy for the adversarial setting. The algorithm for the adversarial setting employs ideas from the primal-dual framework \cite{agde17, agde14} and a novel adaptation of the doubling trick \cite{isss19}.

It combines primal-dual ideas with a new adaptation of the doubling trick. This multiplicative comparison differs from the stochastic additive regret guarantee. Both results are established within the stated Gaussian-perturbation setting, which is central to the analysis.
summary.tldr: Under Gaussian-smoothed contexts, the paper provides resource-constrained bandit algorithms with stochastic regret and adversarial competitive-ratio guarantees.

title: Smoothed Adversarial Linear Contextual Bandits with Knapsacks

abstract: A variety of fairness constraints have been proposed in the literature to mitigate group-level statistical bias. Their impacts have been largely evaluated for different groups of populations corresponding to a set of sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Nonetheless, the community has not observed sufficient explorations for how imposing fairness constraints fare at an instance level. Building on the concept of influence function, a measure that characterizes the impact of a training example on the target model and its predictive performance, this work studies the influence of training examples when fairness constraints are imposed. We find out that under certain assumptions, the influence function with respect to fairness constraints can be decomposed into a kernelized combination of training examples. One promising application of the proposed fairness influence function is to identify suspicious training examples that may cause model discrimination by ranking their influence scores. We demonstrate with extensive experiments that training on a subset of weighty data examples leads to lower fairness violations with a trade-off of accuracy.

paragraphs: Fairness constraints are usually evaluated through statistics aggregated over demographic groups. Those summaries do not explain how individual training examples contribute to the resulting predictions or fairness violations. This paper studies that more granular question using influence functions, which quantify how changes to training examples affect a fitted model.

Under stated assumptions, the authors show that the influence function associated with fairness constraints decomposes into a kernelized combination of training examples. This provides scores that can rank examples by their contribution to discrimination. Such rankings offer a way to investigate the training data underlying group-level effects.

Extensive experiments find that training on selected influential subsets can reduce fairness violations, with a tradeoff in predictive accuracy. The contribution is therefore an instance-level diagnostic and data-selection perspective on constrained learning. An influence score describes behavior of the modeled learning system; it should not be read as an intrinsic moral property of an individual example or person.
summary.tldr: Fairness-aware influence functions identify training examples that shape discrimination and expose accuracy–fairness tradeoffs in data selection.

title: Understanding Instance-Level Impact of Fairness Constraints

abstract: Overparametrization often helps improve the generalization performance. This paper presents a dual view of overparametrization suggesting that downsampling may also help generalize. Focusing on the proportional regime $m\asymp n \asymp p$, where $m$ represents the sketching size, $n$ is the sample size, and $p$ is the feature dimensionality, we investigate two out-of-sample prediction risks of the sketched ridgeless least square estimator. Our findings challenge conventional beliefs by showing that downsampling does not always harm generalization but can actually improve it in certain cases. We identify the optimal sketching size that minimizes out-of-sample prediction risks and demonstrate that the optimally sketched estimator exhibits stabler risk curves, eliminating the peaks of those for the full-sample estimator. To facilitate practical implementation, we propose an empirical procedure to determine the optimal sketching size. Finally, we extend our analysis to cover central limit theorems and misspecified models. Numerical studies strongly support our theory.

paragraphs: Using fewer observations might seem certain to hurt prediction, but this paper shows that downsampling can sometimes improve generalization in ridgeless linear regression. It presents downsampling as a counterpart to overparameterization, examining how the size of a data sketch changes prediction risk on unseen examples.

The analysis focuses on a proportional regime in which sketch size, sample size, and feature dimension are of comparable order. Within that setting, the authors investigate two out-of-sample risks and identify sketch sizes that minimize them. The optimally sketched estimator has more stable risk curves, removing peaks that appear for the full-sample estimator.

The paper also proposes an empirical procedure for choosing the sketch size, bringing the theoretical choice closer to practical use. Further analysis covers central limit theorems and misspecified models, and numerical studies strongly support the theory. The message is conditional but consequential: for the studied estimator and settings, retaining every observation need not yield the best generalization, and sketch size can be chosen for predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Optimally chosen downsampling can improve ridgeless regression's prediction risk and remove peaks in its risk curves.

title: Sketched Ridgeless Linear Regression: The Role of Downsampling

abstract: Despite the effectiveness of ELECTRA-style pre-training, their performance is dependent on the careful selection of the model size for the auxiliary generator, leading to high trial-and-error costs. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of this problem. Our theoretical investigation highlights the importance of controlling the generator capacity in ELECTRA-style training. Meanwhile, we found it is not handled properly in the original ELECTRA design, leading to the sensitivity issue. Specifically, since adaptive optimizers like Adam will cripple the weighing of individual losses in the joint optimization, the original design fails to control the generator training effectively. To regain control over the generator, we modularize the generator optimization by decoupling the generator optimizer and discriminator optimizer completely, instead of simply relying on the weighted objective combination. Our simple technique reduced the sensitivity of ELECTRA training significantly and obtains considerable performance gain compared to the original design.

paragraphs: ELECTRA-style pretraining depends sensitively on the size of its auxiliary generator, making model selection costly through trial and error. This paper systematically studies that sensitivity. Its theoretical investigation identifies control of generator capacity as important and argues that the original optimization design does not manage generator training effectively.

The authors trace the problem to joint optimization with adaptive optimizers such as Adam. In this setting, assigning weights to individual losses does not provide the intended control over their optimization. The proposed change fully separates the generator optimizer from the discriminator optimizer, replacing reliance on a weighted combination of objectives with independently managed optimization.

The resulting technique substantially reduces training sensitivity and produces considerable performance gains over the original design in the reported results. Its significance is that the problem is addressed through how the components are optimized, rather than only through repeated searches for a generator size. The paper connects an analysis of lost optimization control to a simple modular change that restores it.
summary.tldr: Separating generator and discriminator optimizers reduces ELECTRA’s sensitivity to generator selection and improves reported pretraining performance.

title: Understand and Modularize Generator Optimization in ELECTRA-style Pretraining

abstract: Typical generative diffusion models rely on a Gaussian diffusion process for training the backward transformations, which can then be used to generate samples from Gaussian noise. However, real world data often takes place in discrete-state spaces, including many scientific applications. Here, we develop a theoretical formulation for arbitrary discrete-state Markov processes in the forward diffusion process using exact (as opposed to variational) analysis. We relate the theory to the existing continuous-state Gaussian diffusion as well as other approaches to discrete diffusion, and identify the corresponding reverse-time stochastic process and score function in the continuous-time setting, and the reverse-time mapping in the discrete-time setting. As an example of this framework, we introduce “Blackout Diffusion”, which learns to produce samples from an empty image instead of from noise. Numerical experiments on the CIFAR-10, Binarized MNIST, and CelebA datasets confirm the feasibility of our approach. Generalizing from specific (Gaussian) forward processes to discrete-state processes without a variational approximation sheds light on how to interpret diffusion models, which we discuss.

paragraphs: Generative diffusion models commonly learn to reverse a process that adds Gaussian noise. Many kinds of data instead occupy discrete states, motivating a formulation built directly around discrete changes. This paper develops a theoretical framework that allows arbitrary discrete-state Markov processes to serve as the forward diffusion process.

The analysis is exact rather than variational. It identifies the reverse-time stochastic process and corresponding score function for continuous time, and the reverse-time mapping for discrete time. By relating these results to Gaussian diffusion and existing discrete approaches, the framework clarifies how different diffusion constructions fit together.

Blackout Diffusion provides a concrete example: it learns to generate an image starting from an empty image rather than a noisy one. Experiments on CIFAR-10, Binarized MNIST, and CelebA establish that this approach is feasible. The stated finding supports a broader choice of forward processes and starting states for generation; its significance lies in demonstrating this flexibility and providing an exact theoretical account of it.
summary.tldr: Blackout Diffusion demonstrates image generation from an empty image within an exact framework for discrete-state diffusion processes.

title: Blackout Diffusion: Generative Diffusion Models in Discrete-State Spaces

abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) of multivariate time series (MTS) aims to learn robust representations of normal multivariate temporal patterns. Existing UAD methods try to learn a fixed set of mappings for each MTS, entailing expensive computation and limited model adaptation. To address this pivotal issue, we propose a prototype-oriented UAD (PUAD) method under a probabilistic framework. Specifically, instead of learning the mappings for each MTS, the proposed PUAD views multiple MTSs as the distribution over a group of prototypes, which are extracted to represent a diverse set of normal patterns. To learn and regulate the prototypes, PUAD introduces a reconstruction-based unsupervised anomaly detection approach, which incorporates a prototype-oriented optimal transport method into a Transformer-powered probabilistic dynamical generative framework. Leveraging meta-learned transferable prototypes, PUAD can achieve high model adaptation capacity for new MTSs. Experiments on five public MTS datasets all verify the effectiveness of the proposed UAD method.

paragraphs: Detecting anomalies in multivariate time series requires learning normal patterns across several changing variables. Existing methods can depend on learning a fixed set of mappings for each series, which the authors associate with expensive computation and limited adaptation. PUAD instead models multiple time series through distributions over a shared collection of prototypes.

These prototypes represent diverse normal temporal patterns. To learn and regulate them, the method combines reconstruction-based anomaly detection with prototype-oriented optimal transport inside a probabilistic dynamical generative framework powered by a Transformer. This brings the representation of normal behavior and the organization of prototypes into one learning approach.

The prototypes are meta-learned to be transferable, allowing the model to adapt to new multivariate time series. Experiments on five public datasets support the method's effectiveness. The central contribution is reusable normal-pattern structure: representing different series through transferable prototypes provides a way to address adaptation without relying entirely on separate fixed mappings for every series.
summary.tldr: PUAD learns transferable prototypes of normal temporal behavior to support unsupervised anomaly detection and adaptation across multivariate time series.

title: Prototype-oriented unsupervised anomaly detection for multivariate time series

abstract: We consider a federated learning (FL) setting where a machine learning model with a fully connected first layer is trained between different clients and a central server using FedAvg, and where the aggregation step can be performed with secure aggregation (SA). We present SRATTA an attack relying only on aggregated models which, under realistic assumptions, (i) recovers data samples from the different clients, and (ii) groups data samples coming from the same client together. While sample recovery has already been explored in an FL setting, the ability to group samples per client, despite the use of SA, is novel. This poses a significant unforeseen security threat to FL and effectively breaks SA. We show that SRATTA is both theoretically grounded and can be used in practice on realistic models and datasets. We also propose counter-measures, and claim that clients should play an active role to guarantee their privacy during training.

paragraphs: This paper investigates privacy in federated learning with FedAvg, a central server, and a model whose first layer is fully connected. Even when secure aggregation is used, the server receives aggregated models. SRATTA examines what sensitive information can be recovered from those aggregate outputs alone under the paper’s stated realistic assumptions.

The attack does two things: it reconstructs client data samples and groups recovered samples according to which client supplied them. The second capability is the distinctive contribution. Recovering isolated examples already threatens privacy, but linking examples to a shared client reveals additional structure despite aggregation hiding individual contributions.

The authors provide theoretical grounding and demonstrate practical use on realistic models and datasets. They describe the result as a significant threat to the privacy protection expected from secure aggregation in this setting. They also propose countermeasures and argue that clients should actively participate in protecting privacy during training. The finding is tied to the specified model architecture, training setup, and attack assumptions, while showing that aggregate-only access can still support both recovery and attribution.
summary.tldr: Under the studied FedAvg assumptions, SRATTA recovers samples and groups them by client using only aggregated models, exposing a privacy risk despite secure aggregation.

title: SRATTA: Sample Re-ATTribution Attack of Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning.

abstract: We introduce InstaAug, a method for automatically learning input-specific augmentations from data. Previous methods for learning augmentations have typically assumed independence between the original input and the transformation applied to that input. This can be highly restrictive, as the invariances we hope our augmentation will capture are themselves often highly input dependent. InstaAug instead introduces a learnable invariance module that maps from inputs to tailored transformation parameters, allowing local invariances to be captured. This can be simultaneously trained alongside the downstream model in a fully end-to-end manner, or separately learned for a pre-trained model. We empirically demonstrate that InstaAug learns meaningful input-dependent augmentations for a wide range of transformation classes, which in turn provides better performance on both supervised and self-supervised tasks.

paragraphs: Data augmentation applies transformations intended to preserve the information a model should learn. The paper highlights that suitable transformations can depend strongly on the particular input. An augmentation policy that assumes independence between an example and its transformation can therefore miss the local invariances that matter for that example.

InstaAug learns this dependence directly. A trainable invariance module receives an input and produces transformation parameters tailored to it. The module can be trained jointly with the downstream model in one end-to-end process, or learned separately for a model that has already been pretrained. These options let the same central idea fit different training arrangements.

The experiments show meaningful input-dependent augmentations across a broad range of transformation classes. Those learned augmentations improve performance on both supervised and self-supervised tasks. The stated findings support treating augmentation as a decision conditioned on each example, with the learned module capturing variations that an input-independent transformation policy would not explicitly represent.
summary.tldr: InstaAug learns transformations tailored to individual inputs and improves reported supervised and self-supervised task performance.

title: Learning Instance-Specific Augmentations by Capturing Local Invariances

abstract: This work introduces DADAO: the first decentralized, accelerated, asynchronous, primal, first-order algorithm to minimize a sum of $L$-smooth and $\mu$-strongly convex functions distributed over a given network of size $n$. Our key insight is based on modeling the local gradient updates and gossip communication procedures with separate independent Poisson Point Processes. This allows us to decouple the computation and communication steps, which can be run in parallel, while making the whole approach completely asynchronous. This leads to communication acceleration compared to synchronous approaches. Our new method employs primal gradients and does not use a multi-consensus inner loop nor other ad-hoc mechanisms such as Error Feedback, Gradient Tracking, or a Proximal operator. By relating the inverse of the smallest positive eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix $\chi_1$ and the maximal resistance $\chi_2\leq \chi_1$ of the graph to a sufficient minimal communication rate between the nodes of the network, we show that our algorithm requires $\mathcal{O}(n\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}\log(\frac{1}{\epsilon}))$ local gradients and only $\mathcal{O}(n\sqrt{\chi_1\chi_2}\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}\log(\frac{1}{\epsilon}))$ communications to reach a precision $\epsilon$, up to logarithmic terms. Thus, we simultaneously obtain an accelerated rate for both computations and communications, leading to an improvement over state-of-the-art works, our simulations further validating the strength of our relatively unconstrained method.

paragraphs: DADAO addresses optimization when different nodes in a network hold different parts of an objective. The objective is a sum of smooth, strongly convex functions. The method is decentralized and asynchronous, so computation and communication do not have to proceed through a shared sequence of synchronized rounds.

Its key design choice models local gradient updates and gossip communication with separate, independent Poisson point processes. This allows the two activities to run independently and in parallel. The algorithm uses primal gradients without a multi-consensus inner loop, gradient tracking, error feedback, or a proximal operator. The analysis connects a sufficient communication rate to two measures of network connectivity.

Under the analyzed conditions, DADAO achieves accelerated bounds for both gradient computations and communications. The computation bound depends on the square root of the objective’s condition number; the communication bound additionally incorporates the network measures. These results improve on the compared prior work, and simulations support the method. The significance is that separating communication from computation can preserve acceleration while allowing fully asynchronous operation.
summary.tldr: DADAO separates local computation from network communication to achieve accelerated decentralized optimization under smoothness and strong-convexity assumptions.

title: DADAO: Decoupled Accelerated Decentralized Asynchronous Optimization

abstract: Slot attention is a powerful method for object-centric modeling in images and videos. However, its set-equivariance limits its ability to handle videos with a dynamic number of objects because it cannot break ties. To overcome this limitation, we first establish a connection between slot attention and optimal transport. Based on this new perspective we propose MESH (Minimize Entropy of Sinkhorn): a cross-attention module that combines the tiebreaking properties of unregularized optimal transport with the speed of regularized optimal transport. We evaluate slot attention using MESH on multiple object-centric learning benchmarks and find significant improvements over slot attention in every setting.

paragraphs: Slot attention is used to organize images and videos into object-centered representations. The paper identifies a limitation arising from its set-equivariance: it cannot break ties, which restricts its ability to handle videos whose number of objects changes. Addressing this assignment behavior is the central motivation for the proposed modification.

The authors first establish a connection between slot attention and optimal transport. They use that perspective to design MESH, short for Minimize Entropy of Sinkhorn, as a cross-attention module. The module combines the ability of unregularized optimal transport to break ties with the computational speed of regularized optimal transport, aiming to retain useful properties of both.

Slot attention equipped with MESH is evaluated on multiple object-centric learning benchmarks. The authors report significant improvements over ordinary slot attention in every evaluated setting. These findings support changing the attention assignment mechanism to overcome the identified tie-breaking limitation. The theoretical connection also gives a principled way to frame the change, linking the behavior of object assignments to the properties of optimal transport.
summary.tldr: MESH uses an optimal-transport perspective to give slot attention efficient tie-breaking and improve object-centric learning across tested settings.

title: Unlocking Slot Attention by Changing Optimal Transport Costs

abstract: I introduce a novel associative memory model named Correlated Dense Associative Memory (CDAM), which integrates both auto- and hetero-association in a unified framework for continuous-valued memory patterns. Employing an arbitrary graph structure to semantically link memory patterns, CDAM is theoretically and numerically analysed, revealing four distinct dynamical modes: auto-association, narrow hetero-association, wide hetero-association, and neutral quiescence. Drawing inspiration from inhibitory modulation studies, I employ anti-Hebbian learning rules to control the range of hetero-association, extract multi-scale representations of community structures in graphs, and stabilise the recall of temporal sequences. Experimental demonstrations showcase CDAM’s efficacy in handling real-world data, replicating a classical neuroscience experiment, performing image retrieval, and simulating arbitrary finite automata.

paragraphs: Associative memory can recover a stored pattern or connect it to other related patterns. Correlated Dense Associative Memory, or CDAM, brings these two behaviors into one framework for continuous-valued memories. An arbitrary graph specifies semantic relationships between patterns, giving the memory system an explicit structure for moving among related content.

Theoretical and numerical analysis identifies four dynamical modes: recall of a pattern itself, narrow association with related patterns, wider association, and a neutral quiet state. The model uses anti-Hebbian learning rules, inspired by inhibitory modulation studies, to control the range of association. This allows the dynamics to reflect different scales of relationships among memories.

The paper uses these mechanisms to extract graph community structure at multiple scales and stabilize recall of temporal sequences. Demonstrations include real-world data, image retrieval, replication of a classical neuroscience experiment, and simulation of arbitrary finite automata. Together, these applications show how graph-linked memories can support both retrieval and structured sequences of activity within the same proposed model.
summary.tldr: CDAM uses graph-linked memories and controlled association dynamics to support retrieval, community representations, and temporal sequence recall.

title: Semantically-correlated memories in a dense associative model

abstract: In this work, we propose a novel optimization model termed “sum-of-minimum" optimization. This model seeks to minimize the sum or average of $N$ objective functions over $k$ parameters, where each objective takes the minimum value of a predefined sub-function with respect to the $k$ parameters. This universal framework encompasses numerous clustering applications in machine learning and related fields. We develop efficient algorithms for solving sum-of-minimum optimization problems, inspired by a randomized initialization algorithm for the classic $k$-means (Arthur & Vassilvitskii, 2007) and Lloyd’s algorithm (Lloyd, 1982). We establish a new tight bound for the generalized initialization algorithm and prove a gradient-descent-like convergence rate for generalized Lloyd’s algorithm. The efficiency of our algorithms is numerically examined on multiple tasks, including generalized principal component analysis, mixed linear regression, and small-scale neural network training. Our approach compares favorably to previous ones based on simpler-but-less-precise optimization reformulations.

paragraphs: Many clustering-style problems involve several candidate parameter choices, with each objective contribution taking the value of whichever choice fits it best. This paper formalizes that structure as sum-of-minimum optimization. The overall goal is to minimize the sum or average of these minimum values, providing a shared formulation for multiple machine-learning applications.

The authors design algorithms inspired by randomized initialization for k-means and by Lloyd’s algorithm. They extend these ideas beyond the classic clustering objective to the broader optimization model. Their analysis establishes a tight bound for the generalized initialization procedure and a convergence rate resembling gradient descent for the generalized Lloyd procedure.

Numerical evaluations cover generalized principal component analysis, mixed linear regression, and small-scale neural-network training. The methods compare favorably with previous approaches that use simpler but less precise reformulations. The significance is that the minimum-over-candidates structure can be handled directly within a common algorithmic framework, with theoretical guarantees and evidence across several tasks rather than a separate formulation for every application.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes k-means-style optimization to sums of minimum-valued objectives, with tight initialization analysis and convergence guarantees.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Sum-Of-Minimum Optimization

abstract: Graph neural networks are popular architectures for graph machine learning, based on iterative computation of node representations of an input graph through a series of invariant transformations. A large class of graph neural networks follow a standard message-passing paradigm: at every layer, each node state is updated based on an aggregate of messages from its neighborhood. In this work, we propose a novel framework for training graph neural networks, where every node is viewed as a player that can choose to either listen, broadcast, listen and broadcast, or to isolate. The standard message propagation scheme can then be viewed as a special case of this framework where every node listens and broadcasts to all neighbors. Our approach offers a more flexible and dynamic message-passing paradigm, where each node can determine its own strategy based on their state, effectively exploring the graph topology while learning. We provide a theoretical analysis of the new message-passing scheme which is further supported by an extensive empirical analysis on a synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly update each node by collecting messages from its neighbors. Repeating this process lets node representations incorporate information from the surrounding graph. This paper introduces a training framework that gives each node more control over that communication, treating nodes as players that choose how to participate.

A node can listen, broadcast, do both, or isolate itself. Its choice depends on its current state, allowing the communication pattern to change as learning progresses. Standard message passing fits inside this framework as the particular case in which every node both listens and broadcasts to all its neighbors.

This flexibility makes communication itself part of the learning process. Different node states can lead to different patterns of information exchange, effectively exploring the graph’s topology while building representations. The paper provides theoretical analysis of the proposed scheme and supports it with experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. The stated contribution is a broader, dynamic message-passing framework whose behavior is examined through both mathematical and empirical analysis.
summary.tldr: Cooperative graph neural networks let each node choose whether to send, receive, or avoid messages based on its current state.

title: Cooperative Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We introduce Optimal Eye Surgeon (OES), a framework for pruning and training deep image generator networks. Typically, untrained deep convolutional networks, which include image sampling operations, serve as effective image priors. However, they tend to overfit to noise in image restoration tasks due to being overparameterized. OES addresses this by adaptively pruning networks at random initialization to a level of underparameterization. This process effectively captures low-frequency image components even without training, by just masking. When trained to fit noisy image, these pruned subnetworks, which we term Sparse-DIP, resist overfitting to noise. This benefit arises from underparameterization and the regularization effect of masking, constraining them in the manifold of image priors. We demonstrate that subnetworks pruned through OES surpass other leading pruning methods, such as the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, which is known to be suboptimal for image recovery tasks. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the transferability of OES-masks and the characteristics of sparse-subnetworks for image generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Avra98/Optimal-Eye-Surgeon.

paragraphs: Untrained convolutional image generators can already favor useful image structure, making them effective priors for restoration. Their excess capacity, however, can also let them fit unwanted noise. Optimal Eye Surgeon addresses this by pruning a randomly initialized generator until it is underparameterized, before training its remaining weights.

The selected mask alone captures low-frequency image components, even without weight training. When the resulting subnetworks, called Sparse-DIP, are subsequently fitted to a noisy image, they resist overfitting to the noise. The authors attribute this behavior to reduced parameter capacity and the regularizing effect of masking, which constrains the network toward image priors.

Experiments show that OES-selected subnetworks outperform leading pruning approaches, including the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis approach, for image recovery. They also demonstrate mask transferability and investigate sparse subnetworks for image generation. The findings make the initial choice of retained connections an active part of restoration: sparsity shapes what the generator can represent before fitting begins and continues to constrain learning afterward.
summary.tldr: OES prunes image generators at initialization to retain useful image structure and reduce subsequent fitting of noise.

title: Optimal Eye Surgeon: Finding image priors through sparse generators at initialization

abstract: Combining the predictions of multiple trained models through ensembling is generally a good way to improve accuracy by leveraging the different learned features of the models, however it comes with high computational and storage costs. Model fusion, the act of merging multiple models into one by combining their parameters reduces these costs but doesn’t work as well in practice. Indeed, neural network loss landscapes are high-dimensional and non-convex and the minima found through learning are typically separated by high loss barriers. Numerous recent works have been focused on finding permutations matching one network features to the features of a second one, lowering the loss barrier on the linear path between them in parameter space. However, permutations are restrictive since they assume a one-to-one mapping between the different models’ neurons exists. We propose a new model merging algorithm, CCA Merge, which is based on Canonical Correlation Analysis and aims to maximize the correlations between linear combinations of the model features. We show that our alignment method leads to better performances than past methods when averaging models trained on the same, or differing data splits. We also extend this analysis into the harder setting where more than 2 models are merged, and we find that CCA Merge works significantly better than past methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shoroi/align-n-merge

paragraphs: Combining predictions from several models can improve accuracy, but keeping and running all of them is costly. Merging their parameters into one model offers a cheaper alternative, yet independently trained networks may not align in ways that make averaging effective. The paper focuses on improving this alignment before models are combined.

Existing alignment approaches often permute neurons to match one network’s features with another’s. Such matching assumes that a useful one-to-one correspondence exists. CCA Merge uses canonical correlation analysis to align linear combinations of features instead. This broader correspondence can capture relationships between models that a simple rearrangement of individual neurons cannot express.

The authors report better performance than earlier merging methods when averaging models trained on either the same data splits or different splits. They also study the harder case of combining more than two models, where CCA Merge performs significantly better than prior methods. The findings support feature alignment beyond neuron permutations as a practical route toward more effective parameter merging.
summary.tldr: CCA Merge aligns linear combinations of neural features and improves model merging over methods restricted to matching individual neurons.

title: Harmony in Diversity: Merging Neural Networks with Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) is a promising distributed learning framework that addresses data heterogeneity issues across multiple clients by grouping clients and providing a shared generalized model for each group. However, under privacy-preserving federated learning protocols where there is no direct sharing of clients’ local datasets, existing approaches often fail to find optimal client groupings resulting in sub-optimal performance. In this paper, we propose a novel CFL algorithm that achieves robust clustering and learning performance. Conceptually, our algorithm groups clients that exhibit similarity in their model updates by periodically accumulating and clustering the gradients that clients compute for various models. The proposed algorithm is shown to achieve a near-optimal error rate for stochastic convergence to optimal models under mild conditions. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm along with an evaluation on several CFL benchmarks demonstrating that it outperforms existing approaches in terms of convergence speed, clustering accuracy, and task performance.

paragraphs: Clients in federated learning can have substantially different data, making a single shared model a poor fit. Clustered federated learning addresses this by grouping clients and learning a model for each group. The challenge is identifying useful groups when clients do not directly share their local datasets.

This paper proposes using similarities in model updates as the basis for grouping. The algorithm periodically accumulates and clusters gradients that clients compute for various models. These gradients provide information about how clients respond to the models, allowing the grouping process to operate within the stated federated setting without direct access to their datasets.

The authors analyze the resulting learning procedure and establish a near-optimal error rate for stochastic convergence to optimal models under mild conditions. They also evaluate it on several clustered federated-learning benchmarks, reporting improvements in convergence speed, clustering accuracy, and task performance. The combined message is that gradient-based grouping can improve both the identification of client groups and the models trained for those groups.
summary.tldr: Clustering accumulated client gradients improves federated client grouping and learning, with a conditional near-optimal convergence guarantee.

title: Clustered Federated Learning via Gradient-based Partitioning

abstract: Previous efforts using frozen Large Language Models (LLMs) for visual understanding, via image captioning or image-text retrieval tasks, face challenges when dealing with complex multimodal scenarios. In order to enhance the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLM) in comprehending the context of vision and language, we introduce Multimodal Composition Learning (MCL) for the purpose of mapping or aligning the vision and language input. In particular, we introduce two tasks: Multimodal-Context Captioning (MC-Cap) and Multimodal-Context Retrieval (MC-Ret) to guide a frozen LLM in comprehending the vision and language context. These specialized tasks are crafted to improve the LLM’s capacity for efficient processing and utilization of multimodal inputs, thereby enhancing its proficiency in generating more accurate text or visual representations. Extensive experiments on both retrieval tasks (i.e., zero-shot composed image retrieval, visual storytelling image retrieval and visual dialog image retrieval) and text generation tasks (i.e., visual question answering) demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The code is available at: https://github.com/dhg-wei/MCL.

paragraphs: Using a frozen language model for visual tasks requires connecting images with the language context around them. The paper argues that earlier captioning and image-text retrieval approaches struggle with complex multimodal situations. Its proposed Multimodal Composition Learning method focuses on improving how visual and linguistic inputs are mapped or aligned.

The method introduces two training tasks: Multimodal-Context Captioning and Multimodal-Context Retrieval. Both guide a frozen language model toward understanding combined vision-language context. The intended effect is better use of the information supplied across modalities, supporting more accurate generated text or visual representations. Captioning and retrieval provide complementary ways to train this contextual understanding.

Experiments cover zero-shot composed image retrieval, visual storytelling image retrieval, visual dialog image retrieval, and visual question answering. The reported results demonstrate effectiveness across both retrieval and text generation. This range matters because the proposed alignment is evaluated through several uses of multimodal context, rather than through a single output task, while the language model remains frozen.
summary.tldr: Multimodal Composition Learning uses contextual captioning and retrieval tasks to improve a frozen language model's use of combined image and text inputs.

title: Improving Context Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models via Multimodal Composition Learning

abstract: Autoregressive decoding makes the inference of Large Language Models (LLMs) time-consuming. In this paper, we reconsider speculative sampling and derive two key observations. Firstly, autoregression at the feature (second-to-top-layer) level is more straightforward than at the token level. Secondly, the inherent uncertainty in feature (second-to-top-layer) level autoregression constrains its performance. Based on these insights, we introduce EAGLE (Extrapolation Algorithm for Greater Language-model Efficiency), a simple yet highly efficient speculative sampling framework. By incorporating a token sequence advanced by one time step, EAGLE effectively resolves the uncertainty, enabling precise second-to-top-layer feature prediction with minimal overhead. We conducted comprehensive evaluations of EAGLE, including all models from the Vicuna and LLaMA2-Chat series, the MoE model Mixtral 8x7B Instruct, and tasks in dialogue, code generation, mathematical reasoning, and instruction following. For LLaMA2-Chat 70B, EAGLE achieved a latency speedup ratio of 2.7x-3.5x, doubled throughput, while maintaining the distribution of the generated text.

paragraphs: Generating text autoregressively makes large language model inference time-consuming because generation proceeds sequentially. EAGLE revisits speculative sampling through two observations: predicting the model’s second-to-top-layer features is more straightforward than predicting tokens directly, but uncertainty in those feature predictions limits the benefit. The paper makes that uncertainty a central design concern.

EAGLE incorporates a token sequence shifted one time step ahead into feature prediction. According to the paper, this resolves the relevant uncertainty and enables accurate prediction of second-to-top-layer features with little additional overhead. The approach matters because moving prediction into an internal feature space is useful only if the uncertainty in that space can also be handled effectively.

The evaluation spans the Vicuna and LLaMA2-Chat model series, Mixtral 8x7B Instruct, and dialogue, code generation, mathematical reasoning, and instruction-following tasks. For LLaMA2-Chat 70B, the reported latency speedup is 2.7–3.5 times, with twice the throughput. These improvements preserve the distribution of generated text, making the stated result an acceleration of sampling without changing that distribution.
summary.tldr: EAGLE resolves uncertainty in internal feature prediction to accelerate language-model sampling while preserving the generated-text distribution.

title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty

abstract: The inverse reinforcement learning approach to imitation learning is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, it can enable learning from a smaller number of expert demonstrations with more robustness to error compounding than behavioral cloning approaches. On the other hand, it requires that the learner repeatedly solve a computationally expensive reinforcement learning (RL) problem. Often, much of this computation is wasted searching over policies very dissimilar to the expert’s. In this work, we propose using hybrid RL – training on a mixture of online and expert data – to curtail unnecessary exploration. Intuitively, the expert data focuses the learner on good states during training, which reduces the amount of exploration required to compute a strong policy. Notably, such an approach doesn’t need the ability to reset the learner to arbitrary states in the environment, a requirement of prior work in efficient inverse RL. More formally, we derive a reduction from inverse RL to expert-competitive RL (rather than globally optimal RL) that allows us to dramatically reduce interaction during the inner policy search loop while maintaining the benefits of the IRL approach. This allows us to derive both model-free and model-based hybrid inverse RL algorithms with strong policy performance guarantees. Empirically, we find that our approaches are significantly more sample efficient than standard inverse RL and several other baselines on a suite of continuous control tasks.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning can imitate an expert using fewer demonstrations and with greater resistance to compounding errors than behavioral cloning. Its cost is repeatedly solving an expensive reinforcement learning problem. Much of that effort can go toward policies far from the expert's behavior, making the inner policy search unnecessarily demanding.

This paper uses hybrid reinforcement learning, combining online experience with expert data, to focus that search. Expert examples direct learning toward good states and reduce the exploration needed to obtain a strong policy. The method does not require resetting the learner to arbitrary environment states. Formally, the authors reduce inverse reinforcement learning to finding an expert-competitive policy rather than a globally optimal one.

That reduction supports both model-free and model-based hybrid algorithms with policy performance guarantees while reducing interaction in the inner search loop. On a suite of continuous control tasks, the approaches are substantially more sample efficient than standard inverse reinforcement learning and several other baselines. The results support using expert data throughout policy search to preserve imitation benefits with less exploration.
summary.tldr: Hybrid inverse reinforcement learning combines expert data and online experience to reduce exploration while retaining policy performance guarantees.

title: Hybrid Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Graphs with heterophily have been regarded as challenging scenarios for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), where nodes are connected with dissimilar neighbors through various patterns. In this paper, we present theoretical understandings of heterophily for GNNs by incorporating the graph convolution (GC) operations into fully connected networks via the proposed Heterophilous Stochastic Block Models (HSBM), a general random graph model that can accommodate diverse heterophily patterns. Our theoretical investigation comprehensively analyze the impact of heterophily from three critical aspects. Firstly, for the impact of different heterophily patterns, we show that the separability gains are determined by two factors, i.e., the Euclidean distance of the neighborhood distributions and $\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{deg}\right]}$, where $\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{deg}\right]$ is the averaged node degree. Secondly, we show that the neighborhood inconsistency has a detrimental impact on separability, which is similar to degrading $\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{deg}\right]$ by a specific factor. Finally, for the impact of stacking multiple layers, we show that the separability gains are determined by the normalized distance of the $l$-powered neighborhood distributions, indicating that nodes still possess separability in various regimes, even when over-smoothing occurs. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world data verify the effectiveness of our theory.

paragraphs: Heterophilous graphs connect nodes to dissimilar neighbors, but that description covers many different connection patterns. This paper develops a random graph model that accommodates those patterns and uses it to analyze graph convolution within fully connected networks. The central question is how the connections affect the ability to separate nodes.

The analysis identifies two factors governing separability gains: the Euclidean distance between neighborhood distributions and the square root of average node degree. It also shows that inconsistent neighborhoods reduce separability, with an effect comparable to lowering the effective average degree. Thus, the arrangement and consistency of neighbors matter alongside the number of connections.

For multiple layers, separability gains depend on normalized distances between neighborhood distributions propagated through the corresponding number of steps. This yields regimes where nodes remain separable even when oversmoothing occurs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the theory. The findings give a more specific explanation of heterophily than treating all connections between dissimilar nodes as equally problematic for graph neural networks.
summary.tldr: A theoretical model explains how neighborhood patterns, degree, inconsistency, and depth determine node separability in heterophilous graph neural networks.

title: Understanding Heterophily for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Recent advances in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have initiated a new era in repository-level code completion. However, the invariable use of retrieval in existing methods exposes issues in both efficiency and robustness, with a large proportion of the retrieved contexts proving unhelpful or harmful to code language models (code LMs). In this paper, we propose a selective RAG framework to avoid retrieval when unnecessary. To power this framework, we design a self-supervised learning approach to enable a code LM to accurately self-evaluate whether retrieval can improve its output quality and robustly leverage the potentially noisy retrieved contexts. Using this LM as both the selective RAG policy and the generation model, our framework achieves state-of-the-art repository-level code completion performance on diverse benchmarks including RepoEval, CrossCodeEval, and CrossCodeLongEval, a new long-form code completion benchmark. Meanwhile, our analyses show that selectively retrieving brings as much as 70% inference speedup in the online serving setting without harming the performance. We further demonstrate that our framework is able to accommodate different generation models, retrievers, and programming languages. These advancements position our framework as an important step towards more accurate and efficient repository-level code completion.

The paper finds that a large share of retrieved material can be unhelpful or harmful to code language models. Always retrieving therefore creates both an efficiency problem and a challenge in handling distracting context.

Repoformer introduces selective retrieval, with the code model deciding whether additional context is likely to improve its output. A self-supervised training approach teaches this self-evaluation and helps the model use potentially noisy retrieved information. Online-serving analyses show up to 70% inference speedup without performance loss in the evaluated settings. The results support learning when context is useful as a way to improve both completion quality and serving efficiency.
summary.tldr: Repoformer learns when retrieval will help code completion, achieving strong benchmark results and up to 70% reported inference speedup.

title: Repoformer: Selective Retrieval for Repository-Level Code Completion

abstract: Transformers have empowered many milestones across various fields and have recently been applied to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). However, since PDEs are typically discretized into large-scale meshes with complex geometries, it is challenging for Transformers to capture intricate physical correlations directly from massive individual points. Going beyond superficial and unwieldy meshes, we present Transolver based on a more foundational idea, which is learning intrinsic physical states hidden behind discretized geometries. Specifically, we propose a new Physics-Attention to adaptively split the discretized domain into a series of learnable slices of flexible shapes, where mesh points under similar physical states will be ascribed to the same slice. By calculating attention to physics-aware tokens encoded from slices, Transovler can effectively capture intricate physical correlations under complex geometrics, which also empowers the solver with endogenetic geometry-general modeling capacity and can be efficiently computed in linear complexity. Transolver achieves consistent state-of-the-art with 22% relative gain across six standard benchmarks and also excels in large-scale industrial simulations, including car and airfoil designs. Code is available at https://github.com/thuml/Transolver.

paragraphs: Partial differential equations are often represented on large meshes with complex geometry. Applying Transformers directly to their many individual points makes physical relationships difficult to capture efficiently. Transolver instead learns representations of the physical states underlying those points, using them to organize the computation.

Its Physics-Attention mechanism adaptively divides the discretized domain into learnable slices with flexible shapes. Points with similar physical states are assigned to the same slice, and each slice is encoded into a physics-aware token. Attention operates on these tokens to capture relationships across the domain. This construction supports modeling across general geometries and can be computed with linear complexity.

The paper reports consistent state-of-the-art performance and a 22% relative gain across six standard benchmarks. These findings support grouping mesh points by learned physical state as a useful way to combine computational efficiency with the ability to represent intricate physical correlations on complex domains.

title: Transolver: A Fast Transformer Solver for PDEs on General Geometries

abstract: A key challenge in contrastive learning is to generate negative samples from a large sample set to contrast with positive samples, for learning better encoding of the data. These negative samples often follow a softmax distribution which are dynamically updated during the training process. However, sampling from this distribution is non-trivial due to the high computational costs in computing the partition function. In this paper, we propose an $\underline{\text{E}}$fficient $\underline{\text{M}}$arkov $\underline{\text{C}}$hain Monte Carlo negative sampling method for $\underline{\text{C}}$ontrastive learning (EMC$^2$). We follow the global contrastive learning loss as introduced in SogCLR, and propose EMC$^2$ which utilizes an adaptive Metropolis-Hastings subroutine to generate hardness-aware negative samples in an online fashion during the optimization. We prove that EMC$^2$ finds an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$-stationary point of the global contrastive loss in $T$ iterations. Compared to prior works, EMC$^2$ is the first algorithm that exhibits global convergence (to stationarity) regardless of the choice of batch size while exhibiting low computation and memory cost. Numerical experiments validate that EMC$^2$ is effective with small batch training and achieves comparable or better performance than baseline algorithms. We report the results for pre-training image encoders on STL-10 and Imagenet-100.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning improves representations by comparing positive examples with negative ones. Choosing negatives from a large collection becomes costly when the desired sampling distribution changes during training. In particular, a softmax distribution requires a normalization term whose computation can make sampling expensive.

EMC² uses an adaptive Metropolis-Hastings procedure to generate negatives during optimization. These samples account for how difficult the negatives are for the current model. The method targets the global contrastive objective introduced in SogCLR, pairing that objective with a sampling procedure designed to keep computation and memory costs low.

The contribution joins a batch-size-independent stationarity guarantee with practical negative sampling.
summary.tldr: EMC² efficiently samples difficult contrastive negatives and proves convergence to stationarity regardless of batch size.

title: EMC$^2$: Efficient MCMC Negative Sampling for Contrastive Learning with Global Convergence

abstract: As privacy concerns escalate in the realm of machine learning, data owners now have the option to utilize machine unlearning to remove their data from machine learning models, following recent legislation. To enhance transparency in machine unlearning and avoid potential dishonesty by model providers, various verification strategies have been proposed. These strategies enable data owners to ascertain whether their target data has been effectively unlearned from the model. However, our understanding of the safety issues of machine unlearning verification remains nascent. In this paper, we explore the novel research question of whether model providers can circumvent verification strategies while retaining the information of data supposedly unlearned. Our investigation leads to a pessimistic answer: the verification of machine unlearning is fragile. Specifically, we categorize the current verification strategies regarding potential dishonesty among model providers into two types. Subsequently, we introduce two novel adversarial unlearning processes capable of circumventing both types. We validate the efficacy of our methods through theoretical analysis and empirical experiments using real-world datasets. This study highlights the vulnerabilities and limitations in machine unlearning verification, paving the way for further research into the safety of machine unlearning.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specified data from a trained model. Verification methods give data owners a way to check whether a provider has actually carried out that removal. This paper asks whether a dishonest provider can pass such checks while retaining information from the data it claims to have unlearned.

The authors organize current verification strategies into two categories according to the potential dishonesty they address. They then introduce two adversarial unlearning processes capable of circumventing both categories. The central concern is the gap between producing evidence that satisfies a verification procedure and actually removing the information targeted by the request.

Theoretical analysis and experiments on real-world datasets support the effectiveness of these processes. The results expose vulnerabilities in the verification strategies studied and show why a successful check can be misleading under adversarial provider behavior. The contribution is an examination of verification fragility, establishing concrete failure modes that further work on trustworthy unlearning needs to address.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that adversarial unlearning processes can pass existing verification strategies while retaining information supposedly removed.

title: Verification of Machine Unlearning is Fragile

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide excellent text-generation capabilities, but standard prompting and generation methods generally do not lead to intentional or goal-directed agents and might necessitate considerable prompt tuning. Even the best current LLMs rarely ask clarifying questions, engage in explicit information gathering, or take actions that lead to better decisions after multiple turns. Reinforcement learning has the potential to leverage the powerful modeling capabilities of LLMs, as well as their internal representation of textual interactions, to create capable goal-directed language agents. This can enable intentional and temporally extended interactions, such as with humans, the emergence of complex skills such as persuasion, and long-horizon strategic behavior, such as in the context of games. Enabling this requires the community to develop reliable reinforcement learning algorithms for training LLMs. Developing such algorithms requires tasks that can gauge progress on algorithm design, provide accessible and reproducible evaluations for multi-turn interactions, and cover a range of task properties and challenges in improving reinforcement learning algorithms. Our paper introduces the LMRL-Gym benchmark for evaluating multi-turn RL for LLMs, together with an open-source research framework for getting started on multi-turn RL with offline value-based and online policy-based RL methods. Our benchmark consists of 3 Interactive Dialogue tasks and 5 RL Capability tests for a total of 8 tasks, which require multiple rounds of language interaction and cover a range of tasks in open-ended dialogue and text games.

paragraphs: Fluent text generation does not by itself produce an agent that pursues goals across multiple interactions. The paper highlights behaviors such as asking clarifying questions, gathering information, and choosing actions that improve later decisions. Reinforcement learning offers a route toward such behavior, but developing reliable methods requires accessible tasks that evaluate progress over multiple turns.

LMRL Gym provides a benchmark and an open-source research framework for that purpose. The benchmark contains eight tasks: three interactive dialogue tasks and five reinforcement learning capability tests. These span open-ended dialogue and text games, requiring repeated language interaction and covering different properties relevant to training goal-directed agents.

The accompanying framework supports offline value-based and online policy-based reinforcement learning methods. This gives researchers infrastructure for beginning experiments as well as shared evaluation tasks. The contribution is a foundation for studying intentional, temporally extended language behavior. It makes multi-turn decision-making the object of evaluation, so algorithm development can address how an interaction unfolds and whether earlier actions help achieve later goals.
summary.tldr: LMRL Gym supplies eight multi-turn language tasks and a research framework for developing and evaluating reinforcement-learning-based language agents.

title: LMRL Gym: Benchmarks for Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning with Language Models

abstract: Natural gradient methods for PINNs have achieved state-of-the-art performance with errors several orders of magnitude smaller than those achieved by standard optimizers such as ADAM or L-BFGS. However, computing natural gradients for PINNs is prohibitively computationally costly and memory-intensive for all but small neural network architectures. We develop a randomized algorithm for natural gradient descent for PINNs that uses sketching to approximate the natural gradient descent direction. We prove that the change of coordinate Gram matrix used in a natural gradient descent update has rapidly-decaying eigenvalues for a one-layer, one-dimensional neural network and empirically demonstrate that this structure holds for four different example problems. Under this structure, our sketching algorithm is guaranteed to provide a near-optimal low-rank approximation of the Gramian. Our algorithm dramatically speeds up computation time and reduces memory overhead. Additionally, in our experiments, the sketched natural gradient outperforms the original natural gradient in terms of accuracy, often achieving an error that is an order of magnitude smaller. Training time for a network with around 5,000 parameters is reduced from several hours to under two minutes. Training can be practically scaled to large network sizes; we optimize a PINN for a network with over a million parameters within a few minutes, a task for which the full Gram matrix does not fit in memory.

paragraphs: Natural gradients can train physics-informed neural networks with much smaller errors than standard optimizers, but their computational and memory requirements restrict practical model sizes. This paper develops a randomized sketching method that approximates the natural-gradient direction through a smaller representation of the matrix used in the update.

The justification rests on rapidly decaying eigenvalues in the change-of-coordinate Gram matrix. The authors prove this structure for a one-layer, one-dimensional network and observe it empirically in four example problems. Under that structure, their method guarantees a near-optimal low-rank approximation. The scope of the proof and the broader empirical evidence are distinct parts of the argument.

Experiments show large reductions in time and memory, together with accuracy improvements over the original natural gradient that often reach an order of magnitude. Training a network of about 5,000 parameters falls from several hours to under two minutes. A network exceeding one million parameters is optimized within a few minutes, despite its full Gram matrix being too large to fit in memory.
summary.tldr: Randomized sketching makes natural-gradient training of physics-informed networks much faster and smaller in memory, with improved experimental accuracy.

title: Near-optimal Sketchy Natural Gradients for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) solutions with central Differential Privacy (DP) have seen large improvements in their utility in recent years arising from the matrix mechanism, while FL solutions with distributed (more private) DP have lagged behind. In this work, we introduce the distributed matrix mechanism to achieve the best-of-both-worlds; better privacy of distributed DP and better utility from the matrix mechanism. We accomplish this using a novel cryptographic protocol that securely transfers sensitive values across client committees of different training iterations with constant communication overhead. This protocol accommodates the dynamic participation of users required by FL, including those that may drop out from the computation. We provide experiments which show that our mechanism indeed significantly improves the utility of FL models compared to previous distributed DP mechanisms, with little added overhead.

paragraphs: Federated learning systems must balance useful models with protection for participating users. The abstract identifies a gap between two privacy settings: central differential privacy has benefited from the matrix mechanism, while distributed differential privacy offers stronger privacy protection but has lagged in model utility. DMM aims to bring these advantages together.

The main technical contribution is a cryptographic protocol that securely transfers sensitive values between client committees across training iterations. This transfer has constant communication overhead. It also accommodates changing participation and clients that drop out, both of which are practical concerns when training depends on many separate users rather than a permanently available group.

This protocol enables a distributed version of the matrix mechanism. Experiments show substantially improved model utility compared with earlier distributed differential privacy mechanisms, with little additional overhead. The significance is that the utility gains associated with the matrix mechanism can be made available in a distributed privacy setting while accounting for the participation patterns required by federated learning.
summary.tldr: DMM brings matrix-mechanism utility gains to distributed private federated learning through efficient secret transfers between changing client committees.

title: DMM: Distributed Matrix Mechanism for Differentially-Private Federated Learning Based on Constant-Overhead Linear Secret Resharing

abstract: Learning the site-specific distribution of the wireless channel within a particular environment of interest is essential to exploit the full potential of machine learning (ML) for wireless communications and radar applications. Generative modeling offers a promising framework to address this problem. However, existing approaches pose unresolved challenges, including the need for high-quality training data, limited generalizability, and a lack of physical interpretability. To address these issues, we combine the physics-related compressibility of wireless channels with generative modeling, in particular, sparse Bayesian generative modeling (SBGM), to learn the distribution of the underlying physical channel parameters. By leveraging the sparsity-inducing characteristics of SBGM, our methods can learn from compressed observations received by an access point (AP) during default online operation. Moreover, they are physically interpretable and generalize over system configurations without requiring retraining.
