paragraphs: Wireless communication and radar applications benefit from knowing how a channel varies within a particular environment. Generative modeling offers a way to learn this distribution, but existing approaches face difficulties with training-data quality, generalization, and physical interpretation. This paper incorporates channel physics into the generative model to address those issues.

The approach combines the physical compressibility of wireless channels with sparse Bayesian generative modeling. It learns a distribution over underlying physical channel parameters. The model's preference for sparse representations allows learning from compressed observations that an access point receives during its ordinary online operation, connecting the learning procedure to measurements already available in the system.

The resulting models are physically interpretable and can generalize across system configurations without retraining. This connects the representation being learned to properties of the channel, rather than tying it only to one configuration's measurements. The claimed generalization concerns changes in system configuration; the learning objective itself remains the channel distribution associated with an environment of interest.
summary.tldr: Sparse Bayesian generative models learn interpretable wireless-channel distributions from ordinary compressed observations and transfer across system configurations without retraining.

title: Physics-Informed Generative Modeling of Wireless Channels

abstract: Methods with adaptive stepsizes, such as AdaGrad and Adam, are essential for training modern Deep Learning models, especially Large Language Models. Typically, the noise in the stochastic gradients is heavy-tailed for the later ones. Gradient clipping provably helps to achieve good high-probability convergence for such noises. However, despite the similarity between AdaGrad/Adam and Clip-SGD, the current understanding of the high-probability convergence of AdaGrad/Adam-type methods is limited in this case. In this work, we prove that AdaGrad/Adam (and their delayed version) can have provably bad high-probability convergence if the noise is heavy-tailed. We also show that gradient clipping fixes this issue, i.e., we derive new high-probability convergence bounds with polylogarithmic dependence on the confidence level for AdaGrad-Norm and Adam-Norm with clipping and with/without delay for smooth convex/non-convex stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed noise. We extend our results to the case of AdaGrad/Adam with delayed stepsizes. Our empirical evaluations highlight the superiority of clipped versions of AdaGrad/Adam in handling the heavy-tailed noise.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers change their step sizes using gradient information. When stochastic gradients have heavy-tailed noise, unusually large disturbances can make reliable convergence difficult. The paper studies high-probability guarantees, which concern how confidently an optimizer’s convergence can be bounded rather than only its average behavior.

The authors prove that AdaGrad and Adam, including delayed versions, can have poor high-probability convergence under heavy-tailed noise. They then derive improved guarantees for clipped AdaGrad-Norm and Adam-Norm, with and without delay, in smooth convex and non-convex stochastic optimization. The bounds have polylogarithmic dependence on the confidence level. They also extend results to AdaGrad and Adam with delayed step sizes.

Empirical evaluations favor clipped versions when handling heavy-tailed noise. Together, the theory and experiments explain why adaptive step sizes alone may leave an optimizer vulnerable to extreme gradient disturbances, and why clipping can help. The negative result establishes that poor behavior is possible in the studied setting; it does not say every use of unclipped Adam or AdaGrad must fail.
summary.tldr: Gradient clipping improves high-probability convergence guarantees for adaptive optimizers facing heavy-tailed gradient noise.

title: Clipping Improves Adam-Norm and AdaGrad-Norm when the Noise Is Heavy-Tailed

abstract: We introduce $\texttt{TimeMCL}$, a method leveraging the Multiple Choice Learning (MCL) paradigm to forecast multiple plausible time series futures. Our approach employs a neural network with multiple heads and utilizes the Winner-Takes-All (WTA) loss to promote diversity among predictions. MCL has recently gained attention due to its simplicity and ability to address ill-posed and ambiguous tasks. We propose an adaptation of this framework for time-series forecasting, presenting it as an efficient method to predict diverse futures, which we relate to its implicit quantization objective. We provide insights into our approach using synthetic data and evaluate it on real-world time series, demonstrating its promising performance at a light computational cost.

MCL has recently gained attention due to its simplicity and ability to address ill-posed and ambiguous tasks. We propose an adaptation of this framework for time-series forecasting, presenting it as an efficient method to predict diverse futures, which we relate to its implicit quantization objective. We provide insights into our approach using synthetic data and evaluate it on real-world time series, demonstrating its promising performance at a light computational cost.

paragraphs: A time series can have several plausible futures, so forecasting benefits from representing alternatives. TimeMCL adapts Multiple Choice Learning to this task. It uses a neural network with several prediction heads, allowing one model to produce multiple candidate futures for multivariate time series.

Training uses a Winner-Takes-All loss to encourage diversity among the predictions. The authors connect this behavior to an implicit quantization objective: the collection of predictions represents different possible futures through a finite set of alternatives. This perspective helps explain why a multiple-head system can address ambiguity while retaining a relatively simple learning setup.

The paper uses synthetic data to investigate the approach and evaluates it on real-world time series. The reported results show promising forecasting performance at a light computational cost. The contribution is both methodological and explanatory: it adapts Multiple Choice Learning to forecasting and relates the diversity of its outputs to the objective the model implicitly pursues. The findings support an efficient approach to producing several plausible forecasts.
summary.tldr: TimeMCL uses multiple prediction heads and a Winner-Takes-All loss to forecast diverse plausible futures with light computational cost.

title: Winner-takes-all for Multivariate Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Many existing evaluation benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) quickly become outdated due to the emergence of new models and training data. These benchmarks also fall short in assessing how LLM performance changes over time, as they consist of a static set of questions without a temporal dimension. To address these limitations, we propose using future event prediction as a continuous evaluation method to assess LLMs’ temporal generalization and forecasting abilities. Our benchmark, Daily Oracle, automatically generates question-answer (QA) pairs from daily news, challenging LLMs to predict "future" event outcomes. Our findings reveal that as pre-training data becomes outdated, LLM performance degrades over time. While Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has the potential to enhance prediction accuracy, the performance degradation pattern persists, highlighting the need for continuous model updates. Code and data are available at https://agenticlearning.ai/daily-oracle.

These benchmarks also fall short in assessing how LLM performance changes over time, as they consist of a static set of questions without a temporal dimension. To address these limitations, we propose using future event prediction as a continuous evaluation method to assess LLMs’ temporal generalization and forecasting abilities. Our benchmark, Daily Oracle, automatically generates question-answer (QA) pairs from daily news, challenging LLMs to predict "future" event outcomes. Our findings reveal that as pre-training data becomes outdated, LLM performance degrades over time. While Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has the potential to enhance prediction accuracy, the performance degradation pattern persists, highlighting the need for continuous model updates. Code and data are available at https://agenticlearning.ai/daily-oracle.

It also gives little direct insight into how performance evolves as a model's knowledge ages. This paper proposes evaluating predictions of future events as an ongoing test of forecasting ability and generalization across time.

The authors introduce Daily Oracle, a benchmark that automatically turns daily news into question-and-answer pairs. Models are challenged to predict event outcomes, allowing evaluation to keep incorporating new material. The temporal aspect is central: it makes the age of a model's pre-training information relevant to the task being measured.

The reported findings show declining performance as pre-training data becomes outdated. Retrieval-augmented generation, which supplies retrieved information to a model, has the potential to improve prediction accuracy, but the observed degradation over time persists. The results therefore motivate continuous model updates alongside continuous evaluation. Daily Oracle contributes both a renewable source of evaluation questions and a way to observe forecasting performance as the distance from training data grows.
summary.tldr: Daily Oracle uses news-derived forecasting questions to track how language-model performance declines as pre-training information ages.

title: Are LLMs Prescient? A Continuous Evaluation using Daily News as the Oracle

abstract: A recent line of research has exploited pre-trained generative diffusion models as priors for solving Bayesian inverse problems. We contribute to this research direction by designing a sequential Monte Carlo method for linear-Gaussian inverse problems which builds on “decoupled diffusion", where the generative process is designed such that larger updates to the sample are possible. The method is asymptotically exact and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our Decoupled Diffusion Sequential Monte Carlo (DDSMC) algorithm on both synthetic as well as protein and image data. Further, we demonstrate how the approach can be extended to discrete data.

paragraphs: Bayesian inverse problems use observations to infer an underlying object while accounting for prior knowledge about plausible solutions. This paper builds on work that uses pretrained diffusion models to supply that prior. Its focus is linear-Gaussian inverse problems, giving the proposed inference method a specific mathematical setting.

The authors introduce Decoupled Diffusion Sequential Monte Carlo, or DDSMC. It combines a sequential Monte Carlo method with decoupled diffusion, whose generative process allows larger updates to a sample. The contribution connects that alternative diffusion process with Bayesian inference, using the pretrained generative model within a procedure for solving the inverse problem.

DDSMC is asymptotically exact, a convergence property rather than a claim of exact results from every finite computation. The authors demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic data and on protein and image data. They also show how the approach can be extended to discrete data. These findings establish both the method's stated inference property and examples of its use across multiple data types.
summary.tldr: DDSMC combines decoupled diffusion with sequential Monte Carlo for asymptotically exact inference in linear-Gaussian inverse problems.

title: Solving Linear-Gaussian Bayesian Inverse Problems with Decoupled Diffusion Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: We study the bidding problem in repeated uniform price multi-unit auctions from the perspective of a single value-maximizing buyer who aims to maximize their cumulative value over $T$ rounds while adhering to return-on-investment (RoI) constraints in each round. Buyers adopt $m$-uniform bidding format, where they submit $m$ bid-quantity pairs $(b_i, q_i)$ to demand $q_i$ units at bid $b_i$. We introduce safe bidding strategies as those that satisfy RoI constraints in every auction, regardless of competing bids. We show that these strategies depend only on the bidder’s valuation curve, and the bidder can focus on a finite subset of this class without loss of generality. While the number of strategies in this subset is exponential in $m$, we develop a polynomial-time algorithm to learn the optimal safe strategy that achieves sublinear regret in the online setting, where regret is measured against a clairvoyant benchmark that knows the competing bids a priori and selects a fixed hindsight optimal safe strategy. We then evaluate the performance of safe strategies against a clairvoyant that selects the optimal strategy from a richer class of strategies in the online setting. In this scenario, we compute the richness ratio, $\alpha\in(0, 1]$ for the class of strategies chosen by the clairvoyant and show that our algorithm, designed to learn safe strategies, achieves $\alpha$-approximate sublinear regret against these stronger benchmarks. Experiments on semi-synthetic data from real-world auctions show that safe strategies substantially outperform the derived theoretical bounds, making them quite appealing in practice.

A richness ratio α determines an approximate sublinear-regret guarantee in those comparisons, making the benchmark restriction explicit. summary.tldr: A polynomial-time learner finds safe auction-bidding strategies with regret guarantees while satisfying return-on-investment constraints in every round.

title: Learning Safe Strategies for Value Maximizing Buyers in Uniform Price Auctions

abstract: Federated ensemble distillation addresses client heterogeneity by generating pseudo-labels for an unlabeled server dataset based on client predictions and training the server model using the pseudo-labeled dataset. The unlabeled server dataset can either be pre-existing or generated through a data-free approach. The effectiveness of this approach critically depends on the method of assigning weights to client predictions when creating pseudo-labels, especially in highly heterogeneous settings. Inspired by theoretical results from GANs, we propose a provably near-optimal weighting method that leverages client discriminators trained with a server-distributed generator and local datasets. Our experiments on various image classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baselines. Furthermore, we show that the additional communication cost, client-side privacy leakage, and client-side computational overhead introduced by our method are negligible, both in scenarios with and without a pre-existing server dataset.

paragraphs: Federated ensemble distillation combines predictions from client models to label an unlabeled server dataset, then trains a server model on those pseudo-labels. When clients have very different data, the weights assigned to their predictions become especially important. A weighting rule determines how strongly each client influences the resulting training targets.

The paper proposes a weighting method inspired by theoretical results from generative adversarial networks. Clients train discriminators using their local datasets and a generator distributed by the server. Those discriminators supply the information used to weight client predictions. The authors provide a near-optimality guarantee for the proposed weighting approach.

Image-classification experiments show significant improvements over the compared baselines. The paper also reports negligible additional communication cost, client computation, and client-side privacy leakage. It considers both a pre-existing unlabeled server dataset and a data-free route for generating one. The contribution is a theoretically supported way to account for client heterogeneity while keeping the added operational burden small in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Client-trained discriminators provide a provably near-optimal weighting rule for federated distillation, improving reported accuracy with negligible added overhead.

title: Provably Near-Optimal Federated Ensemble Distillation with Negligible Overhead

abstract: We study the linear bandit problem that accounts for partially observable features. Without proper handling, unobserved features can lead to linear regret in the decision horizon $T$, as their influence on rewards is unknown. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel theoretical framework and an algorithm with sublinear regret guarantees. The core of our algorithm consists of (i) feature augmentation, by appending basis vectors that are orthogonal to the row space of the observed features; and (ii) the introduction of a doubly robust estimator. Our approach achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{(d + d_h)T})$, where $d$ is the dimension of the observed features and $d_h$ depends on the extent to which the unobserved feature space is contained in the observed one, thereby capturing the intrinsic difficulty of the problem. Notably, our algorithm requires no prior knowledge of the unobserved feature space, which may expand as more features become hidden. Numerical experiments confirm that our algorithm outperforms both non-contextual multi-armed bandits and linear bandit algorithms depending solely on observed features.

paragraphs: Linear bandit methods use features to guide repeated decisions, but some reward-relevant features may be hidden. Ignoring their influence can lead to regret that grows linearly with the number of decisions. This paper develops a framework and algorithm that account for partial feature observability and provide a sublinear regret guarantee.

The algorithm augments the observed features with basis vectors orthogonal to their row space and introduces a doubly robust estimator. The augmentation supplies additional representational directions beyond those covered by the observed features. The resulting method does not require prior knowledge of the unobserved feature space, including when that space expands as more features become hidden.

Its regret bound grows roughly as the square root of (d + d_h) times T, up to logarithmic factors. Here d counts observed-feature dimensions, while d_h captures how the hidden feature space relates to the observed one. The guarantee therefore reflects the problem's intrinsic hidden-feature difficulty. Numerical experiments report better performance than non-contextual bandits and linear bandit algorithms that rely only on observed features.
summary.tldr: Feature augmentation and a doubly robust estimator enable sublinear regret in linear bandits with partially hidden features.

title: Linear Bandits with Partially Observable Features

abstract: This paper proposes a novel analysis for the Scaffold algorithm, a popular method for dealing with data heterogeneity in federated learning. While its convergence in deterministic settings—where local control variates mitigate client drift—is well established, the impact of stochastic gradient updates on its performance is less understood. To address this problem, we first show that its global parameters and control variates define a Markov chain that converges to a stationary distribution in the Wasserstein distance. Leveraging this result, we prove that Scaffold achieves linear speed-up in the number of clients up to higher-order terms in the step size. Nevertheless, our analysis reveals that Scaffold retains a higher-order bias, similar to FedAvg, that does not decrease as the number of clients increases. This highlights opportunities for developing improved stochastic federated learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Scaffold addresses differences among clients’ datasets in federated learning by using control variates to counter client drift. Its deterministic convergence behavior is well understood, but stochastic gradient updates introduce additional randomness. This paper develops a new analysis of how that randomness affects the algorithm’s performance.

The authors show that the global model parameters and control variates together form a Markov chain that approaches a stationary distribution in Wasserstein distance. This provides a way to analyze the evolving random training state. Using that result, they prove linear speed-up with the number of clients, up to higher-order terms in the step size.

The qualification is consequential: the analysis also identifies a higher-order bias, similar to one in FedAvg, that does not shrink when more clients participate. Increasing client count therefore improves the leading behavior without removing this residual bias. The paper clarifies both the benefit of additional clients and a remaining obstacle in stochastic federated optimization, pointing toward algorithmic improvements beyond simply scaling participation.
summary.tldr: A new Scaffold analysis proves linear client speed-up up to higher-order step-size terms while identifying a bias that more clients do not remove.

title: Scaffold with Stochastic Gradients: New Analysis with Linear Speed-Up

abstract: We present several advances on neural operators by viewing the action of operator layers as the minimizers of Bregman regularized optimization problems over Banach function spaces. The proposed framework allows interpreting the activation operators as Bregman proximity operators from dual to primal space. This novel viewpoint is general enough to recover classical neural operators as well as a new variant, coined Bregman neural operators, which includes the inverse activation operator and features the same expressivity of standard neural operators. Numerical experiments support the added benefits of the Bregman variant of Fourier neural operators for training deeper and more accurate models.

paragraphs: The paper studies neural operators through an optimization perspective. It treats the action of an operator layer as the solution to a Bregman-regularized optimization problem over a space of functions. This gives the layer a mathematical interpretation in terms of what it minimizes, connecting its computation to the geometry used by that optimization problem.

Within this framework, activation operators become Bregman proximity operators that map from a dual space back to a primal space. The framework covers classical neural operators and also leads to a new family called Bregman neural operators. These incorporate the inverse activation operator while retaining the same expressivity as standard neural operators.

The authors test a Bregman version of Fourier neural operators numerically. Their experiments support benefits for training deeper models and obtaining greater accuracy. The contribution therefore combines a broader mathematical description of existing architectures with a concrete architectural variant. The stated advantage concerns training and observed accuracy, while expressive capacity remains equivalent to that of the standard operators.
summary.tldr: An optimization-based interpretation of neural operators leads to a Bregman variant with equal expressivity and experimentally supported benefits for depth and accuracy.

title: A Bregman Proximal Viewpoint on Neural Operators

abstract: Embedding tree-like data, from hierarchies to ontologies and taxonomies, forms a well-studied problem for representing knowledge across many domains. Hyperbolic geometry provides a natural solution for embedding trees, with vastly superior performance over Euclidean embeddings. Recent literature has shown that hyperbolic tree embeddings can even be placed on top of neural networks for hierarchical knowledge integration in deep learning settings. For all applications, a faithful embedding of trees is needed, with combinatorial constructions emerging as the most effective direction. This paper identifies and solves two key limitations of existing works. First, the combinatorial construction hinges on finding highly separated points on a hypersphere, a notoriously difficult problem. Current approaches achieve poor separation, degrading the quality of the corresponding hyperbolic embedding. We propose highly separated Delaunay tree embeddings (HS-DTE), which integrates angular separation in a generalized formulation of Delaunay embeddings, leading to lower embedding distortion. Second, low-distortion requires additional precision. The current approach for increasing precision is to use multiple precision arithmetic, which renders the embeddings useless on GPUs in deep learning settings. We reformulate the combinatorial construction using floating point expansion arithmetic, leading to superior embedding quality while retaining utility on accelerated hardware.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent trees, such as hierarchies and taxonomies, in hyperbolic space while preserving their structure faithfully. Such embeddings can also integrate hierarchical knowledge into neural networks. The authors identify two obstacles in existing combinatorial constructions: inadequate separation between points and the computational consequences of needing extra numerical precision.

The proposed highly separated Delaunay tree embeddings incorporate angular separation into a generalized Delaunay formulation, reducing distortion in the embedding.

The two contributions address fidelity and usability together: improved geometric placement supports faithful representations, and the arithmetic reformulation makes the required precision compatible with GPU computation.
summary.tldr: Improved angular separation and floating point expansion arithmetic produce lower-distortion hyperbolic tree embeddings that remain usable on GPUs.

title: Low-distortion and GPU-compatible Tree Embeddings in Hyperbolic Space

abstract: Machine Unlearning (MU) aims at removing the influence of specific data points from a trained model, striving to achieve this at a fraction of the cost of full model retraining. In this paper, we analyze the efficiency of unlearning methods and establish the first upper and lower bounds on minimax computation times for this problem, characterizing the performance of the most efficient algorithm against the most difficult objective function. Specifically, for strongly convex objective functions and under the assumption that the forget data is inaccessible to the unlearning method, we provide a phase diagram for the unlearning complexity ratio—a novel metric that compares the computational cost of the best unlearning method to full model retraining. The phase diagram reveals three distinct regimes: one where unlearning at a reduced cost is infeasible, another where unlearning is trivial because adding noise suffices, and a third where unlearning achieves significant computational advantages over retraining. These findings highlight the critical role of factors such as data dimensionality, the number of samples to forget, and privacy constraints in determining the practical feasibility of unlearning.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks to remove selected training examples’ influence more cheaply than retraining a model. This paper studies when that computational advantage is possible. It establishes upper and lower bounds on minimax computation time, comparing the best available algorithm against the most difficult objective within the problem setting.

The analysis concerns strongly convex objectives and assumes that the unlearning method cannot access the data to be forgotten. The authors introduce an unlearning complexity ratio comparing the computational cost of the best unlearning method with full retraining. A phase diagram organizes how this ratio changes across the analyzed conditions.

The diagram has three regimes: reduced-cost unlearning is infeasible, adding noise alone suffices, or unlearning offers substantial computational savings. Data dimension, the number of examples to forget, and privacy constraints help determine the regime. The result makes clear that efficient removal depends on the problem’s parameters, with the conclusions grounded in the stated objective class and lack of access to forgotten data.
summary.tldr: For strongly convex objectives without access to forgotten data, the paper identifies when unlearning is cheaper than retraining, trivial through noise, or computationally infeasible at reduced cost.

title: When to Forget? Complexity Trade-offs in Machine Unlearning

abstract: In this paper, we theoretically investigate the effects of noisy labels in offline alignment, with a focus on the interplay between privacy and robustness against adversarial corruption. Specifically, under linear modeling assumptions, we present a unified analysis covering both reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and direct preference optimization (DPO) under different privacy-corruption scenarios, such as Local differential privacy-then-Corruption (LTC), where human preference labels are privatized before being corrupted by an adversary, and Corruption-then-Local differential privacy (CTL), where labels are corrupted before privacy protection. Our analysis leverages a reduction framework that reduces the offline alignment problem under linear modeling assumptions to parameter estimation in logistic regression. This framework allows us to establish an interesting separation result between LTC and CTL, demonstrating that LTC presents a greater challenge than CTL in offline alignment, even under linear models. As important by-products, our findings also advance the state-of-the-art theoretical results in offline alignment under privacy-only or corruption-only scenarios.

paragraphs: Offline alignment learns from previously collected human preferences, but those labels may be altered both by privacy protection and by an adversary. This paper investigates how these two sources of noise interact. Its theoretical framework covers reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization under linear modeling assumptions, allowing both alignment approaches to be studied through a shared statistical problem.

The authors distinguish two sequences of events. In Local differential privacy-then-Corruption, preference labels receive privacy protection before an adversary corrupts them. In Corruption-then-Local differential privacy, the adversary acts first. Their analysis reduces offline alignment under the stated linear assumptions to estimating parameters in logistic regression, making it possible to compare the difficulty of these settings within one framework.

The main separation result shows that privacy followed by corruption is harder than corruption followed by privacy, even for linear models. Thus, the ordering of the processes matters for alignment guarantees. The analysis also improves theoretical results for settings involving privacy alone or corruption alone, extending its contribution beyond their simultaneous presence.
summary.tldr: Under linear modeling assumptions, a unified analysis shows that privatizing preference labels before adversarial corruption makes offline alignment harder than reversing that order.

title: A Unified Theoretical Analysis of Private and Robust Offline Alignment: from RLHF to DPO

abstract: Consumer protection laws are designed to protect consumers from unethical business practices. In this position paper, I argue that these laws serve an emergent dual purpose: if appropriately enforced and strengthened, consumer protection laws can serve as an inalienable defense for AI safety. These laws are well established and can be enforced and strengthened to incentivize businesses to design and deploy safer AI systems. This position runs counter to two prevailing trends in AI policy. The first alternative position is that AI safety requires an entirely new set of focused laws to protect humanity's prosperity. Though I find these efforts valuable, I argue that such focused laws are both hard to write and easy to skirt. The second alternative position is that consumer protection is nothing more than red tape; I argue that existing laws dating back many decades have already reigned in some nefarious business practices related to the development and deployment of AI, and that the litigious society of the United States is well-positioned to use consumer protection laws to encourage new AI safety guardrails. This paper takes a tour of some existing consumer protection laws in the United States and their effects on the development and use of AI systems. This paper also calls to enforce and preserve these laws in a rapidly changing, de-regulatory political landscape.

The proposed mechanism is conditional: with appropriate enforcement and strengthening, these laws can give businesses incentives to build and deploy safer systems. The author presents existing legal protections as resources that already address unethical commercial behavior.

The other treats consumer protection as mere bureaucracy. Against that view, the paper points to existing laws that have already constrained some harmful business practices connected to AI.

The paper surveys consumer-protection laws and their effects on AI development and use, then calls for their enforcement and preservation amid deregulation. It also argues that the United States' litigation-oriented environment is well placed to support this approach. The contribution is a policy case for using and strengthening established institutions as part of AI safety, rather than assuming safety requires only new legislation.
summary.tldr: The author argues that enforcing and strengthening existing U.S. consumer-protection laws can incentivize safer AI development and deployment.

title: Position: Strong Consumer Protection is an Inalienable Defense for AI Safety in the United States

abstract: Influence maximization is an important research area in social network analysis, where the goal is to select a small set of seed nodes so as to maximize the expected spread of influence under a stochastic diffusion process. Classical approximation algorithms for this problem rely on full knowledge of the underlying influence probabilities and operate in an offline manner. In many real-world settings, however, these probabilities are unknown and must be learned from data, raising the question: can one still obtain strong performance guarantees while simultaneously learning the diffusion model parameters through repeated interactions? In this paper, we study the problem of online influence maximization under the independent cascade model, where influence probabilities are unknown and feedback is limited to node-level activation outcomes. Prior work relies on a pair oracle which needs to perform a joint optimization over seed sets and feasible parameters. This oracle is difficult to implement in practice and it was open whether one can achieve sublinear regret using only a standard offline oracle. We resolve this question by designing an online learning algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret using only a standard offline oracle. Finally, we validate our theoretical results via experiments on real and synthetic data.

We resolve this question by designing an online learning algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret using only a standard offline oracle. Finally, we validate our theoretical results via experiments on real and synthetic data.

paragraphs: Influence maximization asks which small set of starting nodes will produce the largest expected spread through a network. Classical algorithms assume that influence probabilities are already known. This paper studies the online version, where a learner must repeatedly choose starting nodes while learning unknown probabilities under the independent cascade model.

The available feedback reveals which nodes activate. Earlier work relies on a pair oracle that jointly optimizes the chosen seeds and feasible model parameters, a demanding computational requirement. The authors instead design an algorithm that uses a standard offline oracle, resolving whether this simpler oracle can support sublinear regret in the stated setting.

Their regret bound grows roughly with the square root of the number of interactions, apart from logarithmic factors. Sublinear growth means the regret per interaction decreases as interactions accumulate. Experiments on real and synthetic data support the theoretical results. The main contribution is therefore a learning guarantee under limited feedback with a more practical oracle requirement.
summary.tldr: An online influence-maximization algorithm achieves roughly square-root regret with node-level feedback using only a standard offline oracle.

title: Efficient Online Influence Maximization under the Independent Cascade Model with Node-Level Feedback

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong empirical gains as self-evolving agents for CUDA kernel generation, driven by feedback-conditioned planning across generations. However, how planning decisions attribute and combine heterogeneous feedback signals remains opaque. Standard end-to-end ablations fail to resolve this question, as iterative planning amplifies early perturbations and conflates feedback effects with trajectory-dependent drift. We introduce CUDAnalyst, a unified analysis layer for controlled, generation-level attribution of planning decisions to feedback components via trajectory freezing and selective feedback injection. CUDAnalyst enables stable generation-level evaluation and principled coalitional-style attribution of feedback effects and interactions. Our results show that explicit planning is beneficial only when feedback is aligned, that effective planning emerges from structured multi-feedback interactions, and that high-level plans from stronger reasoning models can partially transfer to weaker ones. These trends hold across reference backbones, representative workloads, and reference induction regimes, indicating that the identified feedback-to-plan structure is robust within the controlled axes studied.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can iteratively improve CUDA kernels by planning from feedback, but it is difficult to determine which feedback actually drives their planning decisions. Removing a feedback source in an end-to-end experiment also changes later iterations. Those diverging trajectories can obscure the effect of the feedback component the experiment intended to isolate.

CUDAnalyst provides a controlled analysis layer that freezes trajectories and selectively injects feedback at individual generations. summary.tldr: CUDAnalyst isolates feedback effects in CUDA-generation agents, finding that useful planning depends on aligned feedback and structured interactions among signals.

title: Towards Feedback-to-Plan Decisions for Self-Evolving LLM Agents in CUDA Kernel Generation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as efficient annotators for tasks such as generation and classification. While these models offer significant cost and speed advantages over human annotation, a critical challenge remains: existing self-evaluation methods, such as LLM-as-judge, often lack reliable reference-based calibration for error detection. We address this limitation by introducing SAGE (Semantic-Anchored JudGmEnt), a method that leverages semantically similar samples retrieved via $k$-nearest-neighbor as references for annotation verification. We provide a theoretical framework that derives a closed-form expression for the error detection AUROC, which can be decomposed into three factors: intrinsic separability, reference-induced mean shift, and noise reduction through averaging. This decomposition reveals when semantic neighbors help (when references are both semantically matched and correct) and why (by providing reference-based calibration that raises scores for correct annotations and lowers scores for incorrect ones). Experiments on LLM generation, VLM captioning, and classification tasks validate our theoretical framework: SAGE improves error detection when semantic neighbors provide reliable reference-based calibration, and our decomposition offers insights into when direct scoring or alternative strategies may be preferred. Our code is available at https://github.com/dina-1205/SAGE.

paragraphs: AI-generated annotations are fast and inexpensive, but asking a model to judge them can leave its judgments without reliable reference points. SAGE addresses this by retrieving semantically similar samples with nearest-neighbor search and using them as references when checking an annotation. The paper studies both the method and the conditions under which these references help.

Its theoretical framework expresses error-detection AUROC through three factors: how distinguishable correct and incorrect annotations already are, how references shift their scores, and how averaging reduces noise. This decomposition explains the proposed calibration effect: suitable references can raise scores for correct annotations while lowering scores for incorrect ones.

The benefit is conditional on references being semantically matched and correct. Experiments involving language generation, image captioning, and classification support improved detection when neighbors provide reliable calibration. The analysis also helps identify circumstances where direct scoring or another strategy may be preferable. The contribution is therefore both a reference-based detector and an explanation of why retrieving similar examples is not automatically beneficial.
summary.tldr: SAGE improves annotation-error detection when retrieved neighbors are both semantically relevant and correct, with theory explaining that conditional benefit.

title: Detecting Errors in AI-Generated Annotations: When and Why Semantic Neighbors Help

abstract: Standard mixed-precision training of neural networks requires many bytes of accelerator memory for each model parameter. These bytes reflect not just the parameter itself, but also its gradient and one or more optimizer state variables. With each of these values typically requiring 4 bytes, training even a 7 billion parameter model can be impractical for researchers with less than 100 GiB of accelerator memory. We introduce FlashOptim, a suite of optimizations that reduces per-parameter memory by over 50% while preserving model quality and API compatibility. Our approach introduces two key techniques. First, we improve master weight splitting by finding and exploiting a tight bound on its quantization error. Second, we design companding functions that greatly reduce the error in 8-bit optimizer state quantization. Together with 16-bit gradients, these techniques reduce AdamW memory from 16 bytes to 7 bytes per parameter, or 5 bytes with gradient release. They also cut model checkpoint sizes by more than half. Experiments with FlashOptim applied to SGD, AdamW, and Lion show no measurable quality degradation across a collection of standard vision and language benchmarks, including Llama-3.1-8B finetuning.

In standard mixed-precision training, these stored values can make even a seven-billion-parameter model impractical below 100 GiB of accelerator memory. FlashOptim reduces this per-parameter storage while preserving the existing programming interface.

Second, it designs companding functions that reduce the error caused by storing optimizer states with eight bits. summary.tldr: FlashOptim more than halves per-parameter training memory through improved weight and optimizer-state compression, with no measurable quality loss in reported evaluations.

title: FlashOptim: Optimizers for Memory-Efficient Training

abstract: Explainability is essential for applying time series analysis in high-stakes domains. While Time Series Captioning (TSC) offers a pathway to enhance temporal explainability, achieving reliable caption generation usually necessitates high-quality textual annotations. However, as interpreting abstract temporal dynamics requires specialized domain knowledge, acquiring such caption annotations is challenging, thereby impeding the advancement of TSC. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel Caption Label-Free Learning (CLFL) paradigm. Departing from the supervised learning tradition of imitating human annotations, CLFL formulates captioning as an agentic exploration task optimized by feedback from a proxy reward. Specifically, we propose a Dual Loop Agentic Captioning (DLAC) framework to achieve such an exploration-feedback mechanism. In the inner loop, a Time Series Captioning Agent (TSCAgent) reflectively explores potential semantic captions. In turn, the outer loop evaluates these captions via downstream reasoning to derive proxy reward, which feeds back to optimize the TSCAgent. Empirical results validate the effectiveness of the CLFL, proving that the exploration-feedback mechanism is sufficient for learning complex temporal semantics and autonomously generating captions, without any caption label supervision. Furthermore, we release TFTSC, an industrial expert-level time series caption dataset, which is available at: https://github.com/chunhuiz/TFTSC/tree/master.

This paper introduces Caption Label-Free Learning to learn captioning without those annotations. It treats caption generation as exploration guided by a proxy reward, replacing direct imitation of human-written captions with feedback.

The Dual Loop Agentic Captioning framework separates proposal and evaluation. In the inner loop, a captioning agent reflectively explores possible semantic descriptions of the time series. In the outer loop, downstream reasoning evaluates those captions and produces a proxy reward, which feeds back into optimization of the captioning agent.

The authors also release TFTSC, an industrial expert-level time series caption dataset. Together, the framework and dataset advance the study of temporal explanations when high-quality textual training annotations are difficult to obtain.
summary.tldr: A dual-loop captioning agent learns time series descriptions from downstream reasoning feedback without caption-label supervision.

title: Words Towards Explainability: Caption Label-Free Learning via Dual Loop Agentic Time Series Captioning

abstract: Accurate prediction of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) chemical shifts is fundamental to spectral analysis and molecular structure elucidation, yet existing machine learning methods rely on limited, labor-intensive atom-assigned datasets. We propose a semi-supervised framework that learns NMR chemical shifts from millions of literature-extracted spectra without explicit atom-level assignments, integrating a small amount of labeled data with large-scale unassigned spectra. We formulate chemical shift prediction from literature spectra as a permutation-invariant set supervision problem, and show that under commonly satisfied conditions on the loss function, optimal bipartite matching reduces to a sorting-based loss, enabling stable large-scale semi-supervised training beyond traditional curated datasets. Our models achieve substantially improved accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art methods and exhibit stronger generalization on significantly larger and more diverse molecular datasets. Moreover, by incorporating solvent information at scale, our approach captures systematic solvent effects across common NMR solvents for the first time. Overall, our results demonstrate that large-scale unlabeled spectra mined from the literature can serve as a practical and effective data source for training NMR shift models, suggesting a broader role of literature-derived, weakly structured data in data-centric AI for science.

paragraphs: Training NMR chemical-shift predictors usually requires spectra whose measurements have been assigned to individual atoms, a labor-intensive source of labels. This paper develops a semi-supervised method that combines a small labeled collection with millions of literature-extracted spectra lacking those assignments. The goal is to make much larger spectral collections usable for learning.

The method treats supervision as comparison between sets, so the order of unassigned measurements does not determine the training target. Under commonly satisfied conditions on the loss, the authors show that optimal bipartite matching reduces to a sorting-based loss. This conditional result supplies a simpler route to stable training at the scale of the literature-derived data.

The resulting models improve accuracy and robustness over the reported state-of-the-art methods and generalize more strongly across larger, more diverse molecular datasets. Incorporating solvent information at scale also captures systematic effects across common NMR solvents. The findings demonstrate a practical way to learn from weakly structured scientific records while retaining a small amount of explicit atom-level supervision.
summary.tldr: Set-based semi-supervised learning turns millions of unassigned literature spectra into useful training data for more accurate NMR shift prediction.

title: From Human Labels to Literature: Semi-Supervised Learning of NMR Chemical Shifts at Scale

abstract: As LLMs are globally deployed, aligning their cultural value orientations is critical for safety and user engagement. However, existing benchmarks face the Construct-Composition-Context (C$^3$) challenge: relying on discriminative, multiple-choice formats that probe value knowledge rather than true orientations, overlook subcultural heterogeneity, and mismatch with real-world open-ended generation. We introduce DOVE, a distributional evaluation framework that directly compares human-written text distributions with LLM-generated outputs. DOVE utilizes a rate-distortion variational optimization objective to construct a compact value codebook from 10K documents, mapping text into a structured value space to filter semantic noise. Alignment is measured using unbalanced optimal transport, capturing intra-cultural distributional structures and subgroup diversity. Experiments across 12 LLMs show that DOVE achieves superior predictive validity, attaining a 31.56% correlation with downstream tasks, while maintaining high reliability with as few as 500 samples per culture.

paragraphs: Evaluating cultural value alignment requires accounting for both open-ended expression and differences within a culture. The authors argue that multiple-choice benchmarks can emphasize knowledge about values while overlooking these aspects. Their framework, DOVE, compares distributions of human-written text with distributions of model-generated text to evaluate how expressed value orientations align.

DOVE constructs a compact value codebook from 10,000 documents using a rate-distortion variational objective. This maps text into a structured space intended to retain value-related information while filtering semantic noise. It then measures alignment using unbalanced optimal transport, allowing the comparison to reflect distributional structure and subgroup diversity within cultures rather than reducing each culture to one representative position.

Experiments covering 12 LLMs report superior predictive validity, with a 31.56% correlation with downstream tasks, and high reliability using as few as 500 samples per culture. These findings support the usefulness of distributional evaluation for connecting cultural alignment measurements to downstream behavior. The reported correlation is an association with task outcomes, rather than a percentage of cultural values correctly reproduced.
summary.tldr: DOVE evaluates cultural value alignment by comparing human and LLM text distributions in a learned value space that preserves subgroup diversity.

title: Distributional Open-Ended Evaluation of LLM Cultural Value Alignment Based on Value Codebook

abstract: Heterogeneous multi-modal remote sensing object detection aims to accurately detect objects from diverse sensors (e.g., RGB, SAR, Infrared). Existing approaches largely adopt a late alignment paradigm, in which modality alignment and task-specific optimization are entangled during downstream fine-tuning. This tight coupling complicates optimization and often results in unstable training and suboptimal generalization. To address these limitations, we propose BabelRS, a unified language-pivoted pretraining framework that explicitly decouples modality alignment from downstream task learning. BabelRS comprises two key components: Concept-Shared Instruction Aligning (CSIA) and Layerwise Visual-Semantic Annealing (LVSA). CSIA aligns each sensor modality to a shared set of linguistic concepts, using language as a semantic pivot to bridge heterogeneous visual representations. To further mitigate the granularity mismatch between high-level language representations and dense detection objectives, LVSA progressively aggregates multi-scale visual features to provide fine-grained semantic guidance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BabelRS stabilizes training and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods without bells and whistles. Code: https://github.com/zcablii/SM3Det.

paragraphs: Remote-sensing object detection must work across sensors whose images differ substantially, including visible-light, radar, and infrared systems. Existing approaches often align those modalities while simultaneously learning the downstream detection task. BabelRS separates these stages, aiming to reduce the optimization difficulty caused by learning sensor correspondence and detection together.

Its Concept-Shared Instruction Aligning component maps each sensor modality to a common collection of linguistic concepts. Language provides a shared semantic reference for otherwise heterogeneous visual representations. A second component, Layerwise Visual-Semantic Annealing, progressively aggregates visual features at multiple scales to address the mismatch between broad language concepts and the fine-grained information required for detection.

Experiments report more stable training and consistent improvements over leading methods. The approach matters because its shared representation is established through language-guided pretraining before downstream task learning, while its multiscale mechanism preserves attention to detection detail. The findings support this separation of modality alignment and task optimization as an effective design for the evaluated remote-sensing systems.
summary.tldr: BabelRS aligns remote-sensing modalities through shared language concepts before detection training, improving stability and reported detection performance.

title: Unifying Heterogeneous Multi-Modal Remote Sensing Detection Via Language-Pivoted Pretraining

abstract: LiDAR-based 3D object detectors are fundamental to autonomous driving, where missed detections pose severe safety risks. While adversarial attacks are crucial for evaluating the robustness of these detectors, existing point-level perturbation methods rarely cause complete object disappearance and prove difficult to implement in physical environments. We introduce OBJVanish, a prompt-driven text-to-3D adversarial generation framework that enables physically realizable attacks by generating 3D object models that are effectively invisible to LiDAR-based 3D object detectors. We first conduct a systematic empirical study of detection vulnerability in LiDAR-based 3D object detectors, revealing multi-object compositions as the dominant factor. Based on this analysis, the proposed framework iteratively refines text prompts—optimizing verbs, objects, and poses—to generate LiDAR-invisible pedestrian instances as representative vulnerable road users under physical constraints. To ensure realizability, the framework operates over a curated pool of representative real-world 3D object models and restricts generation to their valid combinations. Extensive experiments show that OBJVanish consistently evades six state-of-the-art (SOTA) LiDAR-based 3D object detectors in both simulation and real-world physical settings, exposing critical vulnerabilities in safety-critical detection systems.

Existing attacks that perturb individual points often fail to make an entire object disappear from detection and can be difficult to realize physically. OBJVanish studies adversarial objects whose generated three-dimensional forms can be implemented in physical settings.

An initial empirical investigation identifies compositions of multiple objects as the dominant factor in the studied detection vulnerabilities. The results expose vulnerabilities associated with physically realizable object compositions and demonstrate their relevance beyond point-level perturbations tested only in simulation.
summary.tldr: OBJVanish generates physically realizable object compositions that evade LiDAR object detectors in simulated and real-world evaluations.

title: OBJVanish: Prompt-Driven Generation of Physically Realizable 3D LiDAR-Invisible Objects

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have progressed rapidly with large-scale high-quality data and adaptation strategies, yet remain brittle under real-world corruptions, where both visual recognition and language-grounded reasoning degrade. Beyond cascaded image restoration, a natural alternative is parameter-efficient adaptation that aligns corrupted features with clean references; however, Euclidean alignment alone is not semantics-preserving and can even harm downstream reasoning. We attribute this to a semantic misalignment gap, where features become geometrically closer while drifting off the in-distribution support on which multimodal reasoning is calibrated. To address this, we propose Manifold-Adversarial Adapters (MAA), parameter-efficient layer-wise modules for a frozen vision encoder that explicitly steer corrupted features back onto the clean in-distribution manifold rather than merely shrinking feature-space distance. MAA combines paired feature self-distillation with a token-level adversarial manifold constraint to prevent off-manifold semantic shortcuts. At inference, only the adapters are retained, enabling single-stage robustness with negligible overhead and avoiding the latency and semantic drift of restoration pipelines. Across benchmarks and corruption settings, MAA consistently improves performance over strong baselines.

paragraphs: Image corruption can weaken both visual recognition and language-based reasoning in vision-language models. One response is to make corrupted-image features numerically closer to clean-image features. This paper argues that distance alone is insufficient: features can move closer while still leaving the region of representations on which the model’s reasoning works reliably.

Manifold-Adversarial Adapters add small trainable modules throughout a frozen vision encoder. Their goal is to move corrupted features back toward the clean-data manifold, meaning the supported region of clean representations. Training combines paired feature self-distillation with a token-level adversarial constraint that discourages shortcuts outside that region. This couples feature matching with a constraint intended to preserve semantic usefulness.

At inference, only the adapters are retained, providing a single-stage approach with negligible reported overhead. Across the evaluated benchmarks and corruption settings, the method consistently improves performance over strong baselines. The contribution is a more structured target for robust adaptation: recovering representations suitable for downstream multimodal reasoning, while avoiding a separate image-restoration pipeline and its associated latency and semantic drift.
summary.tldr: Manifold-Adversarial Adapters improve corrupted-image robustness by steering features toward clean-data representations that support multimodal reasoning.

title: Robust Vision-Language Models via Manifold-Adversarial Adapters

abstract: Parameter sharing is a widely used technique in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) that enhances sample efficiency by equipping agents with a unified policy. While effective in homogeneous settings, it often struggles in heterogeneous environments where agents possess diverse capabilities. Conversely, learning customized policies for agents can resolve knowledge conflicts but significantly hinders knowledge transfer, thereby reducing learning efficiency. Existing approaches attempt to balance this trade-off using clustering or agent-specific masks, but they typically rely on strong environment-specific priors and struggle in settings where the team exhibits multi-modal policies. To address these limitations, we propose Dspic, an efficient shared-policy algorithm grounded in the maximum entropy framework. Specifically, Dspic employs self-supervised learning to extract discriminative role embeddings for each agent. These embeddings guide a complete division of the observation space, providing a theoretical guarantee for the optimality of parameter sharing. Furthermore, to handle the increased observation complexity and diversity resulting from this division, Dspic incorporates a diffusion policy, enhancing the capacity to model complex action distributions while enabling efficient learning. Extensive experiments on MaMuJoCo, SMAC, SMACv2, and LBF demonstrate that Dspic achieves superior sample efficiency while maintaining asymptotic optimality.

paragraphs: Sharing one policy across agents can improve learning efficiency, but agents with different capabilities may need different behaviors. Giving each agent an independent policy avoids some conflicts while weakening knowledge transfer. Dspic seeks to retain the benefits of sharing while accommodating heterogeneous roles and multiple possible patterns of coordinated action.

The method uses self-supervised learning to extract discriminative role embeddings. These embeddings guide a complete division of the observation space, for which the paper provides a theoretical guarantee concerning the optimality of parameter sharing. A diffusion policy then handles the more complex and varied action distributions associated with that division, within a maximum entropy framework.

The design combines role differentiation with a shared learning mechanism instead of requiring separate policies for every agent. Experiments on MaMuJoCo, SMAC, SMACv2, and LBF report superior sample efficiency while maintaining asymptotic optimality. The findings support using learned roles and expressive action modeling to address the tension between specialization and knowledge transfer in multi-agent learning.
summary.tldr: Dspic combines learned agent roles with a shared diffusion policy to improve efficient coordination across heterogeneous agents.

title: Towards Complete Multi-Agent Coordination Policy Learning via Denoising Maximum Entropy Optimization

abstract: A natural recipe for intelligent robotic decision-making is initializing from pretrained generative control policies, which have summarized offline experience, and adapting them to self-collected online experience. We present DF-ExpEnse, an exploration technique that improves the quality of online experience collection, thus increasing finetuning sample-efficiency. DF-ExpEnse leverages the multimodal modeling capabilities of the generative control policy to create an expressive and tractably evaluatable candidate set. It then utilizes an ensemble of critics to identify the action that best balances quality with high exploration interest. In fleet settings, DF-ExpEnse further enables cross-agent communication to facilitate collaborative exploration as a group. DF-ExpEnse can be seamlessly integrated with existing strategies that finetune pretrained generative control policies via reinforcement learning. We experimentally validate consistent sample-efficiency benefits through DF-ExpEnse across a variety of manipulation and locomotion tasks, compared to default finetuning and alternative action selection schemes. Project can be found at df-expense.github.io.

The method uses the pretrained policy’s ability to represent multiple possible behaviors to construct an expressive candidate set that remains practical to evaluate. This combines the policy’s existing behavioral knowledge with a separate assessment of which available action is useful for learning.

The technique can be integrated with existing reinforcement-learning strategies for fine-tuning generative control policies. Across manipulation and locomotion tasks, experiments show consistent sample-efficiency improvements over default fine-tuning and alternative action-selection schemes. The findings suggest that better collection decisions can make self-generated experience more valuable during adaptation.
summary.tldr: DF-ExpEnse selects exploratory actions from pretrained generative policies to make online robotic fine-tuning more sample-efficient.

title: DF-ExpEnse: Diffusion Filtered Exploration for Sample Efficient Finetuning

abstract: The low-rank adaptation (LoRA) algorithm for fine-tuning large models has grown popular in recent years due to its remarkable performance and low computational requirements. LoRA trains two "adapter" matrices that form a low-rank representation of the model parameters, thereby massively reducing the number of parameters that need to be updated at every step. Although LoRA is simple, its convergence is poorly understood due to the lack of Lipschitz smoothness, a key condition for classic convergence analyses. As a result, current theoretical results only consider asymptotic behavior or assume strong boundedness conditions which artificially enforce Lipschitz smoothness. In this work, we provide for the first time a non-asymptotic convergence analysis of the original LoRA gradient descent algorithm, which reflects widespread practice, without such assumptions. Our work relies on three key steps: i) reformulating the problem in terms of the outer product of the stacked adapter matrices, ii) a modified descent lemma for the "Lipschitz-like" reparametrized function, and iii) controlling the step size. With this approach, we prove that LoRA gradient descent converges to a stationary point at rate $O(\frac{1}{\log T})$, where $T$ is the number of iterations.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning costs by learning two adapter matrices whose product represents a low-rank parameter change. Its practical simplicity hides a theoretical difficulty: the resulting optimization problem lacks the Lipschitz smoothness used in standard convergence proofs. Earlier analyses therefore focused on limiting behavior or imposed strong boundedness assumptions to restore that condition.

This paper analyzes the original LoRA gradient-descent algorithm without those artificial boundedness assumptions. The proof reformulates the problem using the outer product of stacked adapter matrices. It then develops a modified descent lemma for the reparameterized objective's Lipschitz-like behavior and controls the step size to establish progress.

The result is a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(1/log T) toward a stationary point after T iterations. This ties the guarantee to a finite iteration count rather than only describing eventual behavior. The contribution is a convergence analysis of the algorithm used in practice; the stated endpoint is stationarity, so the guarantee concerns reaching a point with vanishing first-order improvement.
summary.tldr: The paper proves an O(1/log T) stationary-point convergence rate for original LoRA gradient descent without strong boundedness assumptions.

title: On the Convergence Rate of LoRA Gradient Descent

abstract: Foundation models for genomics have the potential to revolutionize therapeutic design, yet the optimal architectural choices for modeling the vast and diverse distribution of metagenomic data remain under-explored. In this work, we present the machine learning methodology behind EDEN, a family of metagenomic foundation models scaled up to 28 billion parameters and trained on 9.7 trillion nucleotide tokens. We provide a systematic empirical study of architectural trade-offs between autoregressive Transformers (Llama-style), State-Space Models (Mamba), and Long-convolutional architectures (Hyena) for nucleotide-level modeling. Contrary to recent trends favoring linear-time sequence models for long-range biological data, we demonstrate that the Llama architecture exhibits superior scaling efficiency and semantic retrieval capabilities as the model capacity grows. We derive a set of quality-aware scaling laws for metagenomics, showing how model performance follows predictable power-law behavior across three orders of magnitude in parameters and data. Through extensive benchmarking, spanning unsupervised zeroshot fitness prediction, semantic completion, and gene recovery, we establish a blueprint for scaling biological foundation models and provide empirical evidence demonstrating why Transformer-based architectures define the current frontier.

The goal is to identify effective ways to model the large and diverse sequence distribution found in metagenomic data.

The study compares autoregressive Llama-style Transformers, Mamba state-space models, and Hyena long-convolution models at nucleotide resolution. As capacity increases, the reported results favor the Llama architecture in scaling efficiency and semantic retrieval. summary.tldr: An empirical study of EDEN finds favorable Transformer scaling for metagenomic modeling and derives quality-aware power-law relationships.

title: Scaling Laws and Architectural Frontiers in Metagenomic Foundation Models

abstract: Reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) generate long chains of thought to solve harder problems, but they often loop, repeating the same text at low temperatures or with greedy decoding. We study why this happens and what role temperature plays. With open reasoning models, we find that looping is common at low temperature. Larger models tend to loop less, and distilled students loop significantly even when their teachers rarely do. This points to mismatches between the training distribution and the learned model, which we refer to as errors in learning, as a key cause. To understand how such errors cause loops, we introduce a synthetic graph reasoning task and demonstrate two mechanisms. First, risk aversion caused by hardness of learning: when the correct progress-making action is hard to learn but an easy cyclic action is available, the model puts relatively more probability on the cyclic action and gets stuck. Second, even when there is no hardness, Transformers show an inductive bias toward temporally correlated errors, so the same few actions keep being chosen and loops appear. Higher temperature reduces looping by promoting exploration, but it does not fix the errors in learning, so generations remain much longer than necessary at high temperature; in this sense, temperature is a stopgap rather than a holistic solution. We end with a discussion of training-time interventions aimed at directly reducing errors in learning.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can repeat text instead of progressing, especially with greedy decoding or low sampling temperatures. This study finds looping is common in open reasoning models under those conditions. Larger models tend to loop less, while distilled students can loop substantially even when their teachers rarely do, pointing toward errors in learning as a key cause.

A synthetic graph-reasoning task exposes two mechanisms. Sampling changes therefore alleviate the symptom without correcting the underlying learning errors. The paper closes by discussing training-time interventions aimed at those errors, framing looping as a learning problem as well as a decoding problem.
summary.tldr: Learning errors and temporally correlated mistakes help explain reasoning-model loops, while higher temperature provides only partial relief.

title: Wait, Wait, Wait... Why Do Reasoning Models Loop?

abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as a flexible alternative to autoregressive (AR) models. They can decode tokens in any order, but the generation quality critically depends on the decoding strategy. Existing approaches predominantly rely on local heuristics, such as confidence or entropy, which may fail to capture sequence-level dependencies and the semantics in the context. To solve this problem, we propose Latent-aware Unmasking Guidance Search (LUGS), a novel decoding framework that leverages the model’s internal hidden states to guide the unmasking process. By incorporating latent-aware scores to compensate for the limitations of local heuristics such as confidence or entropy, LUGS improves the model’s performance. Extensive experiments on various downstream tasks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines on LLaDA-8B-instruct and LLaDA-1.5 models. In Science and Reason tasks, LUGS improved performance by more than 1% on both base models. And LUGS obtains an average improvement of 3.5% in code generation. Remarkably, LUGS outperforms the beam search baseline by more than 5% on average using LLaDA-8B-Instruct on code tasks. These results highlight the potential of latent-aware guidance for advancing controllable and high-quality generation.

Existing decoding strategies often use local signals such as confidence or entropy. Those signals may overlook relationships across the sequence and meaning supplied by the broader context.

Latent-aware Unmasking Guidance Search, or LUGS, adds guidance derived from the model's internal hidden states. These latent-aware scores compensate for weaknesses in local heuristics when selecting the unmasking process. The approach therefore draws on information already represented inside the model to inform generation decisions beyond the immediate token-level signal.

summary.tldr: LUGS uses internal hidden states to guide token unmasking, improving diffusion language-model performance across the evaluated tasks.

title: LUGS: Latent-aware Guidance for Efficient Unmasking in Diffusion Large Language Models

abstract: How does the conversational past of large language models (LLMs) influence their future performance? Recent work suggests that LLMs are affected by their conversational history in unexpected ways. For instance, hallucinations in prior interactions may influence subsequent model responses. In this work, we introduce History Echoes, a framework that investigates how conversational history biases subsequent generations. The framework explores this bias from two perspectives: probabilistically, we model conversations as Markov chains to quantify state consistency; geometrically, we measure the consistency of consecutive hidden representations. Across three model families and six datasets spanning diverse phenomena, our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the two perspectives. By bridging these perspectives, we demonstrate that behavioral persistence manifests as a geometric trap, where gaps in the latent space confine the model’s trajectory.

paragraphs: A language model’s earlier conversation can shape its later behavior, including the persistence of tendencies associated with previous hallucinations. This paper introduces History Echoes to investigate how conversational history biases subsequent responses. Its focus is on connecting observable behavioral persistence with the evolution of the model’s internal representations during a conversation.

The framework approaches consistency in two ways. A probabilistic analysis models conversations as Markov chains to quantify whether conversational states persist. A geometric analysis measures consistency between consecutive hidden representations. These views examine the same phenomenon at different levels: patterns in generated behavior and patterns in the internal states that accompany generation.

Across three model families and six datasets covering diverse phenomena, the authors find a strong correlation between the two perspectives. They connect persistent behavior to a geometric trap in which gaps in latent space confine the model’s trajectory. The contribution is an account of how conversational habits appear in representation geometry, giving behavioral persistence a measurable internal counterpart within the studied models and datasets.
summary.tldr: History Echoes links persistent conversational behavior to geometric confinement in language models’ hidden representations.

title: Old Habits Die Hard: How Conversational History Geometrically Traps LLMs

abstract: Foundation models have sparked a revolution via a pretraining-adaptation paradigm, with recent efforts extending this success to graphs. Unlike other modalities, graphs contain rich structural patterns, yet their structural transferability remains poorly understood. Prior studies consider common substructures in the discrete realm, and we are motivated by a fundamental question: Are common substructures transferable? The underlying theory is largely underexplored. In this work, we shift toward learning transferable structures through the lens of functional behavior. Theoretically, we connect transferable substructures to intrinsic geometry of the representation space. However, characterizing such intrinsic geometry has rarely been touched. To bridge this gap, we develop a new deep learning framework—Geometric Morphology Learning, which parses the local coordinates in the proposed neural vector bundle, learning the intrinsic geometry. Building on this, we design Gauge, a pretrainable neural architecture that constructs the vector bundle, flattening geometrically compatible local coordinates, and a new Dirichlet loss, which also measures the transfer effort. We empirically validate its superior expressiveness in challenging tasks including zero-shot link prediction and graph isomorphism.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models seek to learn reusable knowledge during pretraining, but it remains unclear which graph structures transfer between tasks. This paper approaches that question through the functional behavior of substructures.
