These findings support the usefulness of the proposed geometric representations for the evaluated tasks, alongside the paper’s theoretical account of how substructures can transfer.
summary.tldr: Gauge connects graph-substructure transfer to representation geometry and learns that geometry through neural vector bundles.

title: Are Common Substructures Transferable? Riemannian Graph Foundation Model with Neural Vector Bundles

abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CEs) are essential for actionable recourse, yet their reliability is often compromised in low-density regions, where classifiers exhibit high variance. Unlike existing methods that rely on expensive ensemble intersections to define stability, we propose DensityFlow, a generative framework that constructs robust CEs by adhering to the high-confidence data manifold. Specifically, we model the counterfactual generation as continuous-time dynamics parameterized by Neural ODE, guided by a differentiable density score to actively avoid uncertain, low-density areas. This density score is learned via Noise Contrastive Estimation, effectively leveraging a $(K{+}1)$-way discriminator to estimate density ratios. For black-box settings, we introduce a local proxy distillation mechanism that aligns a lightweight surrogate with the target model strictly within the trajectory of CE generation, enabling efficient gradient-based optimization with minimal queries. Experiments demonstrate that DensityFlow achieves superior validity under model multiplicity while significantly reducing query costs compared to ensemble-based baselines. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/G-AILab/DensityFlow.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe changes that would lead a classifier to a different decision. Their usefulness can weaken in sparsely populated parts of the data, where classifiers vary more. DensityFlow addresses this reliability problem by guiding counterfactual generation through regions that the data support more strongly.

The method represents generation as a continuous trajectory governed by a neural ordinary differential equation. A differentiable density score steers that trajectory away from uncertain, low-density areas. The score is learned through noise contrastive estimation, using a discriminator to estimate density ratios. This provides a density-based alternative to defining stability through expensive intersections across ensembles.

When the target classifier is a black box, DensityFlow trains a lightweight local substitute along the counterfactual’s generation trajectory. That focused approximation supplies gradients while limiting queries to the target. Experiments report better counterfactual validity under model multiplicity and substantially lower query costs than ensemble-based baselines, supporting density guidance as an efficient route to more robust recourse.
summary.tldr: DensityFlow generates more robust counterfactual explanations by steering changes through well-supported data regions and using local surrogates to reduce black-box queries.

title: Density-Guided Robust Counterfactual Explanations on Tabular Data under Model Multiplicity

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have become a dominant architecture in computer vision, yet producing stable and high-resolution attribution maps remains challenging. Architectural components such as patch embeddings and attention routing often introduce structured artifacts in pixel-level explanations, leading many existing methods to rely on coarse patch-level attributions. We introduce DAVE (Distribution-Aware Attribution via ViT Gradient Decomposition), a mathematically grounded attribution method for ViTs based on a structured decomposition of the input gradient. By exploiting architectural properties of ViTs, DAVE isolates locally equivariant and stable components of the effective input-output mapping while suppressing architecture-induced artifacts and instability. Consequently, DAVE produces robust, precise, and class-consistent attribution maps that highlight model-relevant visual features. Experimental results show that across supervised, self-supervised, and inherently interpretable ViTs, DAVE outperforms prior methods on localization, faithfulness, and user studies.

paragraphs: An attribution map highlights image regions that matter to a model’s prediction. For Vision Transformers, producing detailed and stable maps is difficult because patch embeddings and attention routing can introduce structured artifacts. An explanation can therefore reflect aspects of the architecture alongside the visual features relevant to the decision, motivating the frequent use of coarser patch-level explanations.

DAVE addresses this problem by decomposing the input gradient, which describes how the output changes with changes to the image. Its decomposition uses properties of the Transformer architecture to isolate stable, locally equivariant components of the effective input-output mapping. It suppresses components associated with architectural artifacts and instability, aiming to preserve useful visual detail in the resulting attribution.

The authors report precise, robust maps that remain consistent with the explained class. Across supervised, self-supervised, and inherently interpretable Vision Transformers, DAVE outperforms earlier methods on localization, faithfulness, and user studies. These findings support using architectural structure to improve both the spatial detail of explanations and how closely they reflect model behavior.
summary.tldr: DAVE decomposes Vision Transformer gradients to produce more stable and detailed attribution maps with stronger reported explanation quality.

title: DAVE: Distribution-Aware Attribution via ViT Gradient Decomposition

abstract: Training agentic models for terminal-based tasks critically depends on high-quality terminal trajectories that capture realistic long-horizon interactions across diverse domains. However, constructing such data at scale remains challenging due to two key requirements: Executability, since each instance requires a suitable and often distinct Docker environment; and Verifiability, because heterogeneous task outputs preclude unified, standardized verification. To address these challenges, we propose TerminalTraj, a scalable pipeline that (i) filters high-quality repositories to construct Dockerized execution environments, (ii) generates Docker-aligned task instances, and (iii) synthesizes agent trajectories with executable validation code. Using TerminalTraj, we curate 32K Docker images and generate 50,733 verified terminal trajectories across eight domains. Models trained on this data with the Qwen2.5-Coder backbone achieve consistent performance improvements on TerminalBench (TB), with gains of up to 20% on TB 1.0 and 10% on TB 2.0 over their respective backbones. Notably, TerminalTraj-32B achieves strong performance among models with fewer than 100B parameters, reaching 35.30% on TB 1.0 and 22.00% on TB 2.0, and demonstrates improved test-time scaling behavior.

paragraphs: Training a terminal agent requires examples of extended interactions in working software environments. Producing these examples at scale is difficult because different tasks need different environments, and their outputs require different checks. TerminalTraj addresses both requirements by generating tasks together with executable settings and validation code.

The pipeline filters repositories to construct Docker environments, creates tasks suited to those environments, and synthesizes agent interaction trajectories with executable verification. Using this process, the authors curate 32,000 Docker images and produce 50,733 verified trajectories spanning eight domains. The data therefore captures task execution in environments prepared to support the corresponding work.

These results support environment construction and task-specific verification as useful foundations for generating terminal-agent training data.
summary.tldr: TerminalTraj generates verified terminal-agent trajectories in matching Docker environments, improving trained models on TerminalBench.

title: Large-Scale Terminal Agentic Trajectory Generation from Dockerized Environments

abstract: Existing machine unlearning methods primarily focus on removing data influence after training completes, which is effective for many scenarios, but a complementary capability is needed when removal requests arise during ongoing training. We propose LMCleaner, an efficient and certified online unlearning framework that can process unlearning requests at any training step without waiting for training completion. Our key insight is that influence propagation can be decomposed into a trust region where linear approximation is accurate, and a residual that concentrates in a low-dimensional subspace and can be efficiently masked by calibrated noise. Building on this insight, we design an influence propagation truncation mechanism that treats mini-batch influence as atomic units, computes influence within a truncation window for efficient removal, and injects subspace-aware noise for certified privacy. Our theoretical analysis proves that the truncation residual decays exponentially with window size and that the unlearned model is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-indistinguishable from retraining. Experiments demonstrate that LMCleaner achieves over $100\times$ computational savings compared to baselines while maintaining model utility and defending against membership inference attacks.

paragraphs: Requests to remove training data can arrive before model training finishes. LMCleaner addresses this online setting, allowing unlearning at any training step. Its goal is to remove the relevant influence efficiently while providing a formal relationship between the resulting model and a model obtained through retraining.

The method separates influence propagation into a region where a linear approximation is accurate and a remaining component concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. It treats mini-batch influence as the basic unit, calculates influence within a limited truncation window, and adds calibrated noise targeted to the residual subspace. This combines bounded influence tracking with a privacy mechanism for the part left outside the window.

The theoretical analysis establishes exponential decay of the residual as the window grows and an epsilon-delta indistinguishability guarantee relative to retraining. That is an approximate formal guarantee rather than a claim of identical model parameters. Experiments report more than 100-fold computational savings over baselines while preserving model utility and resisting membership inference attacks.
summary.tldr: LMCleaner removes data influence during training using truncated influence tracking and calibrated noise, with certified approximate indistinguishability from retraining.

title: LMCleaner: Efficient and Certified Online Unlearning via Influence Propagation Truncation

abstract: We introduce, to our knowledge, the first direct second-order method for computing Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games. To do so, we construct a Douglas-Rachford-style splitting formulation, which we then solve with a semi-smooth Newton (SSN) method. We show that our algorithm enjoys local superlinear convergence. To augment the fast local behavior of our SSN method with global efficiency guarantees, we develop a hybrid method that combines our SSN method with the state-of-the-art first-order method for game solving, Predictive Regret Matching (PRM$^+$). Our hybrid algorithm leverages the global progress provided by PRM$^+$ while achieving a local superlinear convergence rate once it switches to SSN near a Nash equilibrium. Numerical experiments on matrix games demonstrate order-of-magnitude speedups over PRM$^+$ for high-precision solutions.

To augment the fast local behavior of our SSN method with global efficiency guarantees, we develop a hybrid method that combines our SSN method with the state-of-the-art first-order method for game solving, Predictive Regret Matching (PRM$^+$). paragraphs: The paper studies how to compute Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games, where the players have opposing objectives. Its contribution is a direct second-order solver designed to reach highly accurate solutions efficiently. The authors describe it as the first method of this kind to their knowledge.

The approach first rewrites the equilibrium problem using a Douglas–Rachford-style splitting formulation, then applies a semi-smooth Newton method. The authors prove local superlinear convergence: sufficiently near an equilibrium, the method improves its approximation at an increasingly rapid rate. This is a local result, so it does not by itself establish efficient progress from arbitrary starting points.

To combine fast finishing behavior with global efficiency guarantees, the paper develops a hybrid with Predictive Regret Matching, or PRM+. That method supplies global progress before the solver switches to Newton steps near an equilibrium. Experiments on matrix games report order-of-magnitude speedups over PRM+ for high-precision solutions, supporting the hybrid approach when obtaining a particularly accurate equilibrium matters.
summary.tldr: A hybrid game solver combines global first-order progress with locally superlinear Newton steps, producing order-of-magnitude speedups for high-precision matrix-game solutions.

title: A Direct Second-Order Method for Solving Two-Player Zero-Sum Games

abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate remarkable syntactic fluency, yet the optimization dynamics governing their acquisition of deep semantic dependencies remain poorly understood. We propose a mechanistic framework that models this learning process as a competition between Surface Statistics and Deep Semantics. Our theoretical analysis identifies a "Gradient Starvation" phenomenon where the error signals for sparse semantic dependencies are actively suppressed during early optimization. This suppression impedes the learning of structural reasoning and causes its emergence to manifest as a sudden phase transition. Furthermore, this framework offers a mechanistic basis for the effectiveness of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategies. By externalizing intermediate reasoning steps into concrete tokens, CoT effectively bypasses the suppression regime inherent to implicit reasoning. We validate these findings across scales ranging from toy transformers to production models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B). Finally, guided by this theory, we propose a topology-aligned contrastive objective that explicitly rectifies the gradient geometry. Experiments on variable binding tasks demonstrate that our method achieves an improvement that is over 2$\times$ larger than that obtained via standard cross-entropy fine-tuning. Code will be publicly available at: https://github.com/jr-zhao/Deep-Dependencies/tree/main.

paragraphs: Fluent language generation does not explain how a transformer learns deeper structural dependencies. This paper models learning as competition between surface statistics and deep semantics. Its theoretical analysis identifies gradient starvation: early optimization suppresses error signals associated with sparse semantic dependencies, making those dependencies harder to learn and causing structural reasoning to emerge as a sudden transition.

The framework also offers an explanation for the effectiveness of chain-of-thought reasoning. Expressing intermediate steps as explicit tokens can bypass the suppression associated with implicit reasoning. The authors validate their findings across toy transformers and production models, including Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, connecting the proposed mechanism to behavior at different scales.

On variable-binding tasks, its improvement is more than twice the improvement achieved by standard cross-entropy fine-tuning. That comparison concerns the size of the gain, not a doubling of absolute performance. The work links a learning-dynamics explanation to a targeted training intervention.
summary.tldr: The paper links delayed structural reasoning to suppressed semantic gradients and uses that analysis to improve variable-binding training.

title: Syntax vs. Semantics: How Transformers Learn Deep Dependencies

abstract: The inherent sparsity, lack of structure, and rotation sensitivity of point clouds often lead to high computational and parameter cost in robust feature learning. To address these problems, we present QPoint, a lightweight framework that leverages robust quaternion feature learning. QPoint incorporates a Quaternion-Enhanced local perception module that uses learnable rotations to stabilize local features against geometric transformations, and a Quaternion global attention mechanism that employs quaternion similarity to capture global geometric context with inherent rotation invariance. Extensive experiments show that QPoint achieves top performance across multiple tasks. It achieves excellent 95.0%, 93.9%, and 92.1% on the challenging ScanObjectNN variants (OBJ_BG, OBJ_ONLY, PB_T50_RS), 94.7% overall accuracy on ModelNet40, and 87.0% instance mIoU on ShapeNetParts. Furthermore, QPoint exhibits superior generalization in few-shot learning scenarios. Crucially, it accomplishes this with extremely minimal parameter and computational requirements, establishing a strong and efficient baseline for point cloud processing. Our source code is in the supplementary material and will be released to the public.

paragraphs: Point clouds are sparse, lack a regular structure, and can change substantially in representation when rotated. Learning robust features from them can therefore require considerable computation and many parameters. QPoint uses quaternion-based feature learning to address these difficulties in a lightweight framework for point-cloud processing.

The framework combines local and global mechanisms. Its local perception module uses learnable rotations to stabilize features against geometric transformations. Its global attention mechanism uses quaternion similarity to capture broader geometric context with inherent rotation invariance. Together, these components address both the stability of nearby geometric features and the relationships needed to understand the overall shape.

Reported results include 95.0%, 93.9%, and 92.1% on three ScanObjectNN variants, 94.7% overall accuracy on ModelNet40, and 87.0% instance mIoU on ShapeNetParts. The paper also reports stronger generalization in few-shot learning settings. These results are achieved with very small parameter and computational requirements, supporting quaternion-based representations as an efficient foundation for the classification and segmentation evaluations described.
summary.tldr: QPoint combines quaternion-based local features and global attention for efficient, rotation-robust point-cloud processing.

title: QPoint: End-to-End Lightweight Point Cloud Processing via Robust Quaternion Feature Learning

abstract: Multi-step retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a widely adopted strategy for enhancing large language models (LLMs) on tasks that demand global comprehension and intensive reasoning. Although many RAG systems incorporate a working memory to consolidate information, existing designs primarily function as a passive storage for isolated facts. This static nature overlooks crucial high-order correlations among primitive facts, thereby limiting models’ capacity for multi-step reasoning and resulting in fragmented reasoning and weak global sense-making within extended contexts. We introduce HGMem, a hypergraph-based working memory system, extending the concept of memory beyond simple storage into a dynamic, expressive structure for complex reasoning and global understanding. In our approach, memory is represented as a hypergraph where hyperedges correspond to distinct memory units, enabling the progressive formation of high-order interactions within memory. This mechanism connects facts and thoughts around the focal problem, evolving the memory into an integrated and situated knowledge structure that provides strong propositions for deeper reasoning. We evaluate HGMem on several challenging global sense-making benchmarks. Extensive experiments and in-depth analyses demonstrate that our method consistently improves multi-step RAG and substantially outperforms strong baseline systems across diverse datasets.

paragraphs: Multi-step retrieval-augmented generation gathers information over several reasoning steps, often keeping a working memory of what it finds. The paper argues that memories organized as isolated facts miss relationships involving several pieces of information. This can leave reasoning fragmented when answering questions that require understanding an extended context as a whole.

HGMem represents working memory as a hypergraph, with each hyperedge corresponding to a memory unit. This structure supports higher-order relationships among facts and thoughts. As retrieval and reasoning proceed, those relationships can develop progressively around the current problem, turning the memory into a connected knowledge structure rather than a collection of separately stored observations.

The system is evaluated on challenging global sense-making benchmarks. Experiments and detailed analyses show consistent improvements to multi-step RAG and substantial gains over strong baselines across diverse datasets. The stated findings support the importance of how retrieved information is organized: a memory that develops relationships among facts can provide stronger propositions for subsequent reasoning and more coherent understanding across long contexts.
summary.tldr: HGMem uses evolving hypergraph memory to connect retrieved facts and improve multi-step reasoning over long contexts.

abstract: We present a new machine learning approach for 3D-QSAR, the task of predicting binding affinities of molecules to target proteins based on 3D structure. Our approach predicts binding affinity by using regression on substructures discovered by relational learning. We make two contributions to the state-of-the-art. First, we use multiple-instance (MI) regression, which represents a molecule as a set of 3D conformations, to model activity. Second, the relational learning component employs the “Score As You Use” (SAYU) method to select substructures for their ability to improve the regression model. This is the first application of SAYU to multipleinstance, real-valued prediction. We evaluate our approach on three tasks and demonstrate that (i) SAYU outperforms standard coverage measures when selecting features for regression, (ii) the MI representation improves accuracy over standard single feature-vector encodings and (iii) combining SAYU with MI regression is more accurate for 3D-QSAR than either approach by itself.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict a molecule’s binding affinity to a target protein from its three-dimensional structure. Its approach combines discovering useful molecular substructures with building the regression model that predicts affinity. This connects the choice of molecular features directly to the prediction task.

Two components drive the method. Multiple-instance regression represents each molecule through a set of three-dimensional conformations, allowing several possible configurations to enter the representation. Relational learning discovers substructures, and the Score As You Use method selects them according to whether they improve the regression model. The paper presents this as the first application of that selection method to multiple-instance prediction with real-valued outputs.

Evaluation on three tasks supports each component and their combination. Score As You Use selects regression features more effectively than standard coverage measures, while the multiple-instance representation improves accuracy over single-vector encodings. Combining the two is more accurate for the studied structure-based affinity prediction tasks than either alone. These findings support jointly considering molecular representation and predictive usefulness when constructing features.
summary.tldr: Combining multiple molecular conformations with prediction-guided substructure selection improves binding-affinity prediction across three evaluated tasks.

title: An integrated approach to feature invention and model construction for drug activity prediction

abstract: This paper proposes a new method for comparing clusterings both partitionally and geometrically. Our approach is motivated by the following observation: the vast majority of previous techniques for comparing clusterings are entirely partitional, i.e., they examine assignments of points in set theoretic terms after they have been partitioned. In doing so, these methods ignore the spatial layout of the data, disregarding the fact that this information is responsible for generating the clusterings to begin with. We demonstrate that this leads to a variety of failure modes. Previous comparison techniques often fail to differentiate between significant changes made in data being clustered. We formulate a new measure for comparing clusterings that combines spatial and partitional information into a single measure using optimization theory. Doing so eliminates pathological conditions in previous approaches. It also simultaneously removes common limitations, such as that each clustering must have the same number of clusters or the yare over identical datasets. This approach is stable, easily implemented, and has strong intuitive appeal.

paragraphs: A clustering comparison usually asks which points are grouped together in each result. This paper argues that looking only at those assignments can overlook meaningful differences because it ignores where the points lie in space. The geometry that helped generate the clusters can also matter when deciding how different two clusterings are.

The authors demonstrate failure cases in previous comparison techniques, including an inability to distinguish significant changes in the data being clustered. They then formulate an optimization-based measure that combines group membership information with spatial information. The resulting comparison evaluates both the partition of the data and its geometric organization within a single measure.

The proposed approach eliminates the pathological conditions discussed in the paper and allows comparisons without requiring equal numbers of clusters or identical underlying datasets. The authors also describe it as stable and straightforward to implement. Its broader contribution is to make clustering comparison reflect the data's layout, extending what can be learned from comparing assignments alone.
summary.tldr: An optimization-based measure compares clusterings using both group assignments and geometry, including across different datasets or cluster counts.

title: Comparing Clusterings in Space

abstract: The use of L_1 regularisation for sparse learning has generated immense research interest, with many successful applications in diverse areas such as signal acquisition, image coding, genomics and collaborative filtering. While existing work highlights the many advantages of L_1 methods, in this paper we find that L_1 regularisation often dramatically under-performs in terms of predictive performance when compared with other methods for inferring sparsity. We focus on unsupervised latent variable models, and develop L_1 minimising factor models, Bayesian variants of “ L_1 ”, and Bayesian models with a stronger L_0 -like sparsity induced through spike-and-slab distributions. These spike-and-slab Bayesian factor models encourage sparsity while accounting for uncertainty in a principled manner, and avoid unnecessary shrinkage of non-zero values. We demonstrate on a number of data sets that in practice spike-and-slab Bayesian methods outperform L_1 minimisation, even on a computational budget. We thus highlight the need to re-assess the wide use of L_1 methods in sparsity-reliant applications, particularly when we care about generalising to previously unseen data, and provide an alternative that, over many varying conditions, provides improved generalisation performance.

paragraphs: Sparse learning seeks explanations that use relatively few active quantities. L1 regularization is a popular way to encourage this, but the paper asks whether its popularity translates into strong prediction on unseen data. The investigation focuses on unsupervised latent-variable models, where hidden factors explain observed data.

The authors develop and compare factor models using L1 minimization, Bayesian versions of L1-style sparsity, and Bayesian spike-and-slab distributions. The last approach encourages a stronger, L0-like distinction between inactive and active values. It also represents uncertainty and avoids unnecessarily shrinking nonzero values, addressing two aspects of estimation alongside the desire for sparsity.

Across several datasets and varied conditions, the spike-and-slab methods outperform L1 minimization in predictive performance, including under a computational budget. The authors also find that L1 can underperform dramatically in these comparisons. The findings motivate reconsidering L1 as a default for sparsity-dependent applications, particularly when generalization matters; they establish an empirical advantage across the studied conditions rather than a universal ranking of sparse methods.
summary.tldr: Bayesian spike-and-slab factor models outperform L1 minimization across the studied datasets, including when computation is constrained.

title: Evaluating Bayesian and L1 Approaches for Sparse Unsupervised Learning

abstract: We study the problem of multiple kernel learning from noisy labels. This is in contrast to most of the previous studies on multiple kernel learning that mainly focus on developing efficient algorithms and assume perfectly labeled training examples. Directly applying the existing multiple kernel learning algorithms to noisily labeled examples often leads to suboptimal performance due to the incorrect class assignments. We address this challenge by casting multiple kernel learning from noisy labels into a stochastic programming problem, and presenting a minimax formulation. We develop an efficient algorithm for solving the related convex-concave optimization problem with a fast convergence rate of O(1/T) where T is the number of iterations. Empirical studies on UCI data sets verify both the effectiveness of the proposed framework and the efficiency of the proposed optimization algorithm.

We address this challenge by casting multiple kernel learning from noisy labels into a stochastic programming problem, and presenting a minimax formulation. paragraphs: This paper addresses multiple kernel learning when some training labels are incorrect. The motivation is that many earlier methods assume perfectly labeled examples while concentrating on computational efficiency. Applying those methods directly to noisy labels can produce suboptimal performance because the class assignments guiding learning are themselves unreliable.

The authors express the noisy-label learning problem through stochastic programming and derive a minimax formulation. They then develop an efficient algorithm for the resulting convex-concave optimization problem. This makes label noise part of the learning formulation rather than continuing to optimize under an assumption that every observed label is correct.

The optimization algorithm has a convergence rate of O(1/T), where T is the iteration count. This is a statement about optimization progress, not a matching rate for prediction accuracy or label correction. Experiments on UCI datasets support both the effectiveness of the learning framework and the efficiency of its solver. The paper thus connects a noise-aware modeling objective with a computational method backed by a convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: A stochastic minimax formulation makes multiple kernel learning noise-aware and admits an efficient solver with O(1/T) convergence.

title: Multiple Kernel Learning from Noisy Labels by Stochastic Programming
